WAY are good resolutions like fainting ladiesl Because they want carrying out. THE working horse takes his meals at table d'oafi and does his work a la cart. A YOUNG lady, speaking of one of her aversions, selid—" He's almost a perfect brute; he only lacks instinct." A STUDENT of human nature says anything can be sharpened. Fut a lead pencil in a woman's . hands and see. "Bless me I" be said, looking at the clock, "it's after eleven. How the time flies! I had no idea it was so late." "It's better late than never," she said, hiding a yawn. "In my opinion all men are liars," mid Mrs. Blister to her husband. "Permit me to remark, my dear, in that connection," he responded gal- lantly, "that you are an angel." BooKsELLEE—" What can I do for you, sir." Country Customer—" Have you a nice obituary of Bismarck? I think a good deal of him, and I would like to have his obituary." AGES will come and go; but woman will not be perfectly happy until she can have eyes attached to her shoulders, so that she may look up to and criti- cise her own back hair. "ARE you fond of looking at the stars ?" asked Bromley of De Guy. "Well, yes," answered that engaging young man, "some times; but as a rule the chorus is good enough for me." COUNTRY bride (looking over bill of fare)— "John, what's Patty de fee grass ?' " Groom— "'Sh Don't talk so loud, or people 'll think we're ignorant. It must be French for celery." -

"Is it dangerous to eat before going to sleep 2* We think not. We have heard frequently of persons doing so? But if you are afraid to risk it perhaps you had better eat after you go to sleep. THE most economical man in Maine has been found. He will buy a small load of wood and saw it six times to save fire, make soap with the ashes, wash, cloths with the soap, and grease his boots with the suds. Mn. The young lady (suddenly brightening up)—" Oh, I like French opera; it has such agoto it I like anything that has go 1" He goes. YOUNG WIFE—" Yes, father always gives ex- pensive things when he makes presents." Husband —" So I discovered when he gave you away." And then he went to his library to draw a cheque for the monthly millinery bill. Coirssuir.—" You speak of a bogus statement; are you going to make another in thewitness-box ?" Witness—" Certainly not. When lamon my oath, that is another thing. When I get in the witness- box, I am going to tell the truth." IF anybody wishes to see what utter and as- tounding ignorance prevails among some of our business men, just let him ask any railroad officer about the details of an accident. It would be as well to ask a two-days' babe to expound Herbert Spencer. WIFE, before a lion's cage, to husband—" What would you say if the bars were to suddenly break, and the lion to eat me up ? " Husband, drily—" I should say he had a good appetite." " I NEVER get angry with a fool," was the cutting remark of a man who wanted to crash a rival in argument. "Oh then, that accounts for your always being on such good terms with yourself, was the response. A NATURALIST says that when a lion becomes old and unable to injure a man his mane falls out. If you have a spite against a lion, don't tackle him until his mane falls out. P.s.—And don't tackle him then. Hire another man to do it for you. It woahl be safer. SYMPATHETIC old lady (to convict)—" Ah, my unfortunate friend, your fate is indeed a hard one, and as she thinks of you here in this dreadful Place how your poor wife must suffer." Convict (very much affected)—" Wh—which one, mum? I'm up for bigamy." "Sliz here, my friend," said a farmer to a tramp, " you've been lyin' in the shade of that fence for over thirteen hours. Ain't it 'bout time to move on ?" "If you say so," replied the tramp, struggling to his feet, "I s'pose it is. I'm only tryin' to make my shoes last as long as possible." Hes. BLOOD (to the colonel, who has returned from fighting a duel)—" Oh, colonel, you look dis- treeeed. Is it possible you have injured your antagonist ?" Colonel Blood—" A devilish sight worse, my dear. I killed a valuable mule in an adjoining lot, and I suppose I'll have to pay for him." MoTrutes—" Ella, go to bed. Say good night to the governess, and give her a kiss." Ella—" No, mamma, I don't want to give her a kiss." Mother— " And why not?" Ella—" Because when anyone gives her a kiss she boxes their ears. Ask papa if she doesn't." ":WONDER what is the matter with Mr. Brown," said the landlady ;" he seems to be very angry about something. Why, you should have seen him grind- ing his teeth just now in the hall." "Perhaps," suggested a boarder, "he is only getting them in order before tackling one of your beefsteaks." The landlady smiled, but there was murder in her heed. FLINTY-HEARTED EMPLOYER.—" Well, John, as I wish to deal fairly, any of the men who like to attend the arbitration meeting this afternoon will be paid as if at work." Ground-down Son of Toil. —" Sus' so, sir, we don't mind goin' ; and has som of hus wot don't 'old with harbutration be a-goin' to 'old a strike meetin' this evenin', o' course you'll do the night wot's right, and pay us overtime." "How stupid I am," said Maudie Sarsnet, execu- ting at the same time quite a respectable yawn. "That's true," said Milton Stubbs, rather impul- sively. "Sir I" exclaimed Maudie, "you are impertinent." "But you yourself just now asserted that you were stupid." "I enly said .so without thinking," said Maudie, petulantly. "Yes, and up to the time you spoke I had only thought so without saying it." Hang arape on the door of Miss Maudie. Another lover scratched off the list. _ _

A YOUNG man had himself measured for a new suit of clothes. When he got his clothes from the tailor he discovered that there was no watch-pocket in the vest. "What is the meaning of this I" asked the indignant customer. "Meaning of what 7" "Why, this vest has got no watch-pocket. Why didn't you make the new vest like the old one I sent you as a pattern It had a watch-pocket.' "I know the old vest had a watch-ponket, but as I found nothing but a pawn-ticket in it for your watch, I didn't see what use you were going to have for a watch-pocket in your vest." Sin DAVID WILKIE had a bad habit of answering people by "really," or, as he pronounced it, "raily.' Stewart Newton, R.A., and he were walking home after a dinner party,when the following dialogue -occurred : Newton— "Well, we had A pleasant evening, Wilkie." Wilkie—" Rally." Newton— " But you were very silent." Wilkie—" Rally?" Newton—" In fact, I heard you say only one word." Wilkie—" Newton—" There it goes again. Why, Dawvid, you never do say anything but 'raily" Wilkie—" Rally ?" Two sailors went into a church at Plymouth on a thanksgiving-day, both of whom belonged to the Temera ire, in the ever-memorable battle of Trafal- gar. The clergynan, in the course of his sermon, unentioned the wo.rd vict°l7':' - observed t he er, Hear, Jack, oue orS. L. pronounced h ctt e there's the ictory." The the word " victory " a second +he Victory tar observed, "Mind, Jack, there's again." The clergyman not long after raentiou, the word " victory " a third time, on which the irritated tar left the church, saying to his com- panion, "Catch me, Jack, staying here any longer; that fellow has mentioned the Vidory three times, and never mentioned the Temeraire once, that was in the hottest part of the engagement." "Now, my dear," said Mr. Younghusband to the paatner of his joys, who was about to start forth on Christmas shopping bent, "get presents for all the family-in-law, and bvy a nice lot of things for the boys; but don't spend more than 100 dollars. We must live within our incomn." "Why, George," eeplied the lady in an aggrieved tone, "you told me we had 200 dollars this month—you knoW you did." And Mr. Youghusband only sighed. Harper's Christmas Number. "Hevra you any reason to offer why sentence should not be passed upon you ? " asked the judge of the female pawnbroker, who had been arrested for extortion. "Please, your honour, I throw myself on the mercy of the court. lam a poor loan woman." "CAPITAL CHAT." t,eet
The Lord Mayor Elect is said to be a ,Jtotaler. How will this harmonise with loving cups and City banquets?
The Queen of Roumania has greatly benefited by her visit to England. Her nervousness has entirely disappeared.

The Duke of Clarence is looking much better, and is undoubtedly stronger than he was ; but he is obliged still to be very careful, and to adhere strictly to his doctor's orders in all matters of diet.

Here is an interesting story showing how our gunboats are built. The Sandfly, intended for the Mediterranean station, is unable to leave owing to the fact that whilst coaling last week some bags of coal were dropped on her deck and they went right through it !

Signor Agostino Gatti, of Gatti Brothers the Adelphi Theatre, restaurant, music-hall &c., has lived long enough in London and got enough out of it to take an interest in English affairs, but is still an Italian Swiss, and has just been re-elected to the Swiss House of Commons. He represents the can- ton of Ticino.

Field Marshal von Moltke has suffered more severely than is generally admitted from his recent excitement. Ms attacks of cramp are not cif a very serious kind, but his eyes have suddenly become so inflamed as to cause much anxiety to his friends. lie will leave Berlin for his beloved Creisau, on the Bohemian frontier, AZ soon as the doctors pronounce him fit to trayeL

" General " Booth wrote that he is so well pleased with the reception of his book that he is encouraged to go on with the work suggested in it. To know exactly how he stands, he proposes to hold a meet- ing in Exeter Hall on Monday evening, the 17th inst. He will then be able to tell what he has received, and to ascertain what his prospects are of putting his proposals into practical execution.

The memorial to Father Perry, whose zeal for astronomical study really caused him to sacrifice his life at the observation of an eclipse last December, is to take the form of a new telescope to be erected at his observatory. Stoneyhurst is to be equipped with a telescope of almost double the power of any which the observatory there now possesses. All the leading British astronomers are to be found in the list of the committee of the fund.

Lady students of science in England as well as in Scotland will learn with grateful interest that a West of Scotland gentleman, the late Dr. Muirhead, of Cambuslang, has left the bulk of his fortune to found a science college for women, to be called the Muirhead College. Ladies will be able to obtain there the scientific and medical training which they frequently have to seek south of the Tweed. The idea is to train women not only as medical practitioners, but also as chemists, and dentists, and dispensers.

The British flag has been hoisted at Mount Hamp- den, the destination of the Mashonaland expedition, amid the firing of twenty-one guns and the offering up of prayer by Canon Balfour. This is a neat way of symbolising the inauguration of the new era of Bible and gunpowder for this part of the world. "The salute of twenty-one guns," says the reporter, "echoed the Amen." If the object had been to make ourselves and our religion ridiculous in the eyes of the world, the thing could hardly have been done better.

A queer sto about another of her Majesty's ships is sent to me from the far East. The vessel in which the writer was passing up Carimatta Straits was chased by a British gunboat, whose commander wanted to know "where he was," and" the name of the islands then in sight." This Shows the Royal Navy in an agreeable light. For the sake of anxious relatives in this country, I withhold the name of ship in question, but I shall ex,pect to hear next that she has been lost on some reef" not marked in the Admiralty chart."

Mrs. Alice Shaw, the whistler, starts for Russia next Monday, where she is to appear before the Im- perial Court. She whistled for the last time before her journey on Tuesday afternoon, at Mrs. "Charley" Matthews's pretty flat in Queen Anne's-mansions, where a select gathering of friends assembled to listen to her. Mrs. Shaw whistled a valse by Chopin, and a cradle song by Mr. Theo Warde in a way which made one of the company remark that birds were not in it, but that for the future when people wanted to write sonnets to the nightingale, they would address them to Mrs. Shaw.

People in Ireland are beginning to wonder if the Viceroyalty has been abolished. Dublin Castle, as a rule, is not given to departure from tradition. For the last quarter of a century the Viceroys have ac- cepted residence in Ireland during most of the year, as a duty of their office. From this tradition Lord Zetland has completely departed. The reflection naturally suggests itself, that if Ireland can do with- out a Viceroy during six months, he must be some- what of a superfluity during the other half of the year. In any case, if the incumbent of this office is on duty half the year, his salary should be reduced by one half.

Princess Beatrice has been occupied for some time in translating from the German of Dr. Emil Kraus, the " Adventures of the Life of Count Albrecht of Erbach," which, indeed, are quite as marvellous as those of Mr. Sala's Captain Dangerous. Count Al- brecht, who lived in the seventeenth century, not only travelled all over Europe, but lived for some time with the Knights of Malta, and was captured by Barbary corsairs, and afterwards was imprisoned at Algiers. The book, which will be copiously illus- trated, is to be published by Mr. Murray. The trans- lation is announced to be the work of "Beatrice, Princess Henry of Battenberg."

The complete returns of the municipal elections confirm our conclusions about the decisiveness of the Liberal victory. In thirty-two Boroughs, which are Parliamentary as well as municipal, there are Liberal gains, and the Parliamentary representation in eighteen of these boroughs is at present wholly in the hands of the Tories. These Tories may consider that they have received notice. In the smaller boroughs, which are incorporated in county constituencies, we have gained twenty-three seats. Irrespective of Independents, who are more likely to be Liberal than Tory, the Liberals report a I net gain of forty-two.

A party ot enterprising adventurers are on the warpath with fancy documents. If they are not forged they are of an extremely fishy character. Their first attempt was to make overtures to persons supposed to be unfriendly to Mr. Parnell. They had a very large and fine cock-and-bull story. It west° the effect that they had obtained access to Mr. Parnell's room while he was staying at Brighton, and had surreptitiously rummaged his desk and secured letters of a highly compromising character in connection with the O'Shea case. Persons ac- quainted with the manners and _customs of Mr. Parnell of course shrugged tbOr shoulders at au; fAQTy,

Mr. Parnell said in the House of Commons on 7 June, 1886, speaking on the second reading debate of the Home Rule Bill I say that as far as it is possible for a nation to accept a measure cheerfully, freely, gladly, and without reservation as a final ; settlement, I say that the Irish people have shown that they hare accepted this measure in that sense." How's that, umpire?

It appears that the Prince of Wales is about to receive a singular memorial from the Baptist Welsh Association for Montgomeryshire and Radnorshire, which, at its yearly meeting held at Llanidloes. agreed to address him as follows: "To his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales—We beg to request your Royal Highness to use your great influence against the evil practices of gambling and betting, whether connected with racecourses or the boxing ring, or, indeed, in any way. We feel strongly that these evils are not only ruinous to the worldly interests of many of our fellow creatures, but also exceptionally dangerous in view of their future interests, and as such we beg of you to give no coun- tenance to these practices in any way whatever."

Lord Hartington's visit to Scotland, writes a cor- respondent, has been a disappointing enterprise. His meetings have been in the main Tory meetings, and he has discovered in his travels that his party has nothing to hope for from Scotland. His host, the Earl of Stair, has had bitter experience of the difficulty of getting his sons accommodated with seats for constituencies in Scotland. On Saturday Lord Hartington visited the Earl of Wemyss. For many years, as Lord Elcho, be represented Hadding- tonshire in Parliament, but it is no longer possible ; for a member of the Wemyss family to hold the , representation, and the present Lord Elcho has had to find refuge in an English constituency with an- other Scotchman and near neighbour—Sir Charles Dalrymple. Mr. Balfour, the Irish Secretary, who is ' a landlord in Haddingtonshire, has also to go to , England to get a seat. Year by year the influence of the Tory and Whig political families in Scotland is diminishing. Even the Marquis of Lorne knows that his native county is closed against him; and Sir Jame. Fergusson, who was once a power in Ayrshire, has to go to Manchester for a seat.

What is the mysterious charm bf steam round- abouts? At country fairs nothing, it appears, does so brisk a business as the wooden horses which carry lads and lasses round and round in a fridtly whirl to the grinding of a barrel organ. In the collrOe of proceedings at the Cheltenham Police Court, it was stat.ed by an itinerant showman that in one day at Farruhill, Stroud, the takings ot his roundabout were no less than sixty-six pounds. Shooting at the mark is also much in favour, but it was stated that the takings from this source on the same occasion were not more than a third of the orofits of the inexhaustibly popular revolving hobby horses.

The Bishop of Chichester was eighty-eight on Monday—truly a grand old man. In personal appearance he gnot unlike the great Duke of Wel- lington, with an aquiline nose, white hair, and a ruddy face. It is no exaggeration to say that he is entirely free from the infirmities of age, and can hold his own in a theological argument or a brisk walk across a Sussex down with the most active of his clergy. Bishop Durnford was educated at Eton, became Fellow of the Magdalen College, Oxford, married a daughter of the terrific Dr. Keate, was rector of Middleton, Lancashire, for thirty-five years, was Archdeacon of Manchester till 1870, and was then made Bishop of Chichester by Mr. Glad- stone.

LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS. By L. GORDON RYLANDS, B.A. As intimated in our last issue, we commence this week the biographical sketch of the career of the late Mr. Peter Rylands, as written and recently published by his son, and we propose to continue it until concluded. We are deeply indebted to Mr. Gordon Rylands for his permission to place before our readers the interesting life of his father which he has written. Mr. Peter Rylands was born on the 18th of Janu- ary, 1820. His father, Mr. John Rylands, of Bewse) House, Warrington, was the descendant of a long line of yeomen and manufacturers, who had been settled in South-West Lancashire for several gene- rations. His mother was the daughter of the Rev. James Glazebrook, vicar of Belton, Leicestershire. He was educated at the Boteler Grammar School. at Warrington, at the time when the Rev. Thomas Fere Bayne, 8.C.L., was Head Master; and while there he gave promise, by his industry and ability, of the distinction which he was in after life destined to attain. Mr. Rylands began to take a keen interest in poli- tical matters at a very early age. In the year 1835, when he was 15 years old, a mock election was car- ried out by a number of the sons of electors of War- rington, the Tory candidate being a young gentle- man of the name! of Oliver, and the Whig candidate Master William Marson. Both sides apparently claimed the victory, which each celebrated by a dinner to their member. The dinner of the youth- ful reformers was held in a large room in Bridge-st., I Warrington, on the sth of February, 1835, Peter Rylands was chosen to preside, and his brother, Thomas Glazebrook, was elected one of the vice- presidents. All the proceedings were dignified and orderly, although more than two hundred young men were present. Speeches were made and toasts drunk, and Peter Rylands, in reply to the toast of his health as president, delivered a speech which would do credit to many a public speaker of mature age. But the pursuit in which Peter Rylands was chiefly absorbed at this time and for cocoa years after was the study of Natural History', and in com- piny with his brother, Thomas Glazebrook, he used to make long excursions in search of specimens. The collection of insects which he then made is still in existence, and is of considerable value. But he was not content with the mere pleasure of collec- tion ; he commenced to carry on a correspondence with other naturalists, and contributed to several magazines, among which the chief were "The Eclec- tic Review," " Loudoun's Magazine of Natural His- tory," and "The Naturalist." He also became a member of the Warrington Natural History Society, for which he wrote a series of papers on " The Structure of Birds considered in relation to their Habits," and another paper on the "Mimicries of Birds.' Another subject in which Mr. Peter Rylands took great interest in his younger days was that of Phrenology, in which he was a firm believer. He became a member of the Warrington Phienological Society, and at some of the meetings of this society, in the year 1838, he read a series of papers on the subject, entitled respectively, " On the Primitive Feeling of the Organ denominated by Phrenologists Cautiousness,' " "A few General Observations on Comparative Phreno- logy," " Considerationsrespecting the Organs which do not appear to be possessed by animals." Yet Mr. Rylands was not really of a scientific or philosophical nature, so that when the claims of public life began to clash with those of natural science, the latter Dad to give way, and although a love of birsisand of nature always remained, the turmoil of Municipal and Parliamentary life soon became all-absorbing. But between the period of devotion to seientific pua- suits and the period of devotion to public matters, there was to some extent a break. Up to the age of 21 Mr. Rylands had given no thought to business. He was, indeed, nominally engaged in the office of his father, who carried on business as a sail-cloth manufacturer, and had also a mill, in partnership with Mr. Greening, of Warrington, for the manufacture of iron wire; but the time he spent in the office was almost entirely occpied in reading works upon Natural History, and writing letters and articles upon the same subject. He imagined that his father was a wealthy man, that the iron-wire busi- ness was apaying concern, and that his father was in a position to leave him and his brothers comfortably off ; but he was awakened to the stern realities of life by an unpleasant shock. The sail cloth business had entirely deserted Warrington, and the wire manufactory, which had been left for some time by the elder Mr. Rylands en- tirely in the hands of his partner Greening, was not in reality paying its way. Nevertheless, Mr. John Rylands had regularly drawn an income from the concern, quite in ignorance that no profits were being made. Mr. Peter Rylands and his brothers, having investigated matters, had their eyes opened to the fact that their father's affairs were in anything but a satisfactory condition, and they saw that, to make the wire manufacture pay, the business must be entirely re-organized and carefully developed. In the year 1843, therefore, Mr. John Ry- lands and Mr. Greening were bought out,and a new firm, under the style of Rylands Bros., wast established. The development of this business required all the energies of the three brothers for softie years, but, after a period of "anxiety and slow progress their efforts were crowned with complete success. Their enterprise, their upright dealing, and their determination that they would turn out nothing that was not of excellent quality, eventually brought Rylands Bros., wire into repute, and their firm becartie one of the largest of the kind in England. For acme years past the firm had exported large quantities of iron: and steel wire to all parts of the world. At one time the production rose to nearly 400 tons per week, but of late years the competition of German manu- facturers has made itself very severely felt, and has re- duced not only the price of wire, but also the amount of orders placed in this country. Up to 1864 the iron used by the firm was purchased from Staffordshire and Shrop- shire, but in that year Messrs. Rylands established works at Warrington itself for the production of puddled iron suitable for wire mills. To the production of puddled iron was soon added the manufacture of sheets and hoops, and, in 1874, these works were amalgamated with those of the Dallam Forge Company, at Warrington, and with Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' colleries at Wigan. The capital of the new (company, called "The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited," amounts to nearly a million, the principal shareholders and direc- tors being the former partners. The Pearson and Knowles Company turn out upwards of 2,000 tons of bars, plates, sheets, hoops, and wire iron weekly, while the collieries at Wigan produce about 700.000 tons of coal and cannel yearly. Mr. John Rylands, Mr. Peter Rylands' eldest brother, is now chairman of this company. The success of Mr. reter Rylands and his coadjutors has given a great impulse to the trade in Warrington, which had for some time languished. Many other !similar manu- factories have been established, the town has grown greatly in size, and the value of property has largely in- ' creased. In fact, the piesent prosperity of Warrington is mainly due to Mr. Rylands and his brothers. It will not be necessary for me to say that Mr. Peter Rylands was not a man whose mind could ever be entirely absorbed in money-making. So soon, therefore, as the anxiety and care required by the re-organization of the wire business were somewhat relieved, he began once more to occupy himself in literary pursuits, devoting himself especially to the consideration of religious ques-

div.head: k.47N EXAMINER,
div.p: k.47N EXAMINER,

bions. Mr. Rylands was at this time an earnest Christian, firmly believing that Christianity is the only religion it to be held by civilized men, and that the highest obliga- tion imposed upon the Church is that of Christianizing , the whole world. This conviction naturallyled te a con- sideration of the means by which the Church would beat ' accomplish this great work, and ia the year 1845 Mr. Rylands published a little pamphlet, setting forth the opinions at which he had arrived. This pamphlet was entitled" The Mission of the Church; or the Remarks of the relative importance of Home and Foreign Missionary Effort in the present state of the World," and was in- tended to prove that Home are more important than Foreign Missions. In this little pamphlet it -is pointed out, in the first place, that the more highly civilized a nation is, the greater is its influence upon the world, and that it is consequently important for the Church to thoroughly Christianize England. Again, it is shown that, with the entrance of missionaries into savage lands, also come traders and adventurers, who offer the natives drink, accustom them to the evils of civilization, and do more harm than the missionaries do good; and, that, there- fore, until the English people are themselves truly Chris- ' tian,the English Church can never do much good among the heathen. Then the total number of persons existing on groups of savage islands is compared with the number living in vice and ignorance in one of our large towns; and it is argued that the money, toil, and lives spent upon the conversation of the former few would have worked a wondrous change for the better among the multitudes of the latter. Further, the paucity of ideas in the mind of the savage is shown to put difficulties in the way of his conception of a Diety and of the Christian dogmas, whereas the intellectual activity of the civilized man will lead him to embrace erroneous doctrines, should the truth not be placed clearly before his mind. Most of , the arguments inthe pamphlet are sound, and it must be I a matter of regret to every man who has at heart the welfare of his race, whether he be a Christian or not, , that so much energy and money is wasted by the Church in comparatively futile endeavours in remote lands, while vice, crime, and ignorance floutish in our midst. All these things are bringing the Church into greater and greater discredit. It cannot fail to be observed that, while its revenues are enormous and its dignitaries wealthy, its effects practically nothing in the way of raising the moral and intellectual status of the people. As to their intellectual status, seeing that the Church has for so many centuries striven to keep the people in ignorance, it is, perhaps, too much to expect it to change its habits now ; and, as to their moral statuts, it has always been inclined to wink at breaches of the com- mandments if a man will but worship regularly and repeat his Creed. The only Christian body which really gets at the people is the Salvation Army, and this the Church persecutes and hates. Therefore, although Mr. Rylands' pamphlet was written more than 50 years ago, it is as applicable to-day as it was then, and lean con- fidently recommend it to the careful consideration of all I Churchmen.
(To be contiimed.)

div.head: LARGE ST. HELENS FORTUNE AT STAKE. IN RE TIPPING.-ROBERTS v. WYATT.
div.p: A LARGE ST. HELENS FORTUNE AT STAKE. IN RE TIPPING.-ROBERTS v. WYATT.

In the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on Saturday, Mr. Renshaw, Q.C, with whom was Mr. Farwell, moved on behalf of the de- fendant in the action for change of venue of trial from the West Derby Division of Lancashire to the county of Middlesex. The action was purely a Chancery action,. lasing a next-of-kin action relating to a very large estate worth something like £230,000. The defendant was a barrister, and the administra- tor of the estate, and the plaintiff was Jane Roberts, who was now residing at Chorley, in Lancashire,havinvome overfrom America for the purpose of bringing this action. The defendant and his witnesses resided in the South of England, Sussex and Hampshire, and some of them, who were material, were very old, and would be unable to travel to Liverpool. The real question he (Mr.Renshaw) understood, would be whether the grandmother of the plaintiff was legitimate or not, and that would turn boa , great extent upon documents. The action was a purely • Chancery action, and the only reason why it was sug- gested that it should be heard in Lancashire, was the facl that the testator was a Lancashire man, residing prior to to his death at Bold Hall, near St. Helens, and ' that the plaintiff resided in the county of Lancashire,and was a poor woman. As, however, it was a Chancery suit, he asked that it should be treated in the ordinary way Chancery suits were dealt with, and tried in Lon- don, before a judge in Chancery.—Mr. Justice Kar,with- I out calling upon Mr. Swinfen Eady, who appeared to op- pose the motion, said he thought in this case he ought ; not to alter the venue. The question was a nisi prius issue, and if the plaintiff obtained her decrese,:it would be worked out in the Chancery Court and therefore he saw 110 reason for taking the trial of the issue from the Assize Court. There were several reasons why it should be tried at the Assizes, one being that it would be tried ' much sooner than if left in this branch of the court,, ' therefore he should refuse the motion.—On the applica- tion of Mr. Eady, his lordship gave the respondent the- costs incurred by him.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. The Rev. G. P. Roberts presided; and there were also present Messrs. Long. Heaton, Smith, and Kilshaw, S. Sut- ton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen. (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector). THE ALLOTMENTS Am—The CLERK said he had had a. communication from the County Council in which an inquiry was made as to hoW many applications there had been to put the Allotments Act, 1887, into operation in the Authority's district. The answer he had made to that was that no application had been made and as well as could be judged there was no disposition to apply- Another question was as. to in how many cases the appli cation had been refused. In reply to this he had said that he thought the Authority would be quite willing to deal with applications if the- circumstances made it advisable, but at present they were in ignorance of such circum- stances—Mr. Long asked if the Rural Sanitary Author- ' ty was the medium through which the allotments were got.—The CLERK said it was but they had never had any application and nobody seemed anxious ' about it. He did not think they needed to move ' until a reason was shown for it.—Mr. Einztrox said they could not force people to have allotments.— Mr. LONG questioned whether many people knew about the allotments.—Mr. SMITH thought that people could buy what they wanted cheaper than they could grow it.—Mr. LONG suggested that steps should be taken to make the provisions for the Allotments Act more public, and he approved of a suggestion to post notices on the doors of churches and chapels.—The CLERK thought that was more for the overseers to do, and the Chair- man thought it would be bestito communicate with the overseers.—ln answer to a question, the INSPECTOR said he never heard anything about allotments in any part of the district.—Mr. LONG: Do you imagine they know anything about it P—The INSPECTOR I don't suppose they do.—Mr. HEATON : Is there any district in the out- skirts that would be likely to require it ?----The INSPEC- TOR : I don't think so.—Dr. SEPIiToN thought it would be a very good thing if the Allotments Act was carried out.—lt was then decided that the Clerk should write to the overseers of the different parishes with regard to the Allotments Act.
MORT Sou. Rimovet.—lt was decided to accept the tender of Mr. James Newton, for the removal of night soil in the extra-municipal part of Warrington.

TEE RIETON BURIAiI GROUND.—The Clerk read the minutes of a meeting of the parishioners of Rixton-with- Glazebrook, held on the 16th October, for the purpose of giving the ratepayers an opportunity of expressing their opinion on the question of burial accommodation. It was unanimously decided not to comply with Mr. Shaw's claim of £5O for compensation, and Mr. Davies offered a fresh site for the Cemetry. It was decided to recommend the Rural Sanitary Authority to purchase for £5OO the new piece of land offered by Mr. Davies.—The Chairman said the new site was better than the old one, and the recommendation was adopted. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The Medical Officer re- ported that the district continued very healthy, and al- most free from zymotic disease. NEW HOUSES.—The Surveyor recommended the follow- ing plans for approval :—Addition to works of the War- rington Chemical Company, Sankey Bridges • two houses for Mr. P. Eden, at Penketh ; two houses at Collins Green

for Mr. P. Sutton. LAMPS AND STREET MAEING.-It was decided to erect eight lamps on the Liverpool-road, and to leave over consideration of the question as to whether the cost should be charged, on the general rate or against th& particular locality in which the lamps are placed. 10 was also decided to give the necessary notices for the making of streets off Liverpool-road.

div.p: - T I T-BI TS. TRADITION OF THD 1645 PLATO&

In a wild and secluded spot in Teviotdale, a con- siderable mound of earth is shown, under which it is said the plague was buried. There is a singular and awful distinctness in the tradition connected with the spot. It was originally, say the people, a oottage which contained the large family of a poor shepherd. At the present time, no trace of a place of habitation is discernable; it is a plain ordinary- looking hillock, upon the surface of which the sward grows as green, and the field-daisy grows as sweetly, as if it were not, what it is, the tomb of human misery and mortal disease. The plague was introduced into this house by a piece of finery which the shepherd's wife purchased brain a wan- dering pedlar, and wore for some time upon her head. She was speedily seized with the dreadful distemper, and took to her bed. Some of the children also beginning to feel affected, the shep- herd himself went to the nearest farm-house to seek assistance. The inhabitants of the place, alarmed in the highest degree for their own safety, rose in a body, and, instead of attempting to relieve the infected family, spread the intelligence to the neighbours, who, being equally apprehen- sive with themselves, readily joined them in the dreadful decision, that mercy to individuals should be postponed to a regard for the general health. With this resolution, and disregarding the entieaties of the poor shepherd, they went en maAse, and, closing the door upon the unfortunate family, proceeded to throw up earth round and over the cottage, till it was buried at least five feet beneath the surface. All the time of this operation, about half a day, the inmates, aware of their fate, cried dreadfully; and k was not till a large turf had been laid upon the top of the chimney, and a deep stratum of earth deposited over all, that their wailings were heard finally to subside. The shepherd is described as having for some time gone round and round the place like one demented, uttering fearful cries, and invoking heaven to save his family, till at last, being driven away bfr the people, he de.parted from the awful scene in a state of dis- traction, and was never more heard of or seenin the district.

Long and deeply did he ponder upon the strange business which had called Count Conrad to his shop, and in no way, under no light, could he get any reason from it. Why he, a youth who had never spoken with the proud Duke, save once on common busi- ness, and who was so far down in the social scale, should have been thus called upon to give a virtual consent to the bestowal of Rosalind Valdai'a hand, was beyond his ken. He was but a poor artisan— she, a wealthy heiress and a scion of nobility—and she was under the legal guardianship of the Duke, whose word, 80 far as she was concerned, was law. And again—Conrad Damonoff was a Count, and reputed to be wealthy. To be sure, he was some- what dissolute, but then a majority of his compeers were the same. Now, if this Count loved the lady Rosalind, and had asked for her hand, and the Duke was willing he, should have it, why had this extraordinary proposal been sent to the poor gun-- maker ? Ruric asked this question of himself a hundred times. He would begin and lay down all the premises in his mind, and then he would try to make the deduction; but no reasonable one could, 'he arrive at. One thought clung about him like rx, dim specter at night, which, hope would make an angel, and which fear would paint a demon.. Could it be possible that Rosalind had told her love for k him, and that the Duke would pay some deference to it? He tried to think so. Hope whispered that it might be so. But fear would force itself in, and speak in tones so loud that they could not be mis- understood. Finally the youth resolved upon the only reasonable course.. He concluded to let the , matter rest, so far as his own surmises were con- oerned, until he could see Rbsalind--and that he was determined to do as soon as possible. What more could. he ask for. love ? He had not aimed at this confession so soon. But he put it not from him now.. He gazed a moment into ths.fair maiden's kindling eye, and as. he saw the love-lit tear gatherinehere and the happy smile working its way about the rosy lips, and away in the joyous dimples, he opened his arms and clasped the. fondly loved one to his. bosom. "Oh, I all not deceived in this," he murmured. "Speak, dearest one." "I can not forget the love of the happy times agone," the noble girl replied, gazing up through her happy tears. "Oh, how many and many an hour have I prayed to God that those days might return, and that the one true heart of earth I loved might be mine once more. Rorie, why should I hide the truth tor why set it aside? To me thou art all in all. I have no one else to love, and none to love me else save the noble girl who brought you hither. I can tell you no more." Happy Rune! Happy at that moment—forget- ting all else but the love that gleamed out upon him then, he clasped the cherished object ardently to his bosom. But the moments flew on, and at length his mind came to the subject of his visit. "Rosalind," he said, holding one of her fair hands s

div.head: ANECDOTE OF LORD ADVOCATE JEFFREY.
div.p: ANECDOTE OF LORD ADVOCATE JEFFREY.

This Advocate for Scotland was the son of =under- clerk of Session, and was born in the upper part of a house in the Lawnmarket, Edinburgh, very near the spot where the celebrated David Hume is said also to have irst,tieen the light. The house happened to take fire at the time when the future Lord Advocate was only about a year old, and in the hurry of saving other things, the child in the garret was for a long , time forgotten. Inez it was almost too late, he was ' remembered, and an honest man, by trade a slater, volunteered his services in rescuing the infant, from his perilous situation. With much difikulty, and no little danger, he was brought forth from the burning house, and delivered into the arms of his anxious friends. Thus was a life, which assuredly has been of some importance in Scottish literary and political history, preserved by the courage of a poor tradesman. It is pleasant to have it to record, that many years after this event, when Mr. Jeffrey had commenced his oareer at the bar, the poor slater, happening to get involved, by no misconduct of hix own, in a ruinous series of legal troubles, applied fox advice to Mr. J., who, in gratitude to his disim terested preserver, exerted himself in such a way as completely to extricate him in a very short time We believe we may safely add, that this conduct or , the part of the Lord Advocate is no more than what all who knew him would expect from him unxier suck circumstances.

div.head: OLD SCOTTISH MODE OF DISCOVERING MURDER.
div.p: OLD SCOTTISH MODE OF DISCOVERING MURDER.

In tracing the customs of our ancestors, we alter. siately pity their superstitious usages, and are amused at the credulity of the legislature, in continuing absurdities which would now be scoffed at even by children. There was a superstitious notion, once ex. ceedingly prevalent, regarding the discovery of thc murderer by the touch of the dead body. In Ger. many, this experiment was called bah rechi, or the law of the bier, because, the murdered body being stretched upon a bier, the suspected person wai obliged to put one hand upon the wound, and the other upon the month of the deceased, and in that posture call upon heaven to attest his innocence. If during this ceremony the blood, gushed from the month, nose, or wound, a circumstance not unlikely to happen in the course of shifting or stirring the body, it was held sufficient evidence of the guilt ol the party. The same singular kind of evidence was ' admitted in the Scottish oriminal courts, at the short distance of a little more than a century and a. half. Youstainhall relates a most dreadful instance of this perversion of jurisprudence. The case was that of Phillip Stanfield, tried upon the 30th November, 1687, for cursing his father (which by the Scottish law is a capital crime, Act 1661, chap. 20), and for being accessory to the murder. Sir Jame! Stanfield, the deceased, was a person of melancholy temperament; so that when his body was found in a pond near his own house of Newmiles, be was at first generally supposed to have drowned himself. But the body having been hastily buried, a report arose that he had been strangled by ruffians, Instigated by his son Philip,, a proffigate youth, whom he had disinherited on account of his gross debauchery. Upon this rumour the2rivy Council granted warrant to two surgeons.. of characte; named Crawford and Muirhead, to dig up the body, and to report the state in which they,.slicruld find it. Philip was present on this occasion, and the evi- dence of both surgeons bears. distinctly, that he stood for some titae at a distance•freera the body of his parent; but being called upon to assist in, stretching out the corpse, ha put his hand to the head, when the month and nostiils instantly gushed, with blood. This circumstancei with the evident symptoms of terror and remorse exhibited by young Stanfield, seems to have had considerable weiglit with the jury, and is thus stated:in the indictment: —"That his (the deceased's):nearrist relatives being required to lift the corpse into,the coffin, aftu,rit had been inspected, upon the said Philip Stanfield, touching of it (aceord.rizg,to Gbits usual mo discovering murder It bled afresh upon the said Philip; and that thereupon bet let the body 231%, and fled from it in the greatest eonsternationi pry.. lug, ' Lord have mercy -ripen. me!'" The prisoner to the murder , tber was little p mous.than owfashifsonfnadthgeur, although guilty of being acceseory strong presumptions allaingli him. It is truas he was at the same time saparately convicteik of the distinct crimes of halting cursed his father; and drunk damnation to, the. monarchy ana hies, archy. His sentence, whicilwas to have histougma cut out, and hand struck oft previous to his. being banged, was executediwith thst utmost rig2p4 Be denied the murder with his. last breath. "-Bs Is," says a contemporary judge,, '‘a dark case-oildivina- tion, to be remitted, to thfr great day, whethor he was guilty or innocent. Only, it is certain .he was a bad youth, and may, seruaus a beacon ha,a,ll' profli- gate persons."

div.head: WARRINGTON ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON ELECTIONS.
DECISIVE LIBERAL VICTORY. 7 SEATS OUT OF 9 SECURED.

Two reasons combined give an unusual interest to the municipal elections in Warrington, on Satur- day. The first was that by the recent division of the town into nine wards, in place a the original SIN, the contest would to a great extent reveal the political leanings of the new divisions ; and the second reason was that the contest, in almost thel fullest sense, was an "all-round" one. A Liberal candidate was placed in every ward, but the Tories failed to bring out anyone to champion their cause in the Bewsey district, for which Mr. Shaw Green was consequently returned unopposed on behalf of the liberal party. In each of the other wards there was a spirited contest. As was to be expected, both political parties were placed upon their mettle, andl they laid themselves out for a fight of the most uncompromising description. For a week or two prior to the day of the election there was a great amount of activity at the respective headquarters of the two parties—the central office of the Liberals being at 10, King-st., and that of the Conservatives at 103, Sankey-st. In some of the Wards, meetings were held, but in others the candidates devoted their .energies to organising and canvassing. The politi- cal issue was never lost sight of, but in addition to this, matters of municipal policy were, of nouns°, much enlarged upon both in the addresses and speeches of the candidates. The advisability, or rather the necessity, of improving the public baths seemed to be unanimously conceded to, and there was an almost equal concensus of opinion that the Intercepting Depots should be either "mended or ended," with a pronounced bias in favour of the " ended " remedy in the two wards in which these adjuncts of sanitary work in Warrington are placed. The treatment meted out by the Conservative members of the Town 'Council to the motion which Councillor Flood had intended to propose against accepting tenders from firms who paid less than recognised wages was mentioned at Liberal meetings, but the Conser- vatives kept a significant silence on the subject. The local Trades' Council also sent questions to each candidate, as to the views with regard to the wages and holidays to be given to Corporation workmen, and afterwards the Trades Council put out a placard, advising working-men to vote for its list of candi- dates. In one ward, that of Whitecross, the Liberal candidate gave pre-eminence to the manner in which ex-Police-sergeant Shaw had been treated by the Watch Committee, and references to this matter al- -ware found a cordial response. - -

TOWN HALL WARD. Candidates : Mr. J. H. Fleming (L), tanner' Winmar- leigh-lodge, Springfield-St., and Mr. James Fairclough (C), corn miller, 5, Wilson-Patton-St. No. of voters. 1,109; no. of vGtes polled 831 ; polling place, Drill shed; returning officer, Alderman Davies. Both of the candidates in this Ward were retiring councillors, and both had past services to appeal to, though in regard to this Mr. Fleming had been longer in the Town Council than his opponent. It is said that their claims for municipal honours appeared so equal in the eyes of at least one elector—a Liberal by the way—that in his perplexity as to which should have his vote he set- tled the matter by "tossing up," the fall of the penny being in favour of Mr. Fairclough. Mr. Wm. Walker had charge of the electioneering operations for Mr. Fleming, and in the polling booths the Liberal candidates persona- tion agents were Messrs. Samuel Ryan and Herbert Jones, while Messrs. J. D. Bond and Joseph Marratt acted in the same capacity for Mr. Fairclough. WHITECROSS WARD. Candidates: Mr. H. Roberts (L), builders' merchant, Rose Cottage, Common-lane, Latchford, and Mr. A. Woods (C), jeweller and silversmith, 98, Bewsey-rd. No. of voters, 85; No. of votes polled, 699 • polling place,St. Barnabas' Schools; returning officer, Councillor W. Fierpoint. The contest in this Ward was one of the most spirited in the town. The Tories seemed to exert themselves to the utmost to oust Mr. Roberts from the Town Council,of which he had been an active and out-spoken member for six years. On the other hand Mr. Roberts worked with a determination to win handsomely, and, having had a long experience of electioneering, he acted as his own election agent. In addition to this he was supported by a very representative and vigorous Committee, the mem- bers of which all worked with a will to return the candi- date of their choice. Throughout the day the workers on both sides displayed great activity in bringing up voters, and it did not seem that the supporters on either side could be charged with any laxity in this respect. With-. in the polling booths the personation agents of Mr Roberts were Messrs. G. Booth and E. Heyes, and those of Mr. Woods,were Messrs. A. Titchard and McCoy. ORFORD WARD. Candidates Mr. J. Walker (L), irenfounder, 11, Winnaarleigh-st., and Mr.G. Y. Bolton (C), glass manu- facturer, 93, Bewsey-st. No. of voters, 626; no. of votes polled, 502 • polling place, Silver-st. school.; returning officer, Alderman Harrisoa. For this new Ward both parties had candidates who as yet are new to the duties of tke Town Council. The Conservatives were confident that they had got a strong candidate in Mr. Bolton, who is an employer in the ward, but the Liberals were not less sanguine that in Mr.. Walker they had a powerful and popular champion. Mr. W. Roberts acted as Mr. Walker's election agent,and under his direction a systematic and business-like can- vass was entered upon and from the first the indications were encouraging. The Ward is the smallest in the town, and in the early part of Saturday there was little show that anything in the nature of an election neatest was being conduaed, hut later on matters became brisker. Messrs. J. J. Bunch and J. Upson were Mr. Walker's personation agents, Messrs. J. Bretherton and B. Charnley acted for Mr. Bolton. ST. JOHN'S WARD. Candidates : Mr. U. Blackhurst (L), jeweller, 1. Grappenhall-rd., and Mr. J. Hill (C), builder, 24, Ashton-

street. Number of voters, 1,319; number of votes polled, 822; polling place, Club-room, John-st., returning officer, Alderman Sutton. This is the most populous ward in the town, and a considerable amount of interest was centred in the re- , suit. Mr. Blackhurst was the retiring member of the Council who had been allocated to this ward by the ' government commissioner, and at first his return was challenged by Mr. John Roberts, on behalf of the Con- servatives. But after thinking over it, Mr. Roberts, "the twice-defeated" did not seem to care for a third rebuff, and retired from the field. Mr. James Hill was the next nominee of the Tories, and, although an em- ployer of labour, he was announced as a " wotkingman" candidate. Considering the number of voters in this ward, polling was rather slow for the better part of the day, but in the last hour or two there was considerable "business" done by the poll-clerks. Mr. Blackhurst's personation agents were Messrs. J. Lyons, J. Ashworth, and J. Whitfield ; and those of Mr. Hill were Messrs. E. Carter, W. Taylor and W. Bate. FAIRFIELD WARD. Candidate : Mr. F. Dixon (L). metal merchant, 1, Arpley-st., and Mr. 11. J. Longton, (C), 54, Cross-lane, Earlestown Number of voters, 804 •, number of votes polled, 665 ; polling place, Brick-st., schools; returning officer, Alder- man Wright. Mr. Dixoti came out for this ward as an" independent" but he was supported by Liberal electors, his opponents being a nominee of the Conservatives. Although it could not be said that Mr. ;Dixon was a retiring Councillor, as he dropped out of the Council a year or two cy'm yet he had "past services" to appeal to as he had been a conspicuous member of the Town Council for some Tears. He was, when in the Council, specially interested in the workings of the Gas and Sanitary Committees, not as a member, but as a critic, and the need for improving and cheapening the gas, andof a radical reform at Longford, the intercepting depbts wereput prominently forward in his address. Ills opponent, Mr. Longton, is a young lawyer, who pot up for Latchford two or three years ago but was " thrown " by a faulty nomination paper before the electors had even a chance of recording a vote. The fight on this occasion was as may be seen by result—a narrow majority of five—a tough one, but Mr. Dixon gained the verdict. Mr. Dixon's personation agent was Mr. James Tilley, Messrs.J. Berry and T. Holbrook acting for Mr .Longton. HOWLEY WARD. Candidates : Mr. A. Browne (L), solicitor, 27, Wilson- Patten-st., and Mr. N. B. Percival (C). grocer, 6, Sails- bury-st. Number of voters 1,039; number of votes polled, 782; polling place, National Schools, Chureh-st. ; returning officer, the Mayor (Alderman Francornb). The Liberal candidate, although successful in the end, at first suffered from the disadvantage of being late in the field, while Mr. Pexcival, a retiring councillor,was before the electors from the beginning. In addition to this, Mr. Percival's candidature was supported by both meetings and canvassing, Mr. Brown contenting himself with can- vassing alone. Mr. Percival, as usual under the circum- stances, appealed to services already rendered, but over and above this, he put forward what might be called a physiological argument why he should be returned, namely, that he was an older man than his opponent, and that old men had More brains than young men. The event proved, that the appeal to past services, such as they were, nor to the birth certificate, was of any avail. Polling in this ward, as in some of the others,was slow in the early part of the day-,but more lively towards closing time. Mr. Browne's personation agents were Messrs. J. Maguire and Conway, and Mr. Percival's,Messrs. J.Tay- lor and E. Harrison. ST. AUSTIN'S WARD. Candidates : Mr. J. 'ritchett (L), estate agent, White- cross House, Liverpool-road, and Mr. J. Ilepherd (C), maltster, 3, Wilson Patten-st. Number of voters 666 ; number of votes polled 529 ; polling place, Holy Trinity Schools ; returning officer, Aldan:Al Burgess.

The two candidates for this ward were old antagonists, Mr. Titchett having previously run Mr. Hepherd very close in what was admittedly a Tory ward. Since that contest a number of new voters have been added to the ward, and thisadded an element of uncertainty to the fight which made it all the more interesting. The fear of the Tories that they might lose the seat was evidenced by the fact that they did not hesitate to use the base weapon of slander to ths art the attack of Mr. Titshett. LATCHFORD WARD. Candidates ) Mr. S. B. Stringer (1), gentleman, 150, Wilderspool Causeway, Latchford, and Mr. J. Ashton (C), licensed victualler, 2 and 4, Wilderspool Causeway. No. of voters, 884 ; number of voters polled, 553 ; polling place, St. James's Schools; returning officer, Alderman Chandley. Latchford has been so much of a Tory stronghold that it has not been contested for ten years, and Mr. Ashton, the retiring councillor, kad held a seat in the Town Council for twenty years. The contest was somewhat of the nature of a forlorn hope" as far as Mr. Stringer was concerned, but it will be seen from the result of the poll that a not inconsiderable section of the electors have stamped with approval his protest against the class of representation, which the Tories think good enough for Latchford. The contest was quietly conducted, though neither of the candidates nor their supporters left any stone unturned in bringing up voters. DECLARATION OF THE POLL.

The polliag begun at the different booths at eight I o'cloelt in the morning, aad was continued till eight • o'clock at night, when the booths were closed. Directly after eight o'clock the ballot boxes were conveyed to the ' Town Hall, and there, in the Council Chamber, the counting wag set about in the: presence of the return- ing officers, the Town Clerk, the candidates and others. There was evidently a wide-spread interest as to the I result, and by nine o'clock many hundreds of persons ' had assembled in front of the Town Hall steps from ' which the announcements are made. It was expected, , that the counting would be over shortly after nine o'clock but it was getting towards ten before the Mayor and the other returning officers issued from the Town Hall, , and made public, the anxiously-waited for results. The Liberal victories were evidently very popular in the crowd, and as the six wards in which Liberals were re- turned were first on the list, the cheering increased in volume on each successive announcement. When at length the result for St. Austin's Ward as declared,and it was seen that the Tory bad retained his seat,there was a good deal of hootink mingled with the rather feeble cheers, and there was a burst of counter-cheering on its being announced that the Toryonajority only numbered eleven votes. The results were declared as follows : TOWN HALL WARD. J. H. FLEMING (L) 430 J. FAIRCLOUGH (C) 4Ol Majority WHITECROSS WARD. H. ROBERTS (L) A. WOODS (C) Majority ............... .... 193 ORFORD WARD.
