Maiority AT THE LIBERAL CLUB: ENTHUSIASTIC PRO- CEEDINGS. Tery soon after the declaration of the poll, there was a large and enthusiastic gathering at the Liberal Club, where an extempore meeting was soon formed to celeb- rate the great success at the polls. The successful candi- dates were, as they presented themselves, loudly cheered. Councillor W. Pierpoint presided, and the successful.. newly elected Ceuncillors present were—CeuncillorFlem- hig, Councillor Roberts, Councillor James Walker, and Councillor Browne. There were also present Councillor Garner, Councillor Flood, Councillor Beaman, Messrs. J. Walker, W. Roberts, C. J. Holmes, J. Albinson, Sze. Councillor Shaw-Green was prevented from being present through indisposition. The CHAIRMAN said they were met together on a very joyful occasion, but at the same time they must not have too long speeches as a great many of those present had , been working very hard. (Hear, hear.) Well, where werethey now ? (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had occasion when Mr. Beaman was returned to say that the Liberal party was not a discredited party, and ho had I always maintained that if the Liberal party of Warring- I ton had fair play it would be the dominant party in the town, and what he thought before he felt certain was the fact now. (Applause.) There was a certain paper in Warrington—(oh, oh, and laughter, and a Voice: "It's a disgrace, ')—yes, it was a disgrace to journalism. That paper took upon itself to act as a prophet for the Tory party, and it actually had the dignified ignorance —(" Impudence ")—well, yes, it was impudence. When ' they recollected what the editor of that paper used to be and what political colour he was, be (the chairman) did not envy his feelings that nirht. (Hear, hear.) What he wanted to observe upon was that that paper ventured to prophecy that there would be a Tory major- ity in every ward. (Laughter.) Well, they knew the result. They were all satisfied with it, and he was more than satisfied. It was said they were a party without a leakier, and that they were disorganised. The result that day published the lie to that assertion (Applause.) In conclusion he urged them all to become membecs of the Liberal Club ; and then called upon Councillor FLEMING to address the meeting. Mr. ' Fleming who had a very cordial reception, thanked them all for the noble victory achieved that day, and speaking with regard to the work done in his own ward he said he could not single out any individual from the many. Who had exerted themselves to the utmost. He had fought what was considered a stiff battle, and Mr. John White had said that after he had been all over the place he had gone to the Town Hall Ward to be beaten. (Laughter.) But they knew the result, and they had his gratitude, and that of the Liberal party. He thanked them for himself, but he thanked them more for the cause they had at heart. (Applause, and:" Three cheers for the Grand Old Man.") Councillor H. ROBERT'S was enthusiastically received, I and at the outset expressed his gratitude to the inagni- ficent committee of workers that had assisted him in 1 Whitecross Ward. A few days ago the notorious news- paper that had been referred to ventured to prophecy that they should lose in Whitecross Ward by a majority of 43 votes, and it it had been within the power of that newspaper to decide the fate of Whitecrose Ward perhaps I they should have lost. But it was a fortunate and a creditable thing that the electors in Whitecross Ward I were a bit too respectable for that newspaper. (Hear, hear, and applause.) If there was one thing more than another that he was thankful for in regard to the election it was that, in spite of a great deal of mud-throwing, his private character had come but all right. (Hear, hear.) Although, politically speaking, they had a very consider- ' able majority in the Whitecrose Ward, yet apart from ' that the ,intelligence of the Ward bad asserted itself and had vindicated his conduct and the conduct of his friends in regard to ex-P.S. Shaw. (Applause.) He had no hesitation in saying that if a poll of the borough could be taken on that subject alone, the Chief Constable and the Watch Committee would find themselves in a very small minority. (Hear, hear.) It nteant that as long as Liberalism asserted itself it would assist those who could not help themselves, and indeed that was a fundamental principle Gi their politioal faith. (Hear, hear.) And Liberalism would assert itself in spite of misrepresentation and falsehood. (Applause.) That election was satisfactory for more reasons than one. They had been taunted and jumped ,on "all over the shop," as he might say. Their opponents thought they had them down, and that they were a disorganised and discredited party. But give him the support of the intel- ligent working-men of Warrington, and the aristocracy • could go to the party to which they naturally be- longed. (Applause.) At their meetings in Whitecross Ward they had discussed municipal matters, and it Showed to him that if the candidates on the Liberal side would only take the electors into their confidence the Tory party would not be in it. The Liberals wished to do right all round, and they wanted to repre- sent them in every ward in Warrington thorough men. They could not do with any weak-hearted fellows. They ought to fight every municipal election, and he would guarantee that if those men who took a deep interest in Liberalism in Warrington would only make a little personal sacrifice, they would have such a majority in the Town Counil that they should not have to wait for the election of a Liberal Mayor or aldermen at the hands of the Tory party. (Applause, and a voice: .6 NO compromises.") No, the day of compromises in Warrington had gone; they wanted no favours at the hands of the Tory party—they could afford to take what they wanted, and they would take it. (Applause.) The result of that election would bring them a Parliamentary candidate of a satisfactory character—(applaun.)—and he would guarantee that there was sorrowiffg that night at Walton Hall. (Hear, hear and laughter.) They
and

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1890.

had had such an array of aristocracy in Whitecross Ward that day as they:should net have again for many years to come, and yet they had won the ward in such a fashion that they would have a great many walks over in the future. The Tories spoke of his having been pitehforked into the Town Council, but he was very willing to be again " pitchforked" baby that majority of 193. (Applause.) Mr. Wautan, the newly elected councillor for Orford Ward, next expressed his thanks for having been placed at the head of the poll, and also to those who had helped him and to the gentleman who had lent their convey- acmes. (Applause). 1 Councillor A. BROWER said he was the "youthful op- ponent" whom Mr. Percival would not be afraid of (laughter and applause). Hewes very grateful to all those who had worked for and supported him in attack- ing a Tory ward which had not been won by the Liberals for 22 years. (Hear, hear). He had been thinking that day, after he had seen Sir Gilbert Greenall was being handed round from committee room to committee room, what inspiration and enthusiasm that election would have given to their grand old man of Warrington, Mr. Mcalinnies had he lived till that day. (Hear, hear). He saw by the prophecy that he was to be beaten that day by 59, but that was a wrong result by just 120. (Hear, hear and laughter). Mr. Percival in speaking about him said that whilst boys might have a good gift of the gab, they had not got the brains, but the people of Warring- ton had thought different. (Applause). Mr. Browne again thanked his supporters, and also urged upon members of the Liberal party to support that club by joining it, the subscription being only ss. a year. Mr. JOIIN WALKER moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Pierpoint for presiding. They had secured seven seats out of nine ; a magnificent victory had been won ; and it was but one of the many victories that had been won all over the country to cheer the heart of the Grand Old ;lan. (Applause.) It was no secret that they had had sone difficulty in Warrington in getting what they con- sidered a suitable candidate, because it was thought that the Liberal party in Warrington was not so strong as to ensure a victory. But that message taken to the Liberal leaders in London as to their victory would show them that Warrington could be won for the party at the next election. (Applause.) The Chairman of the Tory party at the first meeting in that contest he attended, declared that so far as they were concerned they were taking politics into account. The Liberals accepted the chal- lenge. They made it a political fight, and they hada won a political victory. (Applause.) That had been a soldiers' battle, won, not by generals, for unfortunately, they had not a great many generals, but the soldiers had fought splendidly, and they deserved every credit. It had been a battle of the masses against the classes. (Applause.) With regard to the two candidates who had not succeeded, Mr. Stringer, who was a comparative stranger, deserved every credit for the gallant fight he had made in what was recognised as a forlorn hope. (Hear, hear.) They who lived at Latchford were deter- mined' that they would at last make some protest against the overpowering influence of the drink trade; and do something, too to let it be seen that such a case as that of Sergeant Shaw should not in the future pass by with iinpunity. (Hear. hear.) Mr.Titchetthad been foully slandered bytheTory*Paxty—(hees,hear)—but now It appeared that after the truth was known, that slander had reacted on the Tory party with the result that Mr. Titchett had, as he might say, escaped having been returned hy the narrow majority of eleven votes. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Walker) considered that a splendid fight on Mr. Titchett's part, and he thought that when an op- portunity arose, and an opportunity might arise before long, the ward that had the opportunity might well con- sider whether Mr. Titchett, who had fought two battles for the Liberal party, should not be candidate for it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had won that splendid victory; and if they intended to profit by it, they must have their ward meetings and get thoroughly organised. (Applause.) Mr. KIERIL&E, in seconding the vote of thanks, con- gratulated them on their victory over the coercion party. As regarded St. Austin's Ward they actually had a majority, but six of their duplicate voters had voted for Mr. Fleming, nine for Mr. Blackhurst, he did not know how many for Mr. James Walker. (Hear, hear.) They, should, therefore, really have had a victory, and at any bye-election they would have one. (Applause.) He believed that they had voted on the coercion question that day, and that at a Parliamentary election they would win the borough. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. W. ROBERTS, in supporting the vote of thanks, congratulated the Liberal party on having elected Mr. Councillor Walker to the Town Council. (Hear, hear.) He could not close without expressing his deep sympathy with Mr. Titchett in the most disgraceful attack which had been made upon him. He had not deserved such I conduct, and he (Mr. Roberts) hoped the Liberal party would remember the gallant way in which Mr. Titchett had fought in St. Austin's Ward. They should not rest satisfied until they saw Mr. Titchett in the Town Council. (Applause.) He urged upon those present to endeavour to make that club as successful, and even more success- ful, than the club in Sankey-st. (Hear, hear.) The vote of thanks was then passed, hearty cheers being given for Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. F. A. Roberts. The Cs:mamma, in responding, explained that the chairman of their executive, Mr. F. A. Roberts, had been unavoidably called away during the whole of that week, so as to render is totally impossible for him to be among them, or he would most certainly have been. He had had a letter at the beginning of the week from Mr. Roberts apprising him of the fact, and asking him if he would take charge of his duties. That lie (the chairman) had tried to do to the best of his abilities. (Applause.) Then there was their friend Mr. Clayton—(applause, and " Cheers for Clayton.") They had seen very little of Mr. Clayton all the week, but he (the chairman) in the exercise of his duties had found him working almost day and night com-
agai

pleting arrangements for the elections, and however much the workers might be entitled, and they were en- titled to the best thanks of the candidates, he was bound to say that Mr. Clayton had done his work in an admir- able manner and deserved the thanks of the entire Liberal party of Warrington. (Applause.) He (the chairman) had done what he had done for the Liberal party because he thought it was his duty, and he had seen no reason to change his mind. (Loud applause.) The gathering then dispersed. ,sarrfunif AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.' ----- 1741, Y • '

" I GREAT DISAPPOINTMENT." The Conservative Club, en Saturday evening, about nine o'clock, presented a very animated appearance. An unusually large anmber of members had assembled eager to herald the joyous news that the Conservative party at the polls had been sncceesful. On every hand there was perfect unanimity that the Conservative candidates in at , least most of the Wards must head the poll. The defeat therefore, came as a terrible disappointment; and as might have been expected, it was attributed to various causes, but mainly to the inertness of the workers and , deficient combination. Mr. ROBBIIT PIHRPOINT. Chairman of the Conservative Association, said he had hoped very much that day to' have been able to congratulate them instead of having to condole with them. He need aot say, as Chairman of the Conservative Association, how sorry he was at the result of thepoll. They had only returned two out of the eight candidates that they put forward. Many gentlemen had worked with unfailing energy, and to them he begged to tender the thanks of the Conservative Association. Those who had worked had done hard work, and had done it well ; but he could not disguise from them a fact that they knew perfectly well, which was, that there were some who might have worked, who had not done so. (Hear, hear.) He said with a certain bitterness of feeling that there were men who could have come forward and done their work, who had not done so; .12ut he hoped that day would be a lesson to them in the future. He took it that it was no playing work to do political work. It was a duty sometimes unpleasant, sometimes a duty which took one away from other things which one would rather do, but still it was a duty which every man could take part in if only by helping a little, and he regretted to think there were some who had done no- thing. It might be that he was speaking some- what too warmly on that occasion no, no ")—but, he was, he thought, on ordinary occasions a cool and quiet man. He assured them that night he felt very strongly on that matter, and he trusted they would learn a lesson from the defeat their party had sustained that day, and that they would take care the future was better than was that day. (Hear, hear.) He seemed to be almost scolding when perhaps he ought to be praising, because he could appre- hend that there were probably few in that room—or per." haps none—who had not done sonic little work that day. He thought it was their duty to thank all those present who had in any way supported the Conservative caidi- dates ; ani he hoped when the next opportunity came they would all work—all who were in that room, and all who were outside—and he would urge upon them that they most not only work at municipal elections, but at the greater election, the Parliamentary election, which was approaching day by day. (Applause.) He could scarcely find words to express how he felt that night. lie was disappointed, and naturally those around him would i be disappointed; but let them take care the next time I they had anything to do that all of them worked as hard as they could, and then, they might depend upon it, they would be victorious again. (Applause.) Mr. Jorrir WHITE said he had nothing much to add to what the Chairman had already said. He felt with him that they had sustained a groat disappointment that evening. He must say he had looked forward to six out of the eight candidates being returned; and the narrow majorities with which they had been beaten in the Wards I showed that with a little more effort they might have had six winners instead of six losers. It was, of course, hard to lose at any time ; but it was still harder to lose as they had done that day, by the apathy of those who , ought to have worked. They heard people sometimes say that Municipal Elections were of little importance; but this was not so, for they were of importance. He thought it was possible by the lesson they had learnt that night that those who had not worked with them as they should have done would, in the future, work hard and the results would then be certainly better than they had proved to be that day. He thought they should tender their thanks to those who had helped the candi- dates, and to the candidates themselves. He Was sure they never had a better let of candidates than they had had during the contest just closed. They were all good and true men who had worked hard themselves. He also thought that they could ccndole with the candidates very much, not only for suffering defeat, but because the workers of the Conservative party had not given them the assistance which they deserved. If they would compare the number of votes recorded with the number of votes in each of the Wards they would find that there was a very large percentage who had not voted at all, and from the way the Liberals had worked it was evident that those who had not voted were Conservatives. (Ap- plause.) Councillor Iluirt thought it was high time that all the members of the Conservative Association should come to the conclusion that every gentleman they returned to the Council was a true Tory—(hear, hear)—for they did not want any weak-kneed Tories in the Council. He found that now they would have a greater necessity for the true Tories; and, if those of their party in the Council would only act according to their principles they would still be in the majority. Mr. A. Woons, who was well received, said he could tell them candidly that for ten days he had worked his utmost in Whitecross Ward, and he had had six hard

working men assisting him, and he meant to say but for the assistance of thew men they would have polled a much smaller number than they had done. (A. voice " Hold on "). They might say hold on, but it was a fact. If the Conservatives who walked about with flowers in their coats all over the town had gone and sup- ported him as they ought to have done, he felt confident, if be had not been returned, the majority would have, been very little over 20. He did not regret the result very much personally, but he did very much regret it for the party. The Liberals had worked tooth amd fasil, with the result that they had been victoricons (Applause.) Mr. H. J. LONGTON said he had done what he could to win the fight for the credit of the party. (Hear, hear.) He had been supported by a fair number of hard working-men—enthusiastic men—and they had done their very best for him, and he was sure he would never forget their kindness. All that he could say was that the Conservatives of Fairfield Ward had not voted quite in accordance with their colours, otherwise the result would have been different. (Applause.) Mr. N. B. PERCIVAL, said if the Conservatives would not come forward and support the candidates they could not expect a different result. He was truly sorry with the result, but all who had worked had done their best. Councillor Ilseunen said he thought it must be a little relief to them to have a winning candidate to say a few words to them. (Laughter.) As far as his ward was concerned, he thought his success was due ts the assist- ance given him by Alderman Wright and Alderman Sutton, and he firmly believed if he had not had the help of those two gentlemen the party would have lost St. Austin's Ward. A gentleman having spoken a few words on behalf of Councillor Ashton, who was successful in again winning his seat for Latchford Ward, Mr. THOMAS MASON, after sarcastically commenting upon the few of committee men who gave a helping hand at the elections, said it was no good mincing matters, and they might as well speak their minds. He was very sorry indeed that Mr. Percival had been unsuccessful ; but they all knew that he had in Mr. Arthur Browne one I of the strongest opponents he could possibly have, and they knew that Mr. Browne was one of the most rising , young men in his profession in Warrington. In conclu- sion, he said they must have more energy put into the ' committee men if they wantsd them to take a more active interest in everything appertaining to the welfare of their party. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT again briefly addressed the assembly. He said the thanks of the party were due to the candidates and those who that day had worked for them. He had spoken to them before with some degree 'of warmth and some degree of bitterness; but he did not know that he had spoken toe strong. He aid not think he had done, and he could, if he liked, say some- thing a great deal warmer, but he would decline doing so. He would, at the same time draw their attention to the fact that they had that day learnt a lesson of victory from their defeat. He sincerely congratulated those gentlemen who had won, and sympathised with those who had lost. Whatever those around him had done, he could only say let those who had worked to deserve praise, praise themselves, and let those who de- served blame, blame themselves. (Applause.) He had: not often an opportunity of appearing amongst them, ' but as long as he held the privilege of being their chair- man, and when he had the opportunity of speaking to them, he would tell them the truth, and he then might tell them plainly that be regretted deeply what had happened that day ; and he implored them to take care that it did noteccur again. They had returned but two candidates at the head of the poll, and those two were gentlemee well deserving of the trust, and he congratu- lated them upon their success most heartily. In con- clusion he said again that he had great pleasure in niov- ing a vote of thanks to the candidates and workers. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously and the audience then dispersed. THE COMPOSITION OF THE COUNCIL. The following is now the composition of the Town Council, but it should be explained that there are two vacancies caused by the resignation of Alderman Crosfield and Councillor Monks. The total number of members is 36. Town Hall Ward.—Messra. William Pierpoint (L), R Heaton (C), and J. H. Fleming (L.) Whitecross Ward.—Messrs. E. Greenall (C), F. Monks (resigned) and H. Roberts (L.) Bewsey Ward.—Messrs. T. Flood (L), S. J. Beaman (L),
and J. S. Green (L.) Orford Ward.—Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins (C), F. A. Roberts (L), and J. Walker (L.) St. John's Ward.—Messrs. J. Garner (L), J. Platt (L), _ _

and G. Blackhurst (L.) Fairfield Ward. —Messrs. T. Flutchinson (L), R. T. Fair. dough (C), and F. Dixon (L.) Howley Ward.—Messrs. W. Bolton (C), J. Cannell (C), and A. Browne (L). St. Austin's Ward.—Messrs. L. Voisey (C), J. Muir (C), and J. Flepherd (C). , Latchford Ward.—J. Taylor (C), W. Tinsley (C), and J. Ashton (C). Number of Councillors, 27. There are also nine Aldermen, viz. :—Messrs. R. W. Francomb (C), J. Burgess (L), JeCrosfield (L) (resigned), J. Davies (C), J. Harrison (C), C. J. Holmes (L), J. E. Wright (C), T. Sutton (C), and S. Chandley (C)-9 ; making a grand total of 36. Seventeen of the above-named gentlemen, including Messrs. Crosfield and Monks, are Liberals, and 19 Con- servatives, so that the Conservatives are still in a major- ity of two, even after the Liberal gains of Saturday.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.

Mr. Gladstone drove from Fasque House on Monday morning to Isinrencekirk on his homeward journey. The ordinary train leaving Aberdeen at 10.20 was specially stopped at Laurencekirk, in order that the saloon pro- vided for the right hon. gentleman by the North British Railway Company might be attached. Mr. Gladstone, who is looking all the better for his rest of the past few days, was loudly cheered by a number of farmers and others who had assembled at the station. Mr. Gladstone met with an enthusiastic reception at Montrose and Arbroath. At Dundee, too, there was a great crowd on the platform, and hope was expressed that it would not be long before he came back again. Mr. Gladstone entered into conversion with one of the city members, Mr. Leng, and, before leaving, proposed from the saloon window, "Prosperity to Bonnie Dun- dee." The cheers were loud and prolonged as the train left. THE RETURN JOURNEY. On Thursday Mr. Gladstone concluded his stay in Scotland. The right hon, gentleman, who was accom- panied by Mrs. Gladstone, drove from The Glen, Sir Charles Tennant's seat, and proceeded to Innerleithan, where a number of people assembled and cheered loudly. special train was provided by the North British Rail- way Co., and Mr. Gladstone and his party started for Carlisle shortly after ten o'clock. No stoppage was made between Innerleithen and Carlisle, but at various stations es rotas numbers of people had collected, and cheered as the special train passed by. At Galashiels there was a particularly large assembly, mainly consisting of work- people. A report had been made that Mr. Gladstone should receive an address there, but he felt obliged to decline. In response to cheers, he repeatedly bowed from the carriage windows. SPEECH AT CARLISLE: THE LICENSING QUESTION. Carlisle was reached soon after noon. Mr. Gladstone met with an enthusiastic reception. He addressed several thousand people in the courtyard, from the County Hotel. He spoke for nearly half an hour. Referring to compensation, he said it was not an immoderate statement to hold that the price the country would have to pay for the redemp- tion of licenses on the principle then laid down would have been in England alone two hundred millions of money, and it would have been the death warrant of temperance reform. Although the Government had said if the bill was thrown out no good whatever would be done, the magistrates, the present defective licensing authority, had already shown a disposition far better than they had before, and were beginning to act on the principle of the present law, and had actually begun to pluck up their courage, and to re- duce the number of public-houses to what they considered the wants of the population. The Liberals had attained a stronger position for approaching that question than ever before, and that stronger position had been attained by the happy and thorough and crushing defeat sustained by the public. house endowment scheme of the present Government. He went on to denounce the Government for not appeal- ing to the country now that popular feeling was shown to be decidedly against them. The Government were like a man with a bad tooth, who knows he must go to the dentist but cannot pluck up courage. Like a timid Iman going to bathe, they had not courage to plunge into the water. The longer he stood the colder he got, but the must jump in (laughter and cheers.) That was really the position of the Government, but,come the dissolution when it might, the Liberal party were ready for it. , Mr. Gladstone reached Preston from Carlisle at 3.18. IHe occupied a saloon. A crowd of Liberal politicians and others awaited his arrival, and cheered him heartily. He was too hoarse to speak. On leaving he was loudly cheered. The train moved on to Wigan, where there was another most enthusiastic reception. The train passed through Bank Quay Station, Warring- ton, at half-past four. Nobody seemed to be aware that Mr. Gladstone would pass through Warrington, the pre- , ' sumption being that he would take the new Midland routs from Carlisle direct to Chester. Consequently there was no demonstration at the station, but the passengers' and others on the platform recognised and cordially , saluted the illustrious travellers. Miss Tennant, who had accompanied Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone so far, con- tinued her journey on the London train ; and the saloon carriage, in which were Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, was attached to the local train for Chester. Several by- standers surrounded the saloon, and shook hands with Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, and a heraty cheer was raised ' as the Chester train left the station. Mr. Gladstone reached Chester General Railway Station shortly after five o'clock, and not withstanding the long journey from Carlisle he looked remarkably well. He continued the journey to Sandycroft Station, on the Holyhead line, where he alighted, and was immediately driven to Hawarden Castle. He arrived at the Castle about six o'clock.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF A MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF A MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT.

Another Parliamentary vacancy will, it is said, shortly occur through the resignation of Mr. Edward Crossley, who has a seat for the Sowerby Division of the West Rid- ing of Yorkshire since 1885. The reason of Mr. Crossley's intended early withdrawal from the House of Commons ;is the delicate state of his health. Steps are now being taken to bring forward a suitable Gladstonian candidate for the constituency. There are over 11,000 electors; the Liberal majority in 1885 being 3,500.

A WOULD-BE MURDERER HANGS HIMSELF. Early on Saturday morning a desperate affray took place at Sparkhill, near Birmingham. A man was being arrested for stealing geese, and when about half a mile from the police station he turned upon the policeman and tried to cut his throat with a pruning knife. A desperate struggle between the officer and his assailant ensued. It required the combined efforts of six men to take the , desperado to the station. Later in the morning he was found in his cell dead, having hanged himself with his shirt. - -

div.head: FATAL QUARREL BETWTYN BROTffERS.
div.p: THE FATAL QUARREL BETWTYN BROTffERS.

On Tuesday afternoon the Sheffield Borough Coroner held an inquest on Edward Hinch, who died on Sunday morning last from wounds alleged to have been inflicted by George Hinch, his brother. The men lived together with their widowed mother at Carbrook, Sheffield. On Saturday night both had been out drinking,and returned , home about eleven o'clock. A quarrel ensued, in the course of which George picked up a large carving knife, and, making a rush at his brother, stabbed him in the arm,eausing a large wound four inches deep, and sever- ing the main artery. Edward died from the injury thus caused about one o'clock on Sunday morning. George was arrested for murder, and now stands remanded on that charge; but the coroner's jury, believing that the stabbing took place while the prisoner was in a rage, and without any premeditation. found a verdict of man- slaughter.
AN AUSTRIAN ARCHDUKE DROWNED.

A Vienna correspondent telcgraphs c—lt seems no longer possible to doubt that "Captain Johann Orth," otherwise the Archduke Johann Salvator, has been drowned. The Archduke. it will be remembered, resigned his imperial rank with the Emperor's consent, and after passing the necessary examinations, became last year the oaptain of a merchant vessel, the Mar- garetha. which he owned. Last spring he sailed for Monte Video with a cargo of saltpetre. and on July 11th he left Monte Video for Valparaiso. It appears tfig at , about the time when the Margaretha ns'e nava been passing Cape Horn terrible cyclones prevailed, and the captain of a Swedish barque, the Robertf ors, which put in at Valparaiso on September 13th, being out from Monte Video, reports that as he passed near Cape Elora he sighted the wrecks of three vessels, one of which he de- clares was that of the Margaretha. The news has created a feeling of deep sympathy in Vienna, where the Arch- , duke was greatly esteemed, as indeedlie was everywhere.

3IARRIAGE OF THE VICAR OF BURTON- WOOD. The ladies of the pariah of St. Michaele, Burton- wood, have been exercised in their minds lately, by the eirculation of a rumour that the Rev. W. Wil- son, vicar of St. Michaels, was about to re-enter the matrimonial state. The surprise was all the greater as it is known that Mr. Wilson has fora long period been an invalid, and unable to undertake the services at the church. The rumour, however, became an accomplished fact on Monday, for on that day the wedding took place. On Monday morning, I Mrs. Jane Forshaw, drove on to the vicarage, and I returned shortly afterwards with the bridegroom, the Rev. W. Wilson. On the arrival in church, the cere- mony was performed by tke Rev. W. Michael, of Man- chester, who has been officiating at Burtonwood during the. illness of the vicar. Mr. Gawtherpe acted as best man, and Miss M. Atherton, housekeeper to Mr. Wil- son, stood as bridesmaid for Mrs. Forshaw. At the conclusionlof the ceremony, Mr. andrlrs. Wilson drove away ea route for Cheadle, the bride's home. Mrs. Wilson retired from the brewery some few months ago, is now residing at Cheadle.

div.head: LIBERA.TION SOCIETY MEETING.
div.p: LIBERA.TION SOCIETY MEETING.

The Council of the Liberation Society held its autum- nal meeting On Tuesday in Mancnester. The chair was occupied by Mr. Henry Lee, and there were also present a number of members of Parliament and other prominent adherents of the movement. Mr. Carvell Williams gave an encmiraging review of the propects of the Disestab- lishment questions, and resolutions were adopted with ' reference to the position of Disestablishment in Scotland and Wales, the attitude to be observed by Liberationists at the nextgeneral election, the tithe question, national education, and the Maltese marriage question. In the evening there was a soiree, under the presidency of Mr. Alfred Illingworth, M.P., at which Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., in an effective speech urged the claims of Wales to the immediate disestablishment and disendowment of a Church which, he said, was the Church of the Mai, tesimal minority,
MEETING OF THE NATIOIcAL LEIGUE.

Mr. Claucy, M.P., presiding at a meeting of the National League, in Dublin, on Tuesday, hoped their English friends would not be deceived by the statements of Mr. Balfour, who said that £lOO,OOO were collected for the Tenants' Defence Fund and only £6,000 expended. He asked where was the remaining £94,000. Mr. Bal- four knew that £6,000 was not as much as had been expended by the National League under ordinary cir- cumstances, and he knew from Mr. Russell that over £30,000 was expended on the Tipperary tenants alone, and in supporting the evicted tenants on the Ponsonby estates. The League would not give Mr. Balfour or any- body else particulars to a penny or a pound of theirexpen- diture. Mr. Balfour never proposed to spend a penny in improvements to relieve distress in the West, except uncoiling red tape for light railways. Mr. Morley had forced that visit on him.

THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 8, 1890.

The Moral Tire published returns of the of the Municipal Elections which Were Elections, held throughout the country, eel Saturday, show that the Liberals have gain between forty and fifty seats. In harmony as they are with the results of the ParliamentarY bye-elections, they add strength to the CO viction that the nation is tired of Toryism an" Coercion, and longs for the opportunity of turning out a Government which blocks the path of progr, ess* Granted that here and there a municipal contest will have turned on purely local issues, there is 0° denying that the emphatic verdict given in seal places as Warrington, Manchester, and Liverpool is in favour of Liberalism as opposed to Toryisrs , The victories are political victories, and they are auguries of the triumph which awaits the Libere party at the General Election. Even as t° municipal elections, it is beginning to be seen that Toryism means, as of old, stagnation and class exclusiveness,. Labour. is asserting itself; it desires to be directly represented in Town Councils, and finds whenit would move in this direction that no real sympathy or help is to be had from the Tory party. So far as Warrington is concerned, was the Liberal journal and the Liberal organisatles3 that made it possible for two genuine werkg- men to obtain seats in the Town Council. In' Helens, labour candidates have contested throe seats, and have won One by a large majorityr the, significant fact being that, taking the of the votes into account, it is fonna that the labour candidates have a larger total o°ll the other, candidates. The Tories are, to be fore' profuse in their, professions of regard for the workers, but the labouring classes are eNtery growing more intelligent,, and are not Vita easily hoodwinked: as they were when this franctf was first given to them- The new generatioa readers and thinkers distrust the Tories as their natural enemies.. In Warrington,, the Liberals haws cause' rejoicing, ,as , they do rejoice, in the magnified/ victory which they achieved on Saturday. something to be proud of to have secured sel7; seats out of nine—six won in the open field--se: one, a walk-over,, conceded beforehand throage* fear of a, contest,. We shall, perhaps, have a Litt!: less of the braggart talk about the Liberal Par" being utterly broken, discomfited, and dis°r...,ags- nised ; and, as we believe there is a. grain Of se:.,, still left amongst the Tories, we venture that.we ha-so seen.the last of sucluboastful„ or oo we say imbecile,. predictions off results as tll,lO which ha-re made; our Tory oontemporarY 41,0" laughing-stook ef, the town. According local organ of the Tory party, the Liberals .„ be beaten in every ward ; and, with a. teinerl'J iwhich was equalled only by its; folly, figures soffe.o _given ae to wbat was called: "a forecast of 14:06 'result.' At:tam:ding to these figures, the Itn;itg, were to win '''allalong the line," with a ra*Prluoi inevemy contested ward, a.r4 a total majority of less than 6til. This was the fiction, but, as it 11-6 pened in fast, the majori4 was against the Tori 0 in six out of the eight contests ; whilst as to oa i°l.lt —St. Austin's Ward—so far from the ma_Y- being 105, against the Liberals, as predicted., it w.° 7 11 only! Taking the result of the whole of tn votes polled on Saturday, we, find that the TaleY party—so far from having a majority of 650-710 ;in a minority of 21)2". To this must be added; LP Liberal majority in Bewsey Ward—where, hild: was no contest—which is at least 100; d: le thus get a Liberal majority in Warringtaa ' present moment of no less than 367. This hopeful; it is highly encouraging; it givSS Pr°- mise of victory at the General Election. The leaders of the Warrington Tories,,sPeaki.,ll6„ after the declaration of the polls, confessed to the great disappointment they had sustained. JOHN WEITE admitted that they expected to win. in six wards, instead of losing in six; but he and others attributed their crushing defeat to lack of ' work and workers. Granted that there is some' thing in this—is it not a sign of the times that the re Conservative party, dependent as the Liberals a , upon volunteers, cannot find the requisite Workers Is it not evidence in itself that the working-rae upon whom they have hitherto h been able to rely, have become. eielc of a Goyeranne _19,44

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

and a policy which have brought no good to them, and wrought nothing but mis- chief in Ireland ? So far as organisation is concerned, we are free to confess that the Liberals of Warrington have been somewkat negligent of late ; they have not had the usual annual meeting and the usual ward meetings; and, if it had not been that the workers were enthusiastic in a cause which they believe to be a winning cause, the victory, if there had been victory at all, would not have been as great as it has proved to be. The Tories did what they could, on Saturday, in their usual way ; they patronised their workers with a sight of Sir GIIDERT GREENALL and other gentry ; but they have found that this won't do in these democratic days; and they will doubtless set about repairing their weak places as well as they can. The Liberals must do the same ; there is undoubtedly room for improvement. They must put themselves in a position to hold what they have got, and to gain more; to go from strength to strength, and from victory to victory.

Bartington LORD HARTINGTON has been de- in liverina at Greenock what is called Scotland. a reply to Mr. Gladstone but what is certainly not an answer. He shows himself consis- tent in that he stands still; and his chief complaint against the Liberal leader is that he is like the rest of the world—he keeps moving on. His lord•• ship makes it clear that, though he recognises that the Unionists may be beaten at the General Eleo- tion, he himself has no thought of yielding. This is what might have been expected; for on the Irish question Lord HARTINGTON is more of a Tory than the Tories themselves. He was the first to suggest a new Crimes Act when Lord SALISBURY was placed in power; and we strongly suspect that it is due to him that the Government have not re- deemed, or made an effort to redeem, their pledges to the nation and to Parliament by granting local self-government to Ireland. In concluding his speech on Tuesday night Lord Hartington said : " Under these circumstances our duty is still as clear as ever to retain at all events our own inde- pendence, to take every means which lies within our reach to prevent power falling into the hands of that party [the Nationalists] or its leaders, who either don'tknow or dare not avow what they pro- pose to do with our constitution and empire." To prevent power from falling into the hands of the Irish leaders—that is, and has been, his lordships aim all through this agitation; and it is for this reason that he has not one word to say about local self-government. He is firm in the matter— stupiel if you will—but he is at least honest, which is more than can be said of Lord SALISBURY and his followers, who have in the past preached ''similarity and simultaneity and "equal laws for the whole kingdom," and will have the hardihood to try it on again, as soon as they know that the hour has arrived when they must face the constituencies' they have bamboozled and betrayed. 13ut they will not succeed again; for " once b iten twice shy" is the motto of the electors. As might be expected, Lord HARTINGTON gives no countenance to the agitation for Home Rule for Scotland, and he truly remarks :—" If we are to have Home Rule for Ireland, and as something of the same kind is suggested for Scotland—some other form of Home Rule for Scotland—then you must remember that we must have Home Rule for England also. If the principle of nationality is to be recognised to this extent I know no reason why England should not claim it also." or do we, nor does anybody else who is liberal in thought, and has given careful consideration to the subject; and that is why the opinion is gaining ground that the only legitimate, consistent and certain way out of the dead-lock on legislation is Home Rule all round. But we are told that the inferior Parlia- ments "could not afford, to the highest ambitions and the highest intellect, the inducements which our present Parliament has offered, and will con- tinue to offer to the highest minds amongst us? And what if that were so? The chief object of a Parliament should be the good government of the country; and not tin gratification of the ambitions of either the highest or the lowest minds. When a Committee is forined for any purpose it is not surely a question cf gratifying ambitions, but of getting the right York done in the right way. And what is a Parliammt but a Committee for doing the work of the nation? But Lord HARTINGTON forgets that it is rot proposed to abolish the Im- perial Parliament,which as the supreme authority dealing with Imperial affairs would afford ample scope for the higiest capacities of the highest minds. So far frail closing the door to aspiring men, the establshment of four Home Rule Parliaments, sid, by side with an Imperial Parliament, woul open new doors for them-- just as it has bed the case with the formation of County Councils As to the difficulty of having four or five Pirko Ministers, we do not see that that need troubl anyone ; call the heads of the subordinate Parktments Presidents, with powers limited along vr,h the authority of their Parliar ments, and the dfficulty vanishes. "What's in a name ?" The clef officer of the United States is called President; ad it neither takes from his great- ness nor causes cnfusion to have other Presidents who are the chics of the States Legislatures. No; Lord HARTINGTN must find better objections to subordinate Paraments, or he will make no stand against the rap progress which the agitation is making. His retedy is a miserably poor one ; it is to deal with "olctruction"; that is to place another gag upon meratrs of Parliament. But we deny that there has ben any obstruction worth nam- ing. Resistancl to bad measures—such as the Public House idowment Bill—there has been, and must be; lot the Imperial Parliament is, in I these days of sten power, express speed, and ex- tensive divisionof labour, altogether unequal to the enormous anever-increasing,business which it is called upon to •ansact. The congestion is great, and it will be gre,er if something be not done to relieve it. Thaomething, to be permanently effective, should lin the nature of domestic Par- liaments for Eiland, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales; in other Drds, it should be Home Rule all round.

Petroleum has been discovered in France. It is rather hard on our neighbours who were pre- viously only too well supplied with natural gas, and other combustible material.

It was not quite the thing for Mr. P. O'Brien to take a photograph of a witness in court, even when the witness was willing; but only a barbarous Bench of Removables would inflict a punishment of seven days' imprisonment for the oflence. Con- tempt of Court indeed ! How is it possible to have anything but contempt for such a court?

Widnes has adopted the Technical Education Act, and, at a meeting, on Tuesday, of the Runcorn School Board a motion was passed to the effect that the Commissioners be asked to adopt the Act in Runcorn. When is Warrington going to move in the same direction ? It is time that the ques- tion was, at any rate, taken into consideration by the Town Council.

The Tory organ's forecast of the Warrington Municipal Elections showed a total majority of 650. The result showed that the Tories were in a minority of 207. Add the two numbers and it will be seen that this precious forecast was out of of it to the tune of 917 votes ! The Sporting Prophet has his place on some journals; but oh! when he makes such a magnificent mess of it they do make Sport of the Prophet.

The Warrington Conservative Club had, it is rumoured, been converted into quite a magazine of fireworks in view of celebrating the win" all along the line." But instead of victory, there was a crushing defeat ; and so many tears were shed when the results of the elections were made known, that the fireworks were flooded with them, and couldn't or wouldn't go off. [N.B. They are now to be disposed of at an enormous sacrifice; no reasonable offer refused.]

Mr. John White was quite merry, on Thursday night week, over the beating that Mr. Fleming was to have in Town Hall Ward; but, as the event reveals, he was just a trifle "too previous" in sug- gesting that the Liberal candidate must wish to leave the Council, and that he had presented him- self in a ward where he was sure to be defeated. The Conservative candidate was certainly a formid- able opponent; but—ah, these " buts' —he was defeated. There has been a good deal of counting of chickens, not only before they were hatched, but when the eggs were addled.

Mr. Robert Pierpoint, the chairman of the War- rington Conservative Association, talked like a sorrowing parent to naughty children, on Satur- day night. He was very hard on them that they didn't "Work, work, work," as they ought to have done, to win the election. But some of them say that it would have looked a littl3 better if Mr. Robert Pierpoint had himself let them see what it was to "work, work, work." An ounce of example is worth a ton of precept. But what then? It is " pretty Fanny's way.' There was a chairman of the Warrington Conservative Association who knew what it was to work.

Earlestown and Newton are at a disadvantage in having no hospital at their doors; but a first step is being taken in that direction by the forma- tion of the " Earlestown and District Medical and Surgical Aid Society." A good start was made at the public meeting which was held on Tuesday evening, and, with the co-operation of aU classes, there is every prospect of the establishment of a most valuable institution. The medical men of the district are like their brethren in other places in showing themselves anxious to render all the assistance they can.

Birkenhead is in a state of righteous indignation at the mal-administration of its Fever Hospital. Out of twenty-five patients suffering from typhus fever, seven have died. The hospital was in such a bad condition that it became an institution for ostnsing rather than curing disease. A most valu- able lesson is being taught, but at a terrible cost. As Carlyle has it, Experience is a mistress who exacteth high wages, but she teacheth like none other.

Millet, the French artist, had a hard struggle whilst living. He could scarcely at times keep the house door open ; but now that he can paint no more his works are fetching fabulous prices. The world-renowned" Angelus" was sold by him when painted for £72. It has passed through various hands, the price constantly increasing; and has just been re-purchased by a Frenchman for £30,000. Poor Millet! If he could, he would groan in his grave. Somebody has made a fortune out of the picture; but it is not the artist.

£30,000 for a picture! It is absurd, and is worse than absurd—it is morally wrong to spend such a sum in sudi a way. £30,000 laid out at interest is over £l,OOO a year; and £l,OOO a year rightly spent would save life and limb, and lift some who are perishing from the depths of misery. Let M. Chauchard, the purchaser, spend a month amongst the crippled, the destitute, the unemployed of Paris, and then ask himself if he is doing right to himself and his kind, in spending £30,000 on a picture

The Mainley Tariff Bill seems to have cooked the goose of the Protectionists of America. It is damaging them at the elections. Democratic victories have been scored in nearly all the States of the American Union, and the " New York Sun" estimates that there will be a clear working Demo- cratic majority of fifty-three. Mr. Mairiley has been defeated by 244 votes. His success has proved to be his defeat. As the old rhyme has it— He digged a pit: he digged it deep; He digged it for his brother; But for his sin he tumbled in That which was digged for t'other.

The Rector of Warrington keeps quietly pegging away at some of the black spots of the town. Speaking at the Parish Church Temperance meet- ing, on Monday evening, he saidhe "looked forward to the time when they would have wider streets, better gas, and a clear atmosphere, and when War- rington would be a sober town." If the Rector had been a candidate and had made this ,his platform, he would certainly have been returned. He does well to touch on these points. He speaks of that which he doth know and testifies of that which he hath seen; and all good citizens say Amen.

Dr. Barnard° does not come well out of the in- quiry as to whether the boy M'Hugh should be given up by him to his mother in order to be brought up in the Catholic faith. According to the decision of the Court of the Queen's Bench, he seems to have made a "scandalous attack" on the character of the mother in order to put himself in a position to keep possession of the son. But he has overshot his mark; the boomerang has returned and struck him. The ruling has gone against him, as "it was evident he was not fit to have the custody of the boy." There will be another, appeal of course, and as much money will be spent in deter- mining whether this one boy shall be Protestant or Catholic as would build another Home. When will there be an end of this shameful sectarianism in connection with public charities?

THE WORKING CLASS AND CHURCH ATTENDANCE. Archdeacon Farrar lately admitted that in Eng- land not 5 percent. of the working classes are com- municants, and not 10 per cent regularly attend zeligiousservices. That statement has excited great i surprise n Wales, where the circumstances of the case are so different, that when, on the occasion of the Congregational Union meeting at Swansea, it was imposed to hold a meeting for the benefit of working-men—as is usual when the Union meets in England—it was locally objected to, on tll/2e ground that in Wales the working-classes are within, and not outside, the churches, and therefore there :was no need for a special meeting for their benefit. In proof of this it is stated that there were more work- ing-men in attendance at the Union meetings than at any previoussessir. And this highly satisfac- tory state of things is due not to the existence of an Established Church, but to the existence of that Nonconformity which it is being sought to weaken, if not to destroy.—" The Liberator.' SHOCKING FATALITY AT WIGAN. A boy named Cooper, residing at 4, Birkett Bank. Wigan, died on Monday evening. The de- ceased was running with pieces of umbrella wire in his mouth, when he ran against a wall, pushing the wire down his throat. lie succumbed to his injuries shortly afterwards. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston, Phaadeldhia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan. Aus- tralia, or New Zonland, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner " Oliz, by Cunard, Gino% American, and other lines.— John Walker, ;tgent. Examiner (Mice, I3ewsey-st., Warrington.—Ativt.

CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES AND APPRENTICES. Mr. Justice Hawkins and Air. Justice Stephen, in the Queen's Bench on Thursday, decided in the case of the Burnley Equitable Co-operative Society v. Casson, that a co-operative society could employ an apprentice in the same way as an individ alai trades- man.

THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES. The canvass of the ratepayers of Widnes with respect to the incorporation of the town has been completed, and the result shows a very large majo- rity in favour of applying for a charter of incor- poration, anl at the monthly meeting on Tues- day next, the General Purposes Committee will re- commend that that course be adopted. The figures will not be made public until that meeting. Reis WATER SWAnATon.—Agent, J. S. Garland, Iron- monger, Warrington .--Advt,
RUNCORN POLICE coma. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. A. Thomag.

.... DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence A boatman named Robert Garner, was fined ss. and costs ; and Teresa Riley and George Jones were each fined ss. and costs. OBSCENE LANGIAGE. —James Jones for using obscene language was fined ss. and costs. A SLEEPY CARTEL—George Astle, a carter in the employ of Messrs. Greenall, brewers, was charged with being asleep while in charge of a horse and dray. The reins were dragging underneath the horses' feet.—A fine of 20s. and costs was inflicted.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. T. S. Timmis and Col. Gaskill. FOOTBALL IN THE STREET.—A number of boys were summoned for playing football in the street and each defendant was fined is. and costs. CHIMNEY ON Fira.—For this offence John Wood, Milton-st., was fined is. and costs, 43. 6d. HIGHWAY OFFENCE.—A tine of ss. and costs was im- posed upon Gordon Cummings, carter, St. Helens, for being asleep in his cart at Dittom—Edward Piercy, Victoria-st., Widnes. was summoned for not having a name on his cart and he was fined ss. and costs. Smoot BOARD CAsEs.—A number of parents were summoned by the School Board for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was inflicted in each case. DRUNKENNESS.—FOF this offence James Hyland, Mary Horan, James Grey, John Howard, and Thos. Tomlin- son, were each fined ss. and costs.—Mary Jane Riley, made her 21st appearance, and was fined 103. and Cods. PAYING FOR HIS FUN—John Deacon, Gladstone-street, was charged with stealing a silver brooch valued at 55., from the Rose and Crown Hotel, the property of Jane Tilley.—On Wednesday the prisoner visited theliotel, and when he left the brooch was missed. Afterwards he was apprehended by P.C. Cummings, who found the brooch in his pocket. The prisoner said he only took it "in a bit of fun." He was fined 20s. iticluding costs. TRESPASS.—WiIIiarn Booth, Ditton, was summoned for trespassing on a field belonging to James Bridge, farmer, and he was fined ss. and costs.

ASSUALT AT DITTON.—James Lee, of Ditton, was sum- moned for assaulting Bridget Feeley, on the 4th inst. Mr. Knowles defended. Mrs. Feeley went to the defend- ant's house to fetch her husband, and, whilst she was en- deavouring to get him out, the defendant, she alleged, struck her on the face and gave her a black eye. Evidence was called to prove that that the woman's husband struck the blow, and the defendant was dismi:csed. TIIkFT BY A SERVANT.—Elizabeth E. Hesketh, domestic servant, 17 years of age, of Vine-street, Widnes, was charged with stealing a gold ring worth 285., the property of her master, Franz Kistamann, Pitville-terrace, Ditton. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and she was Rued 20a. and costs, the Bench not desiring to send her to gaol.

parent society for 1889 was £125,621 6s. 101, and the expenditure -£128,672 14s 7d., leaving a deficiency of £3,051 7s. 9d. This deficiency had been covered by an excess of the annual average for legacies, and the debt of last year had been thereby reduced by the sum of £BlB 13s. id., and now stood at £8,563. In Runcorn the following amounts had been collected for the current year :-St. Paul's Chapel on previous day, £ll 17s. Od. ; Camden Chapel, 10s. 7d. ; by Mr. Soulby, £8 18s. Od. ; Miss Speakman. £6 9s. 68. ; Miss Norman, £lO Bs. 68.; Miss Simister, £lO 10s. 6d. ; Miss Crosby, £5 17s. 6d. ; Camden Schools, boys, £8 3s. 111 d. ; girls, £4 16s. Thd.; collected by books, £l2 12s. 3d. The total amount for Camden Scho,ls including collections in schools was £26 9s. 5,1 d. (Applause.) In Brunswick School there was collected by girls in classes. £4 19s. ; by boys, £7 ss. Sd. ; boys with books, £l9 lie. Id. ; girls, £l7 15s. 6d.; total for Brunswick School, £63 Os. 3d. (Applause.) The total received up to that meeting was £144 is. 38.-(applause)-which included the previous ! day's collections, a total which he was sorry to say showed a decrease of £23 Os. 7d. on last year, when the collections rose higher than they had ever done before.- The Chairman in his opening speech referred to the report as interesting and encourag,ing,and remarked that he 'did not think there was any part of Christian work that had such claims upon the young people as their missions abroad as well as at home. If they were spared to a great age they could not have a better reflec- tion than that of the good they had been the means of doing to those who were living beyond the reach and light of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. (Hear, hear.) Allud- ing, to the amount raised in Runcorn, he expressed his surprise that the amount had decreased because trade was good and he had expected they would eclipse their former efforts. Ile pointed out that in missionary work the sin of drunkenness was a great barrier to all their enterprise and exertions, and said he did not care on what side of politics a man took his stand, hut if neither Party were prepared to remove the evil of drink from our land then the religious men of the country should rise to the occasion. (Applause.) Let them con- sider that if all the churches in Runcorn were to unite together and say that they would not have that evil that was doing such injury, and they would soon be free from the curse which brought poverty and starvation into houses which might be made bright and beautiful. (Applause). As religious people they had never the power to do that and if they only arrived at that purpose, they would have such a wave of missionary spirit spreading throughout the world that would make itself felt. (Applause.) The Rev. James Lewis (deputation) then delivered an interesting speech on the work of the Society in various lands and the good results obtained, and remarked that the present aspect of affairs was highly encouraging:-Die Rev. Smith Spencer (deputation), described his experience of 12 years in South Africa and said the work done there would stand investigation. There was really little known of the work which was being done in the Foreign Mission field ; but he was there to definitely declare that the statement made that the nearer they got to the mission field, the more unatisfactory the work appeared to be, was utterly false. If South Africa was true to her mission, she would be able to provide to a large extent men who enter on Missionary work right up to the equator. They wanted to spend in South Africa £50,000 a year more than they were spending to-day, and if they would hold their posi- tion in Central Africa as they held South Africa as the foremost of Christian Churches. If their Church was true to its ancestry and true to its responsibilities, and above all true to its Master she would take the front place in the evangelization of Africa. (Applause.)-The Rev. H. Burson announced that Mrs. Thomas Hazlehurst had forwarded £5. (Applause.)-On the proposition of Mr. P. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Unsvvorth, a vote of thanks was accorded to the deputation.-Mr. J. R. Frith was appointed treasurer, and Mr. T. Sinister secre- tary. The collections for the evening amounted to £44 Os. 78. During the evening, the choir rendered several specially selected pieces of music in creditable style, Master Musgrove being at the organ.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse on Thursday afternoon. There were present Mr. J. W. Wareing (chairman), Revs. S. A. K. Sylveter, C. W. Wooll, and Dean Finegan, Messrs. W. Tyre; J. Leatherbarrow. J. Marsh, Lowe, E. Birchall, J. Mercer, Davies, J. Birchall, Griffiths, Kenwright, J. 13urchall, Johnson, Middlehurst, Syder, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). INMATES.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 525 inmates this week, 516 last week, and 530 in the corresponding week last year. A WOOLTON APPOINTMENT.—Mr. R. G. Waterman, was re-appointed School Attendance and School Fees Inquiry Officer for the Woolton district at a salary of :280 per annum. .

RAINRILL ASYLUM.—Dr. Wiggleworth, medical super- intendent of Rainhill Asylum, wrote that the Committee of visitors had desired him to inform the Board that the female division of the Asylum was now full and the accommodation available would henceforth be limited to the vacancies occasioned by discharges and deaths.— Mr.Middlehurst rose to say a few words upon the subject, and was referring to what had transpired at a meeting of the Toxteth Board of Guardians,when it was explained that the subject was out of order. CONTRIBUTION ORDERS.—It was decided to issue con- tribution orders on the overseers of the townships wi bin the Union, for the payment of a total sum of £24,429. It was stated that the orders had been prepared in accordance with the estimates adopted in August last. This was the principal business.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present : Rev. J. W. N. TanuerXessrs. Grice,Taylor, P. Speakman, C. C. Lewis Brandreth, Heywood, Smith, W. Whitlow, J. Whitlow, Parr, Pickering. Aaron, Stokes, 11. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).
