div.p: LOCAL NEWS
RUNCORN AND WIDNES,

UNIVERSITY LECTURES AT RUNCORN. The fourth of the series of lectures on political economy will be delivered on Thursday evening next in Bethesda Lecture Hall, by Mr. Llewllyn Smith B.A. B.Sc. The subject for that evening's consideration will be " Rent, Interest, Profits. and Wages. FINEST KIEL Iturritn,i one shilling per pc:aim-I.—lmperial Tea Co.—Advt. ST. JOHNS' AMBULANCE CLASS AT RUNCORN. The success of the Ambulance class last winter has emboldened the promoters to carry on the instruction during the coming season. The first class will be held next week and Dr. McDougall will resume the position of lecturer. Police Clerk Bullock is the secretary. FINEST KIEL BUTTER, one shilling per pound.—lmperial Tea Co.—Advt.

VENETIAN BAZAAR AT RUNCORN. In aid of the fund of building the chancel of St. Michael's Church, Runcorn, a bazaar will he held in Run- corn Public Hall, on Wednesday, and the three following evenings. The attractions for the visitors will be numer- ous and novel. Particulars are given in our advertising columns. C lITCHLEY. Practical Tailor. Bold-st., Warrin zton.—Advt.

SWINE FEVER IN RUNCORN DISTRICT. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Thomas Hen- derson pleaded guilty to moving ten pigs, into a swine fever infected area—from Frodsham to Warrington— without the necessary license.—P.S. Costello said he had previously warned the defendant who,on the other hand; protested that he did not know hills were posted. A fine of 20s. and costs 15s. was imposed. NAUTILUS GRATES.—SoIe agent, Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warriugton.—Advt.

TRAP ACCIDENT AT SUTTON. On Wednesday evening, as Mr. Richard Holcroft, Mr. John !Bate, and Mr. Ralph Tickle, were driving through Sutton, the trap came in contact with the cor- ner of an orchard, and the occupants were thrown into the road. Mr. Holcroft was severely cut above the left eye, and was taken to Mr. Robinson's surgery where his injuries were attended. The others escaped without serious injury. UMBRELLAS RE-cow:RED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Saakev-st.. Warrington.—Adet. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN. Before Major Haziehurst and Dr. Steele at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, George Bartlett, was charged with Wing drunk and disorderly and also with assault- ing P.C. Jones. On Friday evening the prisoner arrived at Runcorn Railway Station and refused to give up his ticket. P.C. Jones arrived on the scene and apprehended the prisoner, who kicked and struck the officer in a vio- lent manlier. He was secured and taken to the police station. In default of paying the total sum of £l7s. 41. fine and costs, he was sent to goal for 21 days. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Adet.

EXTENSIVE THEFTS EY A WOMAN AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mary Rafferty, of no fixed abode was charged with having stolen four aprons worth 4s. 6d. from the shop of Miss E. Marshall, draper, Widnes-road; also with having stolen 6ilbs of beef, value 3s. 6d. from the shop of Archibald Knox, butcher, Albert-road; and further with stealing 3ilbs of boiled ham and a currant loaf, worth is. 6d., from the shop of Benjamin Thompson; grocer, Widnes-road.—P.C. Messenger apprehended the prisoner with the articles in her possession, and she said she had been drunk and had no knowledge of the things. She was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. FINEST KIEL BUTTER, one shilling per pound.—lmperial Tea Co.-4 dvE.

div.head: ROBBF3RY FROM Tam PERSON AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ROBBF3RY FROM Tam PERSON AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Police Court, Mary Riley, of Marsh-st., was charged with haying stolen a purse containing £lO and a gold ring from the person of Geo. Harrison. of 2, White-st. Martin Farracher, labourer, was charged with haying been concerned in tha robbery. On Sunday night Harrison met Riley in Pitt-st., and went with her in an entry behind Wellington-st. Whilst there he missed his purse and he charged the woman with stealing it. She called " Darky " and it was alleged that Farracher came and put himself in a fight- ing attitude and helped the woman to escape. On the application of Superintendent Nobblett the prisoners were remanded. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adet.

ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court on Saturday, Susannah Beans, a tramp from Wolverhampton, was charged with steal- ing a shilling belonging to John Miller. On Thursday the prisoner walked into Miller's house for the purpose of begging and when she left a shilling was missed from the table. The prisoner was arrested and the shilling, wrapped in a piece of linen, was found concealed upon her. She was sentenced to 14 days hard labour.—At the same court George Smith was charged with stealing a knife from the Masonic Hotel, Devonshire-square. On Friday the prisoner was supplied with a plate of bread and cheese and after he had eaten it he walked away with the knife he had been using. He was apprehended by P.C. Woodrow and was now sentenced to 14 days hard labour. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—d. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WOUNDING CASES AT WIDNES. Thomas O'Neil was brought before the Widnes magis- trates on Thursday to answer a charge of having unlaw- fully wounded his son, aged seven, by beating him about the head and body with the buckle end of a strap. The circumstances of the case have been previously re- ported. The prisoner was again remanded, as Dr. Hutchinson, the principal witness, could not attend through illness. It was stated that the boy was now out of danger.—For a similiar reason John Mullarky, labourer, of Sankey-st., was remanded on a charge of stabbing Charles McLoughlin. The prisoner lodged with McLoughlin and on Saturday, when the latter told him he could not stay in the house any longer, he pulled out his pocket knife and stabbed McLoughlin on the arm; Inflicting a wound which bled very freely. McLoughlin had since been seriously ill .—Benjamin Davies, Mid- wood-st., was charged on remand with having caused grievous bodily harm to Michael Brennan on the 25th ult. The prisoner and his wife had a quarrel in the Derby Arms and on leaving, the prosecutor asked the prisoner what he had been doing to his wife, when the prisoner struck him a blow on the head with something he had in his hand.—Dr. O'Beeffe said the wound was circular in shape half an inch in diameter and penetrated to the bone. A piece of flesh was hanging from the wound. The prisoner fainted twice in his surgery through loss of blood.—When apprehended, the prisoner pulled the mouthpiece of a brass musical instrument from his pocket and said: This is what I did it with.— He was committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J.l W. Durrox's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. GREAT FARM Ftniz IN CHESHIRE. An extensive fire was discovered, on Monday night, on the farm of Mr. Boffey, Actbn, near Nantwich. The farm buildings were ablaze, lighting up the country for miles round. A large quantity of hay, corn, and fodder, valued at several hundred pounds. was destroyed. The fire is believed to have been caused by tramps going into an outbuilding, and lighting their pipes. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—l. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey•st., Warrington.—Advt. MR. RYLA NDS'S CORRESPONDENCE. The" Pall Mall Gazette" says :—" The letters of Mr. Peter Rylands, which his son has so rashly and unjutifiably publish ed,h ave given the greatest pos- sible annoyance to the correspondents of the late member for B urnley. It is this fact, no doubt, which has created a considerable demand fora book not otherwise of interest. Mr. Rylands's flu has, it is said, been already threatened with injunctions from three different quarters." THE ROYAL MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL, &C., AGRI-

div.head: CULTURA L. SOCIETY.
div.p: CULTURA L. SOCIETY.

The adjourned general meeting of the members of the above society was held at the Lion Hotel on Monday. The chair was occupied by Mr. George Dickson, of Chester. There was a small attendance. A letter was read from the Town Clerk of Bury (in which town the next show will be held), who ex- pressed his sorrow at being unable to'be present at this meeting, but he added that he would ask the Mayor to attend. Immediately after the elections were over, he purposed calling a town's meeting to appoint a local Committee. He thought it would be advisable for the secretary to be present. He had received a number of local subscriptions. • Lord Derby had promised .£lOO, and Sir Henry James £5O. (Applause.) The Chairman announced that two gentlemen who were appointed vice-presidents at the last meeting had declined to serve, namely. Mr. T. H. Miller and Mr. Fitzherbert Brockholes. After some discussion it was decided to fill up the vacancies thus created at a subsequent meeting of the society.—Mr. Beck (Wigan) drew attention to a printed list of members of the society, and ob- served that there were about 100 defaulters among them. Names of gentlemen appeared on the list who, he had been informed, had not been members of the societycfor six years.—The Chairman informed the meeting that the Secretary was attending to the matter, and had already commenced to revise the list of members. It Was decided that the list be revised at the next meeting of the Council.—Messrs. J. Hammill (St. Helens), G. and J. Tunstall (War- rington), and S. Jude (Liverpool) were separately proposed as auditors of the societV for the next year, and the voting resulted in Mr. Hatnmill being elected.—Mr. llalsall, at the close of the meeting, read a telegram he had received from Mr. Fairhurst, of Wigan, offering a prize of ten guineas for shire mares, the property of bona-fide tenant farmers in the society's district. The offer was received with applause. The revision of the prize list was referred to a committee. OR/TCHLEY, Practical Tailor, Bold-st.,Warrington.—Adr4.

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

The Runcorn Musical Society opened their season on Tuesday evening in the Runcorn Public Hall. That the efforts of the officers and committee of the Society in seeking to provide concerts, illustrative of the choicest musical excepts, were appreciated, was fully demonstrated by the large and fashionable I audience; and the excellent rendering of the various numbers elicited from the critical assembly frequent and genuine applause. The principals secured for the occa- sion were Madame Clara Samuell, who more than sus- tained the reputation gained during former visits to Runcorn. She rendered her songs with great purity of voice and felicity of expression. At the conclusion of each song she received an encore, and to several of the encores she gracefully responded. Mr. E. Grime was , also in good voice, and sang the songs allotted to him in such a masterly manner as to carry away his audi- tory, and in response to repeated calls he bowed his acknowledgements. The Committee were fortunate in the selection of a full orchestra, containing many execut- ants of acknowledged and exceptional ability, and the well-nigh faultless manner in which they rendered the orchestral items, justifies the assertion that their per- formance fully maintained, and, in general, excelled all , previous similar efforts in connection with the Society. The choral numbers were given in splendid style, "The Soldiers Chorus" from " Faust," with orchestral accom- paniment being especially effective. . "The Comrades Song of Hope," was capitally rendered. "The Belfry Tower" and "Good Night Beloved," were unaccompanied and the attention to light and shade evidenced careful training and a considerable degree of musical culture.— Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, the honorary conductor, de- serves the highest credit for providing such a rich musical treat, and the state of efficiency displayed under his direc- tion,by both band and chorus,augurs well for the produc- tion during the season, of Handel's " Messiah "and Men- delssohns's "Elijah," for which the services of the same orchestra have been secured. The full programme was as follows :—Madame Samuel! "Rose softly blooming," (Spohr)" Nymphs and shepherds," (Purcell); " Ye banit and braes." Mr. Grime, " Thou'rt passing hence," (Sullt- van) ; "Oh hear the wild wind blow," (Mattel) ; " Off to Philadelphia," ( Haines.) The Choral Items were "Soldier's Chorus," (Gounod) ; "Comrade's song of hope," (Adams) ; " The belfry tower," (Hatton) ; "Good night beloved," (Pins-uti). The Orchestral Selections consiated of ovartures to " Masaniello," (Aaber) ; and " William Tell," (Rossini) ; selections from Gounod's " Faust ;" Cellier's "Dorothy ; and " Invitation to the Waltz," (Weber.)

RUNCORN SCHOOL ROARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Rev. Canon Wood presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Taylor and Howitt, with Mr. G. Moss (clerk.) • - • --

SCHOOL MANAGEMENT: INCREASES OF SALARY. The School Management Committee reported that eight applications were received for the post of assistant mistress at Greenway-road School, and the blowing were selected candidates to meet the Board : Miss Price, Stoke-on-Trent, Miss Parker, Ulverston, Miss Swales, Rotherham, The 'Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. J. F. Moulton, headmaster at Greenway-road Boys 'Schools,be advanced to £lBO per annum; that the salary of E. W. Rosser, assistant teacher at Greenway-road be advanced to £55 per annum ; that the salary of Miss Simkin, certificated assistant at Greenway-road Board Schools be advauced to £6O per annum. The Clerk submitted an estimate of the revenue of the evening school for the session up to the end of March next showing a total income of £49 from fees and grant. In addition to Mr. J. F. Moulton, the headmaster, the following assistant teachers had been obtained for the evening classes : Messrs. R. H. Jarvis, E. W. Epps, and E. W. Rosser.

div.head: TEgIINICAL EDUCATION.
div.p: TEgIINICAL EDUCATION.

Mr. Hewitt moved that the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners be asked to adopt the Technical Instruc- tion Act, 1889. It had been applied for in other towns in England. If government found people were careless about the higher education of the community, they would no doubt withdraw the money.—The Chairman: I shall be glad to recond the motion.—Dr. Gastaldi said perhaps if the Act were adopted it would involve the great expense of building a technical school. Mr. Howitt said according to the Act not more than one penny in the £ could be' spent. They need not build schools' they could do much as they were doing at the present time in their own schools. In reply to Mr. Taylor, the Chairman explained that if the Commissioners adopted the Act they might appoint the School Board to carry out its provisions, or appoint a special committee on the lines of the Free Library Comraittee.—The motion I was carried unanimously.

WESLEYAN HOME AND FOREIGN MISSIONS. MEETING AT RUNCORN. The annual services in aid of the Wesleyan Home and Foreigh Missionary Society were held on Sun- day, and were attended by crowded congregations. At St. Paul's Chapel the preacher was the Rev. James Lewis, of Manchester ; and at Camden Chapel the Rev. W. Kendrew preached in the morning, and Mr. S. Coventry in the evening. On Monday even- ing the annual meeting was held in St. Paul's Chapel, when a large audience assembled, but was scarcely so numerous as usual, owing to the stormy weather that prevailed. Mr. Robert Shaw, formerly of Runcorn, pre- sided, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs. IL Burson, W. Kendrew, Joseph Lewis (of Manchester), and Smith Spencer (ex-President of the South African Conference) ; Messrs. J. Simpson, P. Speakman, C.C., F. J. Norman, J. R. Frith, F. Taylor, B. Kniveton, J. Uns- worth, and T. Simister (secretary).—Mr. Simister read the annual report, which stated that the income of the

div.head: TYPHOID TETER CASE.
div.p: THE TYPHOID TETER CASE.

In regard to the man who was removed to the Workhouse Hospital a fortnight ago and died next day, Dr. McDougall wrote to the clerk as follows :---I am in receipt of yours of the 22nd inst. With 'reference to the first paragraph of yourletter, I have no reason what- ever to alter my opinion as regards the correctness of the diagnosis in the case mentioned. From the information which I possess I have no doubt that the case was cor- rectly described in my report as " gastritis," conse- quently was not a case for the Infectious Hospital. With reference to the latter part of your fourth paragraph. I certainly have a doubt whether it is my duty to attend parish patients at the Commissioners Infectious Hospital, and will be glad if you will submit the matter to the Local Government Board.—The Clerk said he had written to the Local Government Board, but he had received no reply.

. TEE RELIEF OF TRAMPS. Mr. Aaron then moved the resolution of which he had given notice, that an assistant relieving officer be ap- pointed for Runcorn, at a salary of £8 a year, and that the Chief Constable be asked to allow the police to take the position.—Mr. Aaron pointed out that since Mr. Ward was appointed relieving officer, Clifton and Rock- savage had been taken from Mr. Riley's district, and added to Runcorn, and then there was added to his other duties that of dealing with the vagrants which had previously been managed by the police. No difference was made in Mr. Ward's salary for this extra duty, and ho thought he had bean hardly dealt with, and at all hours of the night was called from his bed to attend to tramps. During the last 18 months the police had the appointment they found 50 tramps with lodgings, and sent 40 people to the House—total 90. Darin.. the last 13 inoltlis Mr. Ward had had it, he had found 158 beds in Runcorn and had ' sent 147 people to the house—total 303.—Mr. Parr : Cheaper to let the police have it.—Mr. Lewis said it was not. The difference was between 203 fourpences and £B.—Mr. Speaktnan seconded the motion, and said the story they had just heard was quite sufficient argument.—Mr. Grice supported the motion.—Mr. Whitlow contended that the practice would drive all the tramps to Preston Brook, and hundreds more would be sent to the Workhouse.—Mr. Lewis said he knew plenty of honest men that applied Un- a night's lodgings, and these would not like to apply to the police for an order.—Mr. Taylor said the figures presented by Mr. Aaron were conclusive. Mr. Smith opposed ther metion strongly and said the greatest part of the poor rates was paid in salaries to officials.—Mr. Aaron thought Mr. Smith was offering a gross insult to the officials. He explained that he had brought this motion forward because the tramp wards at the house were full, and if some measures were not taken, they would have to be enlarged. The motion was car- ried by eleven votes to nine.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also pre- sent, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, J. Whit- low, Lewis, Smith, Pickering, Brandreth, Parr, W. Whitlow, Heywood, Stokes, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and J. Farrington (inspector.) INEFFICIENT WA.TER SUPPLY. ' A letter was read from the Local Government Beard who said they had had under their consideration the annual report of the Medical Officer for 1889. Adyertina, to the remarks as the necessity for an improved supply of water for Frodsham, Helsby, Dutton, Halton Common,' Norley, Bartington Budworth, Clifton, the Board asked what action the Authority had taken or proposed to take in regard to each of these places.—Mr. Stokes said there was now a good supply of water at Clifton, and he did not think there :was a lot of houses so completely supplied.—Mr. Aaron confirmed this statement.—Mr. Brandreth said the supply at Helsby had always been good and was now. There were only one or two points. The medical Officer said it was the distribution of the water at Helsby which wasthe difficulty.—Mr. Brandreth said the Frodsham Gas and Water Company, had the same power to supply Helsby as they had Frodsham, and they had done nothing.—The Inspector said at Halton Common there were a number of cottages which had not a supply at a reasonable distance. The property belonged to Sir Richard Brooke and nothing had

been done yet. The notice had been served upon Sir Richard Brooke. He had a schema for supplying Dutton if it met with the approval of the owners. It would have to be a joint affair between the whole of the owners and if they could not agree, it would be the duty of the Au- thority to deal with the matter and charge the owners. The supply to Norley was the worst in the district, and it was a very difficult matter to deal with. He had had two or three meetings but had not been able to decide on a scheme. He had it in hand. At Bartington, a pump had been put up for some time. In answer to Mr. Aaron, the Inspector said the cottages at Halton Com- mon fetched water from a well in the Park, and the nearest cottage was 350 yards away. He could not say how far the most distant was away.—The Inspector was instructed to present a report to the next meeting.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DVSTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DVSTRICT.

The Medical Officer re—ported a case of diptheria at Stockton Heath. Defects in drainage were found to exist, caused by a cesspool which had not been properly cleaned out. This had now been abolished and the drainage connected with the main sewer. A case of typhoid fever had also occurred at Stockton Heath. It was difficult to account for this case. No sanitary defects were found and the water was derived from the Warrington mains. Another case of typhoid fever had occurred at Overton. Some defects of drainage had been remedied. Two cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Frodsham and also at Preston Brook. He had visited all the cases and had issued the actual instructions.

THE SHIP CANAL AND SEWEILIGE.—AN INJUNCTION SOUGHT. The following correspondence was read :—On October 21st, Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, solicitors to the Authority, wrote as follows to Messrs Grundy, Kershaw and Co.. solicitors to the Ship Canal Co. :—Referring to your letter of the Bth inst. and to ours of the 13th we beg to inform you that at the meeting of the Committee appointed to deal in this matter yester- day, we were instructed to say that the Authority I claim an ancient right of sewering into Folly Brook at Weston and so into the river Mersey and that the existing arrangement with the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners is only a temporary one, that this was explained to the Company's engineer months ago and that now we are told to make some arrangement with the Commissioners which the Authority declines to do. We were further to say, that the Authority insists upon their ancient right being protected and a separate outfall made into the River Mersey and that until the agreement is completed the Authority objects to any interference with any of their sewers and outfalls and that if their requirements be not agreed to by 3rd of November proceedings will be taken to prevent the Com- pany from further interfering with the sewers and out- falls."—ln reply Messrs Kershaw wrote :—" We are very much suprised with the tone of your letter of the 21st which we submit is altogether uncalled for. We have not attempted to debate to the Authority and to tell them to make some arrangement as 3iou state. What we did was to ask that your clients should make the arrange- ments if they required them as they were in so much better position to do it than we are. We have sent your letter to the engineer Iwho as you are aware has carried through the negotiations in this matter.—Messrs. Linaker replied as follows :—We have received your letter and are glad to hear that (although the paragraph in your previous letter certainly read as if you repudiated the responsibility of making arrangements for the Folly Brook Sewer) you did not intend the authority to under- stand that they must make their own arrangements with the Runcorn Commissioners outside the Company. We understand that the Commissioners absolutely decline to allow us a perpetual right through the outfall, and we shall be glad to hear from you after Mr. Williams has had time to consider the :matter.—The Clerk said no further communication hat been received. On the same subject of sewers, Clifford Smith, estate agent, Runcorn, wrote that the Bridgewater Trustees had recently sold some of their land at Wilderspool, fronting the new road from near Twenty Step Bride to near Tom Paynes Bridge, and the persons who had bought the land and erected property complained that there was no outlet sewer provided by the Rural Sanitary Authority. It was absolutely requisite for sanitary purposes, that the sewer should be carried away. On receiving the letter the Clerk wrote to the Ship Canal Company and Mr. Leader Williams replied that they had not been able to get the consent of the Warrington Cor- poration to carry the Stockton Beath sewer into the new river diversion, and as they were not proceeding with the Warrington Dock until after the completion of the Canal, there would not be any interference with the Authority's sewers for some considerable time.—Mr. Aaron said month after month was passing away, and the Ship Canal Company would do nothing.—The Clerk said that the Ship Canal Company had no right to touch any sewer until they had provided another.—Mr. Aaron: They have done.—The Clerk: Oh, yes; and he pointed out the inconvenience and difficulty created through this interference.—The Chairman said the Autho- rity must make a stand, as it was a very important mat- ter.—Mr. Brandreth : What action can we take P—The Clerk: Apply for an injunction to restrain the company from interfering with the sewers.—Mr. Stokes: Will the expense be paid by the Ship Canal Company 2—The Clerk: Whoever pays the expense, you must do it. It is provided for in the Act that all the expenses shall be paid by the Ship Canal Com pany.—Mr.Brandreth moved, and Mr. J. Whitlow seconded that the Committee apply for an injunction to restrain the company from interfer- ing with the sewers of the Union.—The motion was car- ried unanimously.

div.head: Tllll POLLUTION OF ICNIIIIWICH BROOK.
div.p: Tllll POLLUTION OF ICNIIIIWICH BROOK.

Mr. Aaron inquired if there was any communication from the Local Government Board on the subject. The Clerk replied in the negative.—Mr. Aaron said when the Guardians delayed the Local Government Board quickly found fault, and now the Local Government Board were dalliying month after month with the important matter, and the farmers still ran the risk of losing their cattle. Ho thought they ought to turn about and ask the Local Government Board if they were doing their duty.—Mr. Parr: I beg to second that. —The Clerk: I suppose you mean that I must write and tell them the matter is pressing.—Mr. Aaron: You must write and tell them all I have said. (Laughter.)—The Clerk: I must ask you to put it in the form of a resolution.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: POACHING AT STOCKHAM.
div.p: POACHING AT STOCKHAM.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Thomas, Joseph Foster and Joseph Hallman, of Frodsham Bridge, was charged with coming from land at Stockham, when it was suspected they had been in pursuit of game, they having in their possession certain game which had been unlawfully obtained in addition to nets and pegs used for the purpose of taking game. A man named John Mercer, of the same place was charged with aiding and abetting. Foster pleaded guilty and the other defendants were defended by Mr. Burton—ln- spector Bowyer deposed that about three o'clock on the morning of the 18th ult., he saw Foster and Hallman running towards the direction of Hallwood from the ' direction of Northwich-road. On seeing witness and ' other officers Foster dropped a bag which it was after- wards found contained a net and pegs and Hallman I dropped 18 rabbits which he was carrying and ran away like a grey hound. Foster was captured by P.C. Fryer and three pegs were found in his pockets.—P.C. Fryer and P.C. Brew corroborated and stated the defendants threw stones at them.—Witnesses were called to prove that Hallman never left home that night and Foster denied that the other defendants were with him. In reply to Superintendent Large, Foster said he worked the net himself although it was 60 yards in length.—The Bench considered the case proved, and fined each defendant 40s. and costs or a month's imprison- ment. The nets and pegs were forfeited.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor, the chairman, presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., . Fisher, J. Pritchard, W. Timmins, H. J. Once, F. Wiswall, J. Dobson, P. Smith, W. Hankinson, E. W. Humphreys, F. A. Lake,/ Law Clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. 31cDougall (medical officer) M. Barker (surveyor).
TEE DEATH RATE.

The Medical Officer reported that during October there were 38 deaths registered, of which four were inquest cases, of the remaining 34, four were due to bronchitis, three typhoid fever, two heart disease, two cancer, two natural decay, three rheumatism and three to mesente- ric disease. The death rate was 25.3.

NEW PROPERTY. The minutes of the Highway and Buildings Committee I contained the following recommendations :—That the plans of Mr. James Kirkham for the erection of four cot- tages in Picow-st. and seven cottages in Byron-st., sub- ject to the passage being made four feet wide instead of three feet as shown on the Glan ; planof the Manchester Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater undertaking) for the erection of a house in Heath-road ; plans of Mr. John J. Waterworth for the erection of three houses in Greenway- road and three houses in Victoria-road, subject to a four foot passage instead of three feet.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Fisher. THE FIRE BRIGADE. On the recommendation of the Canal, Boats, and General Purposes Committee, the offer of Mr. H. Jackson for the hire of horses in connection with fires on the following terms be accepted: two horses 4s. 6d. per mile and 4s. per hour waiting; three horses 6s. per mile and ss. per hour waiting; four horses Ss. per mile and 7s. per hour waiting. FINANCE.
The Finance Committee reported that the receipts amounted to £l7O, and accounts amounting to £495 13s. —The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Light- burn. _ _
A GRANT TO THE LAW CLERK.

In the absence of Mr. Imison, chairman of the Finance Committee, Mr. Lightburn moved" That resolutio n No, 1160 dealing with the Law Clerk's duties and salary be amended, by adding the following words after tbe words "Parliamentary business "—" But the Law Clerk may charge for work incidental to the preparation of con- tracts where the parties contract'bing with the Commis- sioners pay the costs thereof, and may also in case of legal proceedings recover costs from the parties opposed to the Commissioners. That the consent of the Local

Government gottrd be obtained to a grant of MO to the Law Clerk for extra services (to be enumerated in letter), and that such sum be paid on such consent being ob- tained "—Mr. Lightburn said during the last 12 or 18 months the work of the Law Clerk's department had been very much increased in consequence of the development of the town. The number of contracts with the Ship Canal, in connection with Waterloo Bridge, &c., had been very numerous indeed.—The Secretary gave full details of the extra work, and said had it been charged for in the ordinary way,the amount would have been consider- ably ever a hundred pounds.—Mr. Fisher seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: FREE HOSPITAL.
div.p: A FREE HOSPITAL.

The Health Committee re-cOrnMerided that Mrs.E. A. Whitby, of 6, Peel-st., Runcorn, be appointed nurse and caretaker at the hospital, at a salary at the rate of LI per week whilst engaged in nursing; to have the use of the house free of rent and rates, and to be provided with coal, water, and oil. The appointment to be sub- ject to termination on one month's notice being given on either side. That notices be served on certain property owners' set forth in the Sanitary Inspector's report book, to abate nuisances by substituting glazed earthenware stench traps for the brick traps now in use, and in the event of noncompliance with any of such notices that legal proceedings be taken.—Mr. Lightburn Moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr.Dobson said now they had appointed a nurse at the hospital, he hoped the Board would see the advisability of making the hospital free. His experience during the past few years was that had the hospital been free, a number of people suffering from infectious disease, would have availed themselves of the privilege of entering the institution. It was built for the benefit of the ratepayers, and they ought to receive the benefit by it being made free. Dr. Spiers re- commended this course highly.—Mr. Lightburn said this matter had been under serious consideration, and in a short time they would have a report which would be in general harmony with the remarks made by Mr. Dobson The minutes were adopted.
MR. WALTER TIMMINS.
Mr. Walter Timmins was appointed a member of the Waterloo Bridge and of the Baths Committees.
TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

The Secretary read a letter from the School Board,ask- ing the Commissioners to adopt the Technical Education Act ; and a letter from the National Association for the promotion of Technical Education on the same subject.— Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys moved that it be an instruc- tion to the Parliamentary Committee to consider the provisions of the Technical Instruction Act, 1889, and to report to the Board as to the advisability or otherwise of putting the Act into operation, having regard to the cir- cumstances of the district." He also moved " that pesding, the report of the Parliamentary Committee, the Clerk be instructed to enquire from the Cheshire County Council what proportion of the funds allocated to the Council under the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Act, 1890, would be available for the Urban Sanitary Authority for the purposes of techniaal education with- in the meaning of the Technical Instruction Act, 1889 ; and to request the Council to reserve such proportion for the use of such authority."—Mr. Light- burn seconded the resolution.—Mr. Pritchard said the School Board had made a considerable advance in the way of higher education by the establishment of evening schools in which the subjects taught were mathematics, shorthand, &c., and there were also drawing classes in which building and machine construction and geometry, were taught. He was pleased to be in a position to state that these classes were numerously attended and appre- ciated, and very successful.—Mr. Wiswall said he was very were pleased that this question had been raised.— Mr. Speakman and Mr. Grice having also spoken, the resolutions were passed.

div.head: -TILE LATE MR. TIMMINS.
div.p: -TILE LATE MR. TIMMINS.

The following letter was read :—" Null Cottage, Run- corn, November, let, 1890. E. Marshall Esq., Town Hall, Runcorn. My dear sir,—On behalf of my sister and brothers we tender our sincere thanks to each and every member of your Board of Commissioners, for their kind expression of sympathy towards my late and res- pected father. His object through life was for the good and welfare of others, and your remarks and those of the members are characteristic of him. He has left an excellent example for us to follow and it reminds me of a few favourite words he often quoted from Bedfod. Thy work speaks better of thy worth, Than all that we can say; Immortal it will live on earth, Though thou bast passed away. I remain, my dear sir, yours faithfully, WALTER TIMMINS."

div.head: HOMING OF THE WORKING CLASSES.
div.p: HOMING OF THE WORKING CLASSES.

A circifiar-ier was read iriCn-iir:Charles-71'. Ritchie, president of the Local Government Board, drawing the attention of the Commissioners to the Housing of the Working Classes Act 1890, and asking them to carefully consider its provisions and not let it remain a dead letter. There could be no doubt that a very material improvement in the present condition of the labouring classes may be effected by a strenuous and judicious exercise of the large powers which were given to Local Authorities by the Act,and he trusted the Commissioners would fully realise the responsibility which devolves on them of putting these powers in force in every case in which the circumstances are such as to require that action should be taken under the Statute. The letter was referred to the Health Committee, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: TERRIBLE RAILWAY FATALITIES AT
div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY FATALITIES AT
ST. HELENS. "A MUTILATED BODY FOUND."

About nine o'clock on Monday night a shocking discovery was made on the railway at the Raven-st., crossing near St. Helens Railway Station. A brakes- man in the employ of the London and North- western Railway Company was walking along the side of the St. Helens and St. elens Junction line when .he stumbled over a body lying in the six foot. Assistance was at once obtained, and the body was found to be that of a strongly-built young fellow, about 30 years of age. It was terribly mutilated, and the man appeared to have been dead some time. The body was removed to the public mortuary, add Dr. Jackson was summoned. How the deceased came by his death is not known. Near the spot where the body was found is a footpath, which crosses the line and the canal, and leads from Raven-st., to Lyon's bottle works. The deceased appears to be a collier, and in one of the pockets of his clothing was found a letter addressed to John and Michael Horan or Horne, without any address. The body of the unfortunate man was identified on Tuesday afternoon as that of John Horne, a navvy, who arrived in the town on Monday from Ashton-in-Makerfield. He asked Mr. Riddle, contractor for the new sewer works in Raven-st., if he could find him a job, and Mr. Riddle started him at noon. Later in the day, however, he was seen to be under the influence of liqudr, and Mr. Riddle, discharged him. He was afterwards seen walking along the footpath which crosses the line at the level crossing, but no one appears to know when, or from what train, he received his terrible injuries. He had no friends nor relations in the neighbourhood, but his father in Ireland had been communicated with. An inquest on the body was held before Mr. S. Brighouse. coroner, at the Police Court,at the Town Hall, on Thursday afternoon. Evidence in accordance with the above facts was given, and it was stated that all the trains which passed over the crossing between seven and nine o'clock on Monday night had been examined, but no blood marks or anything was found to denote how deceased came by his death. The jury returned an open verdict of "Found dead." TERRIBLE DEATH OF A SCHOOL GIRL. On Tuesday morning, Jane Faircloug,h, nine years of age, daughter of Robert Fairclougrh, collier, of 74, Back Grove-st., St. Helens, was instantaneously killed by being run over by a locomotive at what is known as Marsh's Level-crossing, near her home. The girl was on her way to school, and attempted to cross the lines in front of an approaching engine engaged in shunting operations. The gatekeeper, a man named Thomas Barrow, attempted to prevent her doing so, but the girl rushed across. When she was just clear of the lines the engine caught her, she was knocked down, and was dragged about a dozen yards. She was then found to be dead. The girls' right arm was clean cut off, and the right side of her head was smashed in. The sad fatality occasioned a painful excitement in the neighbourhood. On Thursday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Town Hall. The evidence went to show that it was the gate- keeper's duty to keep the crossing gates closed when any trains were approaching and on the occasion in question the gate nearest to deceased's home was open. At this point the gatekeeper (Barron), asked the coroner to ad- journ the inquest so that he could obtain legal assistance. The coroner said he thought it was the duty of himself' and the jury to comply with Barron's request, as he no doubt felt the responsibility of the position in which he was placed,. It was a question as to whether or not he had been guilty of negligence or it might be a question for the jury to consider whether he should not be com- mitted for trial. It was then arranged that the inquiry should be adjourned until next Tuesday.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DISGRACEFUL B6E11'101:32- At the Warrington Borough Police Court, en Tuesday, Frederick Stephens was charged with assaulting Peter Sutton, who keeps a refreshment house in St. James's- street, on Saturday night ; also with breaking three panes of glass, and two panels in the shop door, doing damage to the; extent of 15s. Complainant said after he had closedithe shop for the night, the prisoner, in company with others thumped at the door. His son went to see what was the matter, and, seeing the men, said that it was after time ; but the men tried to make a way in. Witness then rushed out and tried to ,et them to go away. This,however, they would not bdo, whereupon a struggle ensued, during which witness was assaulted by defendant, who also broke the panels of the doer, but witness could not say who broke the windows. Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, and ordered to pay the 15s. damages, or in default one month's imprisonment with hard labour. DARING JUVENILE PILFERERS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, John Morley and Frederick Morley, aged respectively twelve and ten years, sons of George Morley, were charged with stealing from the coat room at Trinity School, on Friday, the 31st ult., an overcoat belonging to Herbert Johnson, and another overcoat, the property of Herbert Jowette. Mr. Hunt said the two little boy complainants left their coats in the cloak room of Trinity school at noon on the day in question, and when they went for them towards night found them missing. The police received information of the affair on Friday after- -noon, and inquiries were made. Mr. Briggs, pawn- broker, looked through his stock, and found the coat belonging to the first complainant which the elder pri- soner had pledged for 2s. ed. about three o'clock the same day. The boy also offered the second coat in pledge, saying that his father had sent it because he was short of money. Mr. Briggs, did not, however, take the second coat into pledge. Afterwards Detective Monoghan went to Mr. Brigg's shop, aad as the result of some conversa- tion which took place there, he took possession of the first coat, and then proceeded to Morley's house. He there saw the prisoner John and questioned him about the coat, and finally got both the boys together and they ad- mitted stealing the coats. Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, said th% father would be summoned the follow- ing day for not sending his youngest son to school, and this would make the fifth time he had brought the same case into court in twelve months. Both boys were ordered to receive six strokes of the birch-rod, and detained iia custody until six o'clock.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) pre- siding, Alderman Davies, Alderman Chandley, and Alderman Harrison. DRUNKENNESS AND DISORDERLY CONDUCT.--John Small- wood, at Market Gate, on Saturday afternocn.—Fined ss. including costs.—Mary Ann Binkey, in Buttermarket- st., on Saturday. On promising to leave the town she was discharged.—Henry Broome, at Market-Gate, on Sunday.—Fined Ss. including costs, or seven days.— Thomas Pannell, for a similar offence in Bank-st., was fined ss. and costs. TRANSFER OF LICENSRS.—The magistrates granted transfers of the licenses of the following public-houses The Woolpack Inn, to Herbert Hollingworth from Robert Rose; the Three Pigeons, to William ClAalmers from Her- bert Hollingworth ; the Marquis of Ganby to Mary Whittle from her late husband ; the Waggon and Horses, to Hannah Jones from Isaac Jones ; the Talbot Inn, to Peter Holt Lake from Maria Clayton: the Coopers' Arm s to Henry Evans from William Eddowes ; the Mersey Hotel, to William Henry Bailey from David Smith. DESERTION OF A CHILD—Mary Ann Holmes was charged with having on the 24th October, unlawfully run away and leaving her child chargeable to the War- rington Union.—Mr. B. Shearer stated that he would consent to a djdurn the case for a week to give the defen- dant an opportunity of taking charge of her child, and if she did so, he would then withdraw the charge.—The magistrates agreed to this suggestion. BREACRES or Tar. PEACH.—John Reardin, James Caslin, James Quinn, and Thomas McGuire were charged with committing a breach of the peace, by fighting near Arp- ley iron bridge, on the 25th ult. Another man, named Peter Ford was included in the charge ; but, as he did not put in an appearance at Court. a warrant was issued for his attendance. The prisoners, after fighting among themselves, participated in throwing defendant Caslin into the river. The magistrates reprimanded the pri- soners on their disgraceful conduct, and discharged Cas- lin. Quinn was bound over on his own recognisances of £5, to keep the peace forsix months ; and Reardin and McGuire for a like period, on one surety each of £5, orin default seven days' imprisonment. A DESERTER—Thomas Cragg, was charged with deserting from the Pembroke Militia, stationed at Mil- ford Haven, on the 2nd June last. Mr. Hunt said he had written for orders as to what he should do with de- fendant from the commanding officer, and he would have to receive a reply before he could deal with de- fendant. The case was accordingly adjourned until Friday. Cragg was brought LID again on Friday, when he was fined 40s. including costs. Tursnay.—Before Messrs, .. R. Garnett (in the chair)

div.head: and William Owen.
div.p: and William Owen.

DIFUNICENNESS. —John Cotton was charged with having been drunk in the Police Station on Monday night. Fined ss. and costs or seven days.—Jane Owinn, in Sankey st., on Monday night. Fined ss. and costs or seven days. REFUSING TO QUlT.—Lawrence Mannion was charged with having been drunk and refusing to quit the Stran- gers' Arms beeehouse in Dyer-st., on Monday night. The defendant was refused drink by the landlady, and because he would not leave when requested by her she sent for a constable and had him ejected. Defendant, who pleaded guilty, but denied that it was with diffi- culty he was put out of the house, was fined ss. and costs or seven days imprisonment. ALLEGED SIIOCKING ASSAULT. —Patrick Dooley was charged with assaulting Annie McLoughlin. Complainant said on Saturday night she was proceeding home, when the defendant went up to her and Mused her in a shock- ing manner. He thumped her, kicked her, and when she was on the floor he did not dmist beating her.—Evi- dence in support of this statement having been given, the defendant denied having assaulted the woman. The Bench thought there was a little element of doubt in the case, and this being so the prisoner would be dealt with lightly, and fined only ss. and costs or seven days' im- prisonment. SCF/OOL BOARD —ThO following persons were dealt with as stated below for failing to send their children regularly to school :—Mary Marsh, hawker, Winwick-st. Fined ss.—Peter Hind, forgeman, Cockhedge. Fined Sc. or seven days.—Peter Murray, labourer, Town Hill. 24. 6d.—John McDonald, labourer, Ship Yard, child ordered to be birched.—George Morley, labourer, Price- st. Fined ss.—Thos. Egan, labourer, Crossley-et. Fined 2s. 6d.—Chas. Greenough, labourer, Hind-€t., child ordered to he birehed,—Thos. Rowland, cabdriver, Bridge-st. Fined 28. 6d.—Thomas Taylor, tanner, Mercey-st. Fined 55.—W ;ri . Evans, butcher, Bridge-st. Fined ss.—Henry Jervis, forgeman, Kean-st., child ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. W EDNFSDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough.

DRUNKENNESS AND DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Jane Gwinn was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., the previous evening. P.S. Chantler said the defendant was fined ss. for drunkenness on Monday. Her husband paid the fine, and as soon as she left the court she went and got drunk. Defendant was fined ss. and costs or seven days' imprisonment.

Rasacx or THE PEACE --Bodelia Knockton, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting Harriet Dainteth in Butterrnarket-et., on the 24th ult. Defendant, who admitted the offence was bound over to keep the peace for six months on her own recog,nisances of £5, and one surety of a like amount. DRUNKENNESS. —John Johnson was fined ss. and costs or seyen days for having been drunk in Sankey-st., on Tuesday night. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton (in the chait), and

Captain Ridgway. DESERTERS .—John Chambers was charged with being a deserter from the 34th (border) regiment stationed at Preston ; Tames Tuite was charged with being a deserter from the 2nd battalion Grendier Guards, stationed at London. They were both ordered to be taken to Liver- pool under escort. A SERIES OF THEFTS. —Catherine Draper, Cow-lane, Burtonwood, was charged wadi stealing from the stall of Matilda Bunby in the Market Place at 11 am., on Wednesday, a musical box, value 44. ; also with stealing from the stall of Albert Halliwell, in the Market Place between 10 a.m., and U. am.,on Saturday,a silk muffler, a silk handkerchief, and a silk cape, value in all 'as. Bd. It seems that the muffler and tie were missing from Halliwell's stall on Saturday ; and, in consequence of this, a watch was instituted. On Wednesday the prisoner was seen in the Market Place, and she was seen to pick up the musical box by Detective Sergeant Monoghan, who afterwards visited prisoner's house, and there found the other articles. Prisoner was discharged but it was ordered that a conviction should be recorded against her. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair) and L. Voisey.

ALLEGYD CRUELTY TO A HORM—Peter Clare was Sum- moned for working a horse which was in an unfit condi- tion, on the 22nd Oct.—Mr. Charles Wilson, Inspector for the R.S.P.C.A., said on the day in question he was walking near Bridgefoot, when he saw defendant driving a spring cart, drawn by a pony, over the bridge into Mersey-st. The pony was absolutely unfit to work, and he was sure it was suffering great pain from its several wounds.—Defendant was ordered to pay the costs. A DESTRAINT CAM—Joseph Cox was summoned by John Dobson for removing goods from his dwelling,-house to avoid destraiat. The defendant offered to pay what was owing, and on this understanding the magistrates adjourned the case for a month. and, if at the end of that time he had fulfilled his promise, the summons would be withdrawn.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. .J. Crosfleld (in the chair) and W. H. Blecklv. DRUNKENNESS.—banid Buckley, On the 18th ult. at

Warrington. Fined ss. and costs. Charles Jones, on the 21st ult. Fined ss. and costs. James Coyne, at Sankey, on the 18th ult. Fined 10s. and costs or 14 days Samuel Marsh, at Rixtoa on the 31st ult. Fined ss. and costs. . _

A SIMPLE OFFENCE.—James Newton was charged, being the owner of a cart, with allowing the same to he on the highway, without having his name painted thera- on, at Woolston on the 17th ult. Fined Is. and costs. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Poter Ashcroft was charged with assaulting James Ellison, farmer, Sandy-lane, Orford, on! the 23rd ult. at Warrington. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defence. Complainant stated that he was work- ing on the highway at Winwick-road when the defendant drove up in his cart, and, without provocation, gob out and struck him on the nose. Mr. Davies denied the as- sault, and Mr. John Fisher said he witnessed the alter- cation on the day in question and he saw the complainant and his son following the cart driven by defendant. Complainant started the affair, by endeavouring to hit defendant with a brush. Defendant warded off the blows, and got out of his cart, when complainant again brandished the brush, and his son a scraper. The evi- dence, the magistrates thought, was not conclusive that Ashcroft had committed an assault, and dismissed the case.

DRUNKENNESS AND DISORDWRLY CONDUOT.—Henry Green and William Moody wore charged with having been drunk and disordeely ern the Ist inst. at Warrington. Green was fined ss. and costs and Moody was dis- charged. Doc; CASES.—For allowing their respective dogs to be at large unmuzzled, Wm. B. Skelton, and Wm. Haslam were each fined is. and costs. For a similar offence a fine of 10s, and costs was imposed on Elizabeth Warburton. AN UN'SIISTAINED CHABGB.—John Kay was charged with travelling on the London and North-Western Rail- way, from Liverpool to Newton, without haying paid his fare. It was stated that the prisoner had purchased a ticket at Carnforth to bring him through to Warring- ton. The magistrates failed to see that the charge was substantiated, inasmuch as the prisoner had paid hia fare to Warrington, and the case was consequently dis- missed.

div.head: WARRINGTON Y. WIDNES.
div.p: WARRINGTON Y. WIDNES.

Visitors to the Widnes football ground on Saturday were afforded a rare treat when the above-named clubs played one of their finest exhibitions. Throughout the whole eighty minutes played the game never flagged in the least, the brilliant passing movements of both sides, which were so frequently indulged in, raising the en- thusiasm of the spectators to a high pitch. Both sides had good teams for the occasion, and Smith kicked off for the home team before five thousands spectators, some 1,200 of these having travelled from Warrington. Loose scrimmaging was the order of the first five mieutes, until Morris mulled a pass from Brennan, and John Bate being handy, was instrumental in Widnes defending. Stubbs followed up a free kick taken by Smith, but James Bate, backed up by Barnes, Jolley, Ashton, and Bandies, transferred the game back to the Widnes quar- ter. The Bates again passed splendidly, and tha three- quarters were constantly kept busy. Hartles repeatedly got the oval away, and then a grand spell of passing between James and John Bate, Bandies, Ashton and Thornley, almost ended in a tangible score. Drummond luckily cleared, but it was momentary, for John Bate, securing from a pack near the half way flag threw wide to Webster, and this player soon being in his stride, a sterling run along the popular side found him crossing the line, a loud cheer announcing his success. The kick at goal was short. Bate made his mark from the kick off, and Widnes by renewed exertions worked the oval into Warrington territory, and after several futile endea- vours to place the teams on a level, Evans, Barnes and Webster each in succession again pressed the homesters. A sterling run by Evans from a pass by Barnes took play to the Widnes line, and a beautiful spell of passing by the visiting forwards certainly deserved a better fate. The play of Warrington at this point was excellent, the game on their side now being a series of passes which all had a futile ending. Barber cleared for a moment, and Morris further aided his effort with a long kick to Boscoe, who was as safe as usual. A screw kick by Boscoe, a couple of good runs by Barnes and Evans, again placed Warrington in the ascendancy, but Widnes retaliated in strong force, taking the oval in the mouth of the visitors' goal. Barnes cleverly got it away, Hartles responding but poorly. Povey, Ashton, Berry, and Holmes put in useful dribbles, and then Berry and Thornley came through leading play to the Widnes line. Again Warring- ton were at fault in their final essay, and Peters kicked dead. A grand display of passing amongst the" vrirepul- lers' "backs raised the siege once more,and Barnes dribbled grandly, Hartles luckily saving. Boscoe next compelled a minor, and Jolley directly after the drop passed finely to Webster, a third minor having to be conceded. This was followed by another from the last named personage, and immediately after Bandies had the goal at his mercy, when he slipped and the chance was lost. Holmes saved what appeared a certain try from a long dribble by Stubbs. Webster initiated a passing movement, which was taken up by Barnes and Evans, but Morris tackled surely, and,half time was called with no addition being made to the score, which read as follows—Warrington, 0-1-4 ; Widnes, nil. The game was restarted, and again Warrington showed their superiority, and a beautiful run and pass by John Bate to Jolley saw the latter being pulled up on the line. Barnes floored Barber in his en- deavour to relieve, but by combined efforts Widnes, who were now playing stronger than at any period of the match, forced the game at the Warrington end. Morris had a narrow shave for a drop at goal, and Boscoe saved again from some sterling work by Drummond and Barber. Another fine dribble by Stubbs was checked by John Bate, and Widnes were having the best of it. All their efforts to break through the defence set up by Warrington were fruitless, and towards the close the visitors again rallied. James Bate shone with a capital run to the Widnes line, and Hartles being collared near the posts, a shot at goal was productive of a minor, which was the last point scored, a grand game being brought to a conclusion as Warrington, 0-1-5 ; Widnes, 0-0-2. Teams :—Warrington, J. Boscoe, back ; H. Webster, T. Barnes, and J. W. Evans, three quarter backs ; John Bate and James Bate, half backs; H. Ashton (captain), E. Dillon, J. Jolley, W. Povey, W. Randle,s, J. T. Thorn- ley, B. Berry, J. Holmes, and T. Davies, forwards. Widnes : J. Hartles, back ; H. Peters, D. Brennan. and S. Morris, three quarter backs; J. Drummond and Bar- ber, half backs ; J. H. Smith (captain), G. Hewitt, J. Whelan, E. Gordon, H. Farmer, J Johnson J. Pearson, T. Carroll, and W. Stubbs, forwards. Referee, Mr. T. Hunter.

WARRINGTON " A " Y. WIDNES "A."—The above teams met at Wilderspool, on Saturday, in splendid football weather. Only a moderate number of people wore pre- sent when Isherwood started towards the pavilion goal, play resting at the halfway flag. Capital passing by Rowe and Williams saw Jolley putting in a huge kick, and Welsby, Barnes, and Russell rushed the oval to the visitors' quarters. Rowe and Daniels further improved the home team's position but the Widnes forwards, taking advantage of a mull, removed the venue to the opposite end. Hard lines were experienced by the visi- tors, but Rowe relieved slightly. Forster ran to the quarter flag, and a free kick fell to the visitors for off side play. Daniels came to the rescue with smart kick- ing, and Jolley securing a tremendous kick, and quick following up by the front van, saw Widnes again defend- ing. Williams, Jolley, and Lally all showed up well, and fine passicg by Rowe, Tolley, and Daniels saw the latter cantering over, after completely puzzling Mullinger. Isherwood tailed at the difficult place. The drop-out gave no relief, and Williams was nearly in after pretty footwork. Another fine display of passing by Rowe, Williams, and Jolley was witnessed, and Ishnwood made his mark, nothing resulting from Jolley's kick at goal. Forster, Craig, and Harrison relieved to half-way, but Jolley almost landed a goal from a penalty kick. A minor was forced, and then from some loose play by Widnes, Jolley again got possession and dropped a grand goal from the thick ot his opponents. Loud cheers greeted this success, but Widness played up pluckily on the restart, the oval being taken to touch near the home line. Lloyd was prominent with a grand dribble fully half the length of the field, and Williams, Rowe, and Jolley again passed finely. The short, quick transfers of the home halves completely mesmerized the Widnesians, and from another grand display by Williams, Rowe, Jolley, and Daniels, the ball was taken over and the last-named scored his second try, no goal resulting. Craig and Jolley exchanged kicks on the drop out, and Warrington were still pressing when half-time arrived, the score standing as Warrington 1-2-3, Widnes nil. The visitors restarted, and two minors at once accrued to

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOYE.MI3ER 8. 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOYE.MI3ER 8. 1890.

the,. wirepullers." The home halves were prominent, but Widnes played up pluckily, Jolley relieving ha splen- did style. Barnes, Lloyd, and Isherwood dribbled neatly until stopped by Craig. Mullinger put his side on the attack with a judicious run and kick, but Knowles, Jolley, and Russell removed the danger. Jolley got in a huge kick to the visitors' line, but only a minor accrued after a prolonged attack. The latter part of the game was finished in semi-darkness, and Widness were passing severely during the last ten minutes. However, they failed to negotiate anything more tangible than a minor, and at the close of an interesting game the score stood as follows :—Warrington, 1 goal, 2 tries, 7 minors; Wid- nes, 1 minor. Teams :—Warrington : Massey, full back; Daniels, Jolley (captain), and Lally, threequarter- backs ; Rowe, and Williams, half-hacks ; Isherwood, Lloyd, A. Barnes, Russell, Catterall, Molineaux, Knowles, Welsby and Creaghan, forwards. Widnes, Lightfoot, full back ; Craig, Forster, and Mullinger, threequarter backs ; Harrison and Burgess, half backs ; Minton (captain), Lines, Kenyon, Ridgway, Cook, Tomkins, Hardman, Holt, and Wade, forwards. Mr. S. Pollitt, Swinton, referee. BIRKINTURAD PARK v. EIINCORN.—The Runcorn fifteen are always welcomed in this district, and on Saturday last a large gathering lined the ropes on the Upper Park enclosure to witness the fortunes of the Park against the the crack Cheshire team. Prompt to time the sides faced as follows :—Birkenhead Park—N. Gaskell, back; R. Steel, G. H. Court, and E. T. Nicholson, three-quarter backs; A. B. Spence and A. Fachiri, half-backs; A. G, Wood, T. W. Lockwcod, P. H. Lockwood, W. T. Wood, G. F. Knipe, F. H. Smith, A. J. Chadwick, D. J. Brood- rit, and G. D. White, forwards. Runcorn—S. Houghton, back ; T. H. Davies, J. 11. Crompton, and G. Pendlebury, three-quarter backs; W. Evans and S. Abrams. half- backs ; W. Faulkner, W. H. Broady, P. Riley, R. Dolan, Gayter, 11. Barker, A. Hampson, J. Davies, and H. May, forwards. Two thirty-fives having been agreed upon, A. G. Wood kicked off towards Davies, whoSe return was followed by a splendid dribbling move- ment by the Runcorn forwards, led on by Faulkner, the game atones becoming very fast. A free kick was given to the Park for off-side play, with the result that the Park forwards at once began to press their opponents, but from some loose play, well maintained by the Run- cornians, Crompton nearly scored a flying goal, a minor point ensuing. Houghton returned to the Park line, and after a long maul Gayter was :awarded a try for Runcorn. but Faulkner failed to convert the point. The Park backs ran and passed finely, led on by Spence, and the forwads sharing in the movement drib- bled splendidly, taking the ball close to the Runcorn line —a minor point only rewarding their efforts. After the drop out, the front line of the Park time after time drib- bled,almost the length of the field, but could not score. A drop at goal by Court was knocked down, and a second minor point was added to the home team score. The drop out brought no relief, for the Parkites were con- tinually pressing, and experienced very hard lines in not scoring. The backs at this juncture were running strongly and the forwards were playing magnificently, but strive as they would they could not get on terms of equality, and ends were changed with Runcorn leading by a try and a minor to 2 minors. Faulkner opened the second stage of the play, and the visitors nearly scored a try owing to a mull by White For fully five minutes the home lot were penned in their quarters, and several times their opponents nearly crossed their line. The forwards came to the raeme, and again made a splendid dribble to the Runcorn 25 line, Lock- wood, Knipe, and Alec Wood being prominent. The play contieued to be mostly confined to the forward ranks, but it was very open and exciting, the home scrimmagers especially playing a brilliant game; but the Runcorn backs were in an impassable mood, and scoring was frequently prevented. Relief came from Houghton, and after a few close packs the game again became very Interesting, and the Park should have scored substan- tially. All the forwards, White especially, and thehalves were playing a faultless game, and gave their opposing backs an anxious time. At length Runcorn gradually forced their way into the home half, after Crompton registered a minor point from a shie at goal, May and Broady dribbled well up, and Abrams, being in readiness, ran in under the posts, Crompton successfully landing the premier point. The Park appeared somewhat fagged. but dribbled again to the other end. Runcorn retu to the attaok, and after a fine exposition of the passing game. Crompton ran in under the posts and kicked a goal exactly intime, a good game resulting in favour of Run- corn by 2 goals, 1 try, and 1 minor, to 2 minors.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
ASSOCIATION.

There was more inconsistent form shown in the League same on Saturday. Everton were beaten for the second week in succession, Notts being their conquerors at Trent Bridge by three to one. Two of the three Scotch- men lately captured by Everton took part in the match. Notts have now climbed to the third place in the League table, only one point below Everton and Wolverhampton Wanderers. The last-named were unexpectedly van- quished at Burnley, although the Turf Moor team was far from representative. A check was in store for Black- burn Rovers, who went all the way to Sunderland to be beaten by three goals to one. The gate was the best ever seen on the Sunderland ground. The North End could not defeat Accrington at Deepdale, as they did in the first fixture three weeks back, and had to be content with a draw. Aston Villa are going much better since they were joined by Campbell and Brown, of Benton, r and astonished the world by beating West Bromwich , Albion pointless.

Followers of the North End are just now suffenng from a depressing state of despondency. Just imagine the most famous club in the three Kingdoms being able to score only one goal in three fixtures. No wonder that consternation is rampant in football circles on the banks of the Ribble. And yet, after all, the North End are doing quite as well as their eleven great rivals. They have chalked up 11 points in eight engagement, which is comparatively as good as anything accomplished in tho League tournament up to date.

As regards the question of goal scoring, Accrington and Derby County are at the extreme ends of the pole. 'The " Reds " have only recorded nine goals in nine matches, whilst the Derby men have had no fewer than 33 registered against them in eight contests. Preston have apparently still the best defence, only seven goals being booked against them in eight fixtures ; and Ever- ton are the most deadly in front of goal, having obtained 30 in ninegames.

div.head: FOOTBALL-RUGBY.
div.p: FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

There is one matter mnnected with Lancashire Rugby football which it will be just as well to explain. Some time ago M. Berry, an ex-Kendal Hornet, was suspended by the committee, and the general impression is that the redoubtable "Buff," the new county half-back, is one and the same person as the suspend. It happens, how- ever, to be "Billy," his brother, who came under the ban of the officials.

The following team has been chosen to represent Lan- cashire against Cheshire in the match to be played at Birkenhead to-day :—T. Coop (Leigh) back; J. Valen- tine and J. Marsh (Swinton) and E. H. Flower (Brough- ton), three-quarters; W. Bumby (Swinton) and W. Berry (Tyldesley), half-backs; J. Jackson (Broughton Bangers). W. Atkinson and E. Bullough (Wigan), T. Whittaker (Manchester), E. Blomley (Oldham), J. Elides (St. Helens Recreation), Herbert Hasleham (Manchester Rangers), F. Treweeke (Barrow), and T. Kent (Salford), forwards. Reserves :W. B. Steel (Manchester), back; T. Sudlow (St. Helens), D. Gwynn (Oldham), and W. M'Cutcheon (Oldham), three-quarters; J. Nolan (Old- ham) and W. Cross (St. Helens), half-backs; T. Craven (Salford), J. Wilson (Liverpool Old Boys), T. Mellaslew (Rochdale Hornets), and T. Brayshay (Wigan), forwards.

Says the "Athletic News" :—The match between Widnes and Warrington last Saturday attracted a big crowd to the Widnes ground, but the result was not very gratifying to the home supporters, for though Warring- ton had the good fortune to win, the chances that fell in the way of Widnes, and which were either fearfully mulled or thrown away, was awfully discouraging. There was an entire lack of combination, and a profound absence of ability shown by some of the players, which was not very lively to look at, and is calculated to dis- hearten the strongest enthusiast and supporter of a club. The Warrington team is composed of some very remarkable specimens of the gouu,s homo, from the lengthy Webster to the slim feather-weight, Thorniley ; but all played a rattling good gatna in the first half, and while Widnes had the best of a fierce struggle in the second half, they failed to take the chances offered, and consequently suffered defeat again.

Runcorn are still the Cheshire champions, judging from the way they walked round Birkenhead Park on Saturday. A Cheshire club rapidly coming to the front is Sale, who beat New Brighton last week end. There was a time—ft good many years ago—when Sale were as strong as any of the crack Lancashire clubs, and it to be hoped they will soon regain their ancient prestige. .

There is nothing like being in time. The Runcorn club have already completed their fixtures for season 1891-2. The clubs on the list are :—Leeds, Swinton, Bradford, Salford, Broughton, Liverpool Old Boys, Bur- ton-on-Trent, Old Edwardians, Moseley, Cardiff, New Brighton, Birkenhead Park, Widnes, Sale, Broughton Rangers, Stockport, Tuebrook, and Rochdale Hornets.
Sudlow, the St. Helens three-quarter, created a very favourable impression in the Lancashire trial match last Saturday, and he should stand a chance of getting his cap before the season is over.
