A young man named Arthur Smith died at Kingston- on-Thames early on Monday morning from injuries re- ceived in a football match on Saturday.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT BITRTONWOOD.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT BITRTONWOOD.

In connection with the Burtonwoud Liberal Club, a well-attended meeting was held at the Bridge Inn on Tuesday evening. Mr. Thomas Belfield pre- sided.—Mr. Thomas Horton in the course of an address on Free trade and Fair trade, said lie was proud to see the Burtonwood Liberal Club in such a flourishing condition, and such a large number pre- sent. It was now 40 years ago since the corn laws were passed, and he had no need to explain to that intel- ligent audience, the benefits derived by tho passing of those laws. We found, since the year 1840, our trade and commerce had increased 75 per cent, in comparison Co our population. Since the year 184-0, the comsump- Ural of tea, sugar, rice, &c., per head had increased over 50 per cent. Ho went on to show at length that the con- sumer had the benefit. Therefore he considered this free and fair trade was a benefit to the working classes of this country. We send our goods to America, and they like- wise forward their goods to us, on which a tariff had to be paid. He considered that the same should be given to England, as America demanded from England. He con- tended that if the blessing of cheap tea &c. were being enjoyed, it was the working class who obtained it.—Mr. G. Anders said his contention was that labour would not eompete with capital. He had known firms to remove their works to other countries where they could grow their own cotton, and forward their finished goods to England. He referred to certain mowing machines being manufactured in America and being sold to English farmers for £l6 10s. Od., whereas the English maker could not supply his machine to America under a cost of £29. This,he considered, was not fair trade.—Mr. Horton replied in a most satisfactory manner.—Mr. W. Hume speaking on the manufacture of Belgi urn Iron, asked why other countries were allowed to usurp our Markets. He said our skilled labour was the only thing we had to de- pend upon, and the working classes were the backbone of England to-day. Did they pretend to tell him that steel rails, silk, cotton and other goods, manufactured in ether countries, were being landed in England without is tariff, and we were bound to pay a heavy tariff on all such goods going' to other countries ? Was that fair trade? He said we find them sending coals into England, why, he asked should we not tariff one thing we could well do without, viz., coals? Was that fair trade?—Mr. Horton said that was all very good, but perhaps those present would agree with him that our Government had tried, persuasively to work with other Governments, and he contended that England rode Monarch of them all. He contended that the working clasges were in a better con. dition to-day, and were able to do more with ten shillings now than they could without free trade. We were not decaying, but were advancing every year. (Hear, hear.) This he could prove from the figures of the Board of Trade. Mr. Anders said Birmingham was a great place for tinware, but tinware could be manufactured abroad for less money than we could do it at home. Birmingham had used to do well, but Belgium was usurping her rights, she was delivering wire &c., in our own towns cheaper than we could produce it.— Mr. Horton asked the last speaker where he obtained his information, but Mr. Anders did not vouchsafe a reply.— Mr. J. T. Meirs thought before India or Canada could supply us with cotton or iron ore, it must be colonized. If our coal and iron is getting, worked out, then why, he asked, did we put a tariff upon it? In regard to the tariff question, Mr. A. Simcock asked if the farmer was getting a proportional interest on his capital.—Mr. M. Goffrey would like to hear of the farmer who could make his farm pay, whilst he was burdened with such an. ex- tortionate rent, such as were charged in that neigh- bourhood. Ho thought the farmer was working for the landlord, and not for himself. He contended that Home Rule was requisite in Burtonwood as well as in Ireland. The debate was then adjourned, after the lusual vote of thanks had been accorded.

div.head: FARM FIRE Aa POOLE HALL.
div.p: FARM FIRE Aa POOLE HALL.

A disastrous fire occurred at Poole Hall, on the Manchester Ship Canal, near Ellesmere Port, on Wednesday night, on the premises occupied by Mr. Pickering. Two fire brigades were quickly on the spot, but notwithstanding their services the whole of the farm buildings, together with about 200 tons of hay, were destroyed.

div.head: ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER.
div.p: ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER.

On Mondsy, at the Whitehaven Police Court, James Lyon, forty years of age, labourer, Whitehaven, was charged with attempting to murder his wife, who was engaged at the Fever Hospital at Whiteheven, by cutting her throat with a razor. Dr. Fisher stated that since the wound was inflicted the woman had developed symptoms of fever. She was quite unfit to attend the court; in fact, she was dangerously ill.—The magistrates remanded prisoner for a week.

div.head: SUSPECTED MURDER AT GATESHEAD.
div.p: SUSPECTED MURDER AT GATESHEAD.

The Durham police are enquiring into the death of a young man named Forsyth, clerk to a cement manu- facturer at Gateshead, whose body was found on Tues- day morning within the works premises bearing marks about the throat indicative of severe violence, while in addition his skull had been fractured by a blow from a bar of iron found close beside him. It was the deceased's duty to lock up the works, but he had evidently not left the place on Monday night, and the supposition is that he was attacked from motives of plunder.

div.head: TERRIBLE ENCOUNTER WITH A WHALE. THREE SEAMEN KILLED.
div.p: TERRIBLE ENCOUNTER WITH A WHALE. THREE SEAMEN KILLED.

A despatch from San Francisco, received at Queens- town on Tuesday, contains intelligence of the arrival at San Francisco of the whaling barque John Arinthrop on the 30th October. On September 23rd a large whale was sighted, and two boats were sent to capture it. As soon as the whale was struck by the harpoon it wrecked both the boats, • killing three men and breaking the legs of three others by striking them with its tail. Ten seamen were thrown into the sea, but were rescued by a third boat sent from the ship.

div.head: TIPPERARY PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: THE TIPPERARY PROSECUTIONS.

At the sitting of the Crimes -Act Court on Monday, the cross-examination of Sub-sherrlff Power was proceeded With. At one point Mr. Ronan said Mr. P. O'Brien had a photographic-earner levelled at Mr. Power. The matter was allowed to drop, however, on Mr. O'Brien promising not to use the instrument. When it came to Mr. O'Brien's turn to cross-examine, ha asked if the witness objected to be photographed. Witness said he did not, whereupon Mr. O'Brien took a snap shot. For this he was committed for seven days for contempt of court.
YR. BALFOUR IN IRELAND.

On Tuesday morning Mr. Balfour left Dublin for Donegal, to inspect the site of the proposed extension of the line from Donegal to Killybegs, and inquire into the circumstances of the peasantry, and the probable extent of the potato blight. He goes direct to Strabane, and thence over the Finn Valley to Stranorlar and Donegal Town, whence he will drive to the route of the proposed line, visiting Glenties and Gweedore as time permits. On Wednesday Mr. Balfour' inquiry excursion in county Donegal was resumed. The party left Carrick in the morning on cars, and proceeded to Teelin and Kilear, where the Chief Secretary held long conversations with the local priests on the state of the country, and the possibility of relievlng the distress which is likely to follow on the failure of this year's potato crop. The journey was continued through Ardara to Glenties, at both of which places the Chief Secretary met deputa- tions, with whom he talked over the prospects for the winter.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER BY A. BRADFORD MANUFACTURER.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER BY A. BRADFORD MANUFACTURER.

About nine o'clock on Wednesday morning Mr. Win. Whitley, manufacturer, of 8, Chellow Terrace, Bradford, attempted to murder his wife by beating her about the head with his fists. He locked the bedroom door before he attacked Mr. Whitley, and when hethought he had beaten her to death he rushed out of the room,shouting he would kill his child, which is only six weeks old. He asked the nurse where it was, and she, to put him off the scent, pointed to the front door. Whitley rushed out into the front garden, where he was stopped by neighbours who had been attracted by the wife's screams. He was clad in his nightshirt, the right sleeve of which and both his hands were covered with blood. He told the neighbours that he had murdered his wife and was going to murder the child, and wildly asked where the child was. He, howeVer, made no resistance when he was taken into the house, where he was afterwards arrested by the police. Doctors were telephoned for, and were soon in attendance upon the injured woman. It is sup- posed that the cause of the outrage was homicidal mania, it having been noticed that Whitley's behaviour has been peculiar for some days. So serious was Mrs. Whitley's condition on Wednse night that her depositions were taken. She stated that; her husband was restless all night, and told her he had gob to kill her. He attacked her as she was getting out of bed, tried to throttle her, and beat her about the face, asking frequently if she was dead. At last she said she was dead, and he left her. He had always been a good husband, and kind to her and the children. Her face is scarcely recognisable, but her jaws are not broken. Whitley's comment on the occurrence was, "It's been the visitation of God ; it's been the curse of my life."l He has been pronounced insane by four medical gentle- men. Whitley has since his arrest preserved a perfectly calm and unconcerned demeanour.

div.head: BAZAAR IN THE DRILL HALL.
div.p: BAZAAR IN THE DRILL HALL.

On Wednesday a bazaar in aid of the building fund of St. Peter's Church was opened in the Dril Hall, by the Hon. John Powys, son of the Right Hon. Baron Lilford. It may be here explained that . the work of St. Peter's Mission was begun in 1863 by the Rev. P. R. Moore, continued from 1870 to 1886 by the Rev. M. Schonberg, from 1886 to 1888 by the Rey. Cl. D. Wray, and from 1889 by the pre- sent vicar, the Rev. T. Rigby. All previous efforts to build a church for the parish have been unsuccess- ful, but now the building is finished, and it is expected that it will be opened in the course of a few weeks for public worship. The land for the site was generously given by Mr. W. Sharp, solicitor, of Warrington, and the subscriptions amount to .£3,530 but still nearly .£1,500 is needed in order to open the church free from debt. A curates' fund will be raised, and, we understand, a gentleman will be ordained to St. Peter's at the Advent Ordina- tion. Mr. Sharp has also promised a piece of land near to the church as a site for a parsonage. There was a large and fashionable gathering at the opening of ths bazaar, the company present including Major and Mrs. Muldille, Miss Emily Powys,Miss Theresa Powys, Mrs. Ireland Blackburne, Mrs. Willis (Flalsnead, Whiston), the Misses Willis, the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis) and Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Long, Mrs. Reynolds, Mrs. Parr, the Mayer (Alderman Francomb), the Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Rev. J. J. Langham, Dr. White, Rev. Cl. D. and Mrs. Wray, Rev. T. Rigby, Rev. 0. P. P. Whalley, Rev. Canon Whitley, Rev. Morley Stevenson, Rev. S. Slater, Rev. Gibson Smith, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Mr. John Roberts, Councillor E. Greenall, Mr. J. Smethurst, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. Vere Davies, Mr. James Fairclough, Mr. J. D. Buckton, Mr. H. Broadbent, Mr. Jas. Tinsley,Mr. C Hutchins, Mr. W. Sharpe, Mr. J. R. Buckton, Mr. John White, Szc. The room was very tastefully decorated, the work of decorating being carried out by Messrs. Hitchen and Sons, of Liverpool. The stalls, all of which were laden with an unusually rich assortment of goods, were arranged along the side of the walls aim up the centre of the room. Each of them was canopied by a beautiful Japanese umbrella and ornamented with fans and banners. The stalls were presided over as follows No. 1 stall: Mrs. Lyon, Mrs. Charlton Parr, as- sisted by Miss Mary Lyon, Miss S. Macrae, Miss Townsend, Miss Mabel Waide. No. 2 stall: Mrs. F. W. Willis, the 3elisses Buckton, Mrs. R. Fairclough, Mrs Litton, Mrs. Reynolds, Mrs. Stevenson, Mrs. Woods, assisted ,by Mrs. Hodgson, Miss Allen, Miss Fairclough, Miss Hodgson, Misses Littm, Miss Powys, Miss D. Rey- nolds, Miss Willis and. Miss C.Willis. No. 3 stall : Mrs.

Carleton, Mrs. Darwell, Mrs. James Fairclough, Mrs. Gibson Smith, Mrs. John White, assisted by Miss Black- lock, Miss Broadbent, Miss Butterworth, Miss Dun, Miss Mabel Fairclough, and Miss Melville. No. 4 stall : Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Vera B. Davies, assisted by Mrs. G. D. Wray, Miss Dodd, Miss Long, Miss Milner, Miss Maud Powys, Miss Theresa Powys, Miss Pownall, Miss Thack- well, and Miss Thomas. No. 5 stall : Mrs. Stubs, Mrs. E. Greenall, Mrs. H. Greenall, assisted by the Hon. Mrs. J. E. Cross, Miss L. R. Davies, Miss Joanna Dun, Miss Stubs, and Miss L. Stubs. No. 6 stall : Mrs. Blease, Mrs. Edgar, Mrs. Green, Mrs. Hill, Mrs. H. W. Richardson, Miss Jones, Miss Madeley, assisted by Mrs. Thomas Roberts, the Misses Balshaw, Miss R. Crompton, Miss Edgar, Misses Green, Miss Worrell. Refreshment stall: Mrs. A. Browne, Mrs. Higham, Mr. Alfred Woods, assisted by Miss Armstrong, Miss Ada Birtles, Miss N. Birtles, Miss Highain, Miss L. Higham, Miss F. Higham, Miss E. Higharn, Miss Ada Leigh, and Miss Marian Robinson. Official stall: Mr. G. F. F. White and Mr. C. H. Wood. The gentlemen's Committee consisted of the following: Messrs. John Roberts (chairman), F. Apple- ton, W. H. Atkin, J. E. Birtles, A. Browne, H. Buckton, R. Chorley, H. W. Cookson, G. F. F. White, C. H. Wood, A. Woods, J. McGregor (hon treasurer), Rev. T. Rigby (hon. sec.), P. Edgar (assistant sec.) The Rev. T. RIGBY said that for a bazaar of that des- cription he did not think there was any power so great to attract as weakness and the greatest strength of any bazaar was in its object. If that were the case he was sure all those conditions were well fulfilled in the object of that bazaar. Most people knew that the case of St. Peter was a case of extreme destitution and of great long suffering, but he did not think that people quite knew all the details. The mission work began 27 years ago and the parish was actually cut off in 1874. Up to the present there had not been a church for a parish of close upon 8,000 people all of the working classes and most of them very poor. In fact quite three quarters of the baptisms in the parish were of children and men who were classed as labourers, unskilled labourers, not earning large wages. There had been neither a church nor a parsonage, nothing but a school and a small school at that,and very inconvenient. There was generally a fight going on outside during service, aud there were many other little inconveniences which they had almost learned to disregard, and which, perhaps, when they got into a new church they should miss more than they should like. (Laughter.) The cry of the contents of' the Sunday papers mingling with the reading of the litany, and shrill whistles in the middle of the lessons and the sermon were not conducive to attention, but that was what had been patiently endured at St. Peters for more than twenty years. In addition there was a great dearth of works at the present time. They had at last got a church, and in five or six weeks at most they hoped to be in it. There was a little draw-back—comparatively unimpor- tant—for they had not yet succeeded in getting all the money they wanted. They had raised altoget her £3,500 and they wanted in all, to complete everything even to the boundary wall, about £5.000, so that they required at least £1,500 more. He had now given them an outline of the state of things, and there only remained one thing more to be done and that was to introduce to them the opener of the bazaar. They all knew how long a con- nection there had been between the town of Warrington, and the name of Powys, and it was a thing of which they were all proud that St. Peters was to have the chance of rivettine, a new link in the chain of the connection. (Applause.) The Hon. JOHN POWYS, in opening the bazaar, said it was with the very greatest pleasure he received, a short time ago, an invitation to come there and open that bazaar, because he felt that in so doing he should have the chance of doing something, however small, of furthering a good work, and also because the opportunity was given him of paying his first visit to a place with which his family had been for some years in- timately connected. (Hear, hear.) After what they had just heard, he did not think much remained for him to say as to the work in aid of which that bazaar was held, because Mr. Rigby was much better acquainted with all that than lie could pcssibly be, but lie might perhaps say that upon the amount of money collected depended the consecration of the church, and also upon the consecra.- tiou he believed depended further grants of money. That was a fact they ought not to forget. There was £1,500 further required, and he sincerely hoped that the profits of that bazaar might go a long way towards it. He hap- pened to be present a short time ago at a very interesting ceremony, the reopening of Peterborough Cathedral, after its restoration. As he saw there a large crowd of people, and listened to the very im- pressive service, and marked also the attention given by the large congregation to the bishop's eloquent address, also when lie thought all this had been done and a very large sum collected in a comparatively short time by some earnest workers, and that in an agricul- tural community which had suffered very severely, in the recent hard time, he thought there was in these things a very conclusive answer to the charge some- times made by the church's enemies—the charge of in- difference on the part of her congregations. (Hear, hear.) He was quite sure that Warrington was not going to be beaten by Peterborough. From what he had seen during the short space of time he had been there, and recognising as they all must do the very pressing claims St. Peter's had upon them ho thought a large sum would be forthcoming at the conclusion of that bazaar. (Applause.) He then declared the bazaar open. On Thursday the bazaar was opened by the Bon. Ellinor Wilsm-Patten in the presence of a large gather- ing. The Rev. T. RIGBY in a preliminary statement men- tioned that the sale on Wednesday had realised a little over £4OO. The Hon. ELLlsiort WILSON-PATTEN in declar- ing the bazaar open said she was sorry Lord Winmar- leigh was unable to be present, but it would be a grati- fication to him to hear of the kind manner in which his name had been received. The RECTOR (the Rev. F. W. Willis) announced, amidst applause, that Lord Winmar- leig,h had sent a cheque of £lOO. On Friday the opening ceremony was performed by the Rector of Warrington. The Rev. T. RIGBY men- tioned that the proceeds from all sources up to that time must be at least £750. The RECTOR referred to the generous Jubilee gift of Sir Gilbert Greenall, £1,500 of which had gone to St. Peter's parish, and also to the donation cf £5OO 'from Lord Lilford, Lord Cross had also been kind enough to contribute a yearly sum towards the stipend of the additional clergy of St. Peter's. He should also mention the name of Mr. Wm. Sharp to Whom they were indebted for the site of St. Peter's Church and for additional money help. (Applause.) Mr. T, J. Down's well-known band was present at the bazaar and rendered numerous selections, and the per- formances of Madame Ainsworth, " The mystic marvel" were much enjoyed. The room was kept warm and comfortable by foot-stoves which had been kindly lent by Messrs. T. Fletcher and Company. The cooking de- partment was under the oharge of the chief waiter from the Adelphi, Liverpool, and was also supplied with cook- ing stovss by Messrs. Fletcher and Company.

div.head: GENERAL BOOTH'S SCHEME.
div.p: GENERAL BOOTH'S SCHEME.

General Booth, speaking at Wood Green, London, on Monday night, on his new movement, said he had been inundated with letters on the subject from Royalty, Bishops, Cabinet and ex-Cabinet Ministers, clergymen, and atheists. Archdeacon Farrar has given £5O toward the fund, and promised to preach upon it in Westminster Abbey.

Cardinal Manning has written to " General" Booth a letter: warmly approving his effort. for the benefit of the outcast classes. His Eminence is very severe on modern political economists, and says that every man has a right to bread or to work.

The Press Association says :—We learn that Mrs. Piercey on the day of her arrest admitted to the female searcher, who examined tier clothing in the cell at Holloway, that she sent the invitation to Mrs. Hogg. She said, "I invited Mrs. Hogg to my house. We had a few words. One word led to another. But there, I had not better say anything more about it." The searcher, who comes from Holloway Gaol, was taken to the Treasury this morning. She did not say any- thing to the authorities about the matter uatil Thurs- day evening.

FUNERAL OF THE VICTIMS. On Sunday morning the funeral of Mrs. Hogg and her baby took place at Finchley Cemetery, in the midst of scenes which cannot but be considered as otherwise but disgraceful. Anticipating the presence or a large crowd of spectators, the police authorities had made elaborate arrangements to cope with any attempts at disorder. The weather during the morning was very wet and inclement, but despite this fact a considerable crowd haclgathered in the vicinity of the undertaker's, from where the bodies were to be removed. By half-past eight between 3,000 and 4,000 persons were waiting around the house dis- cussing the circumstances of the crime. About a hun- dred constables were engaged in Camden High-st.' whilst about half that number were placed at intervals further alonc, the route. At twenty minutes to nine o'clock a hansom cab con-, taming Mr. Hogg, husband of the deceased woman, and Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Hogg drove up to the undertaker's. The husband was at once recognised, and amidst groans and hisses from the crowd, an omnious rush was made towards the vehicle, which it required the utmost exer- tions of the constables to repel. The procession consisted of two mourning coaches and a four wheel cab, the , mourners consisting of Mr. Hogg, Mr. and Mrs. Edwin, Hogg, Miss Clara Hogg, Miss Martha Styles, a sister of , the deceased; Miss Elizabeth Styles, a niece ; and two brothers, from Cambridge. The coffin was of polished elm, with black fittings, and.bore the following inscrip- tion ;---" Phcebe Hogg, aged. 32; died 24th Oetober. 1890. Phcebe Hanslope Hogg, aged 18 months, died 24th October, 1890, daughter of the above." Upon it were several wreaths, sent not only by relatives, but bystran- gers as well. Just as the husband •of the murdered woman entered the mourning coach, the mob renewed their efforts to approach it, and for si moment it looked •as if something serious was going t 4 occur. However, the police managed to restrain the hooting crowd, whilst the appearance of some mounted constables from a side street, rendered material aid. For a short dis- tance the crowd accompanied the procession, con- tinuing to groan, but the horses breaking in- to a trot, the majority of the spectators fell behind. At one or two places on the way crowds had gathered and indulged in hooting. A disorderly crowd had congregated at the cemetery, and an unseemly rush was made for the chapel. No special reference was made by the clergyman to the circumstances of the poor woman's death. Upon the termination of the service a most disgraceful scene occurred, the manifestation of hostility towards the husband being renewed, and con- tinued dispite the remonstrances of the clergyman and the chapel attendants, and the police did all they could to prevent him from being molested. It was some dis- tance to the grave; the burial taking place not in the grave belonging to the Hogg family, but in the uncon- secrated portion of the cemetery allotted to common in- terments. During the ceremony at the graveside the behriour of the crowd was more decorous, and in resillinse to the invitation of the minister, many of the , spectators joined in the Lord's Prayer. The service over, the crowd surged around the mourning coaches, and resumed once more the groans and hostile cries in spite of the appeals of many bystaaders "to respect the dead." Escorted by the mounted police the coaches were then driven quickly away, and, mingling with other coaches of a similar character, eluded the recognition of the mob, which soon left the cemetery.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST MRS. PIERCY.
div.p: THE CHARGE AGAINST MRS. PIERCY.

Marylebone Police Court, on Monday afternoon, Mrs. Piercy was charged with the murder of Mrs. Hogg and her baby girl. The court was densely crowded. Mr. Gill. instructed by the Treasury, prosecuted, and the prisoner, whose demeanour was less dejected than last week, was defended by Mr. Freke Palmer. Mr. Gill hav- ing opened the case, Frank S. Hogg, husband of the deceased, was called. He appeared very nervous, and his evidence given last week having been read over, Mr. Gill further examined him. Witness deposed that he married deceased two years ago, and had known the prisoner fouror five years. He first became intimate with the prisoner soon after his marriage, and he had visited her two or three times a week, but he was not supporting her. He believed his wife first became acquainted with the prisoner last Christmas, when ho and his wife stayed at prisoner's house two days. On the night of the murder, not find- ing his wife at home, he went to prisoner's and let him- self in. The prisoner was out and he wrote the follow- ing note:—" Twenty past ten. Cannot stay." Nothing strange attracted his attention. He did once suspect his wife's fidelity, but their relationship had not been strained.

Clara Hogg said she saw the desameed woman leave her house on the afternoon of the tragedy, and go in the direction of the street where the accused lived. Amongst other witnesses called was a neighbour named Piddington, who said she heard windows broken in the prisoner's house, and a baby crying as if in pain. The case was again adjourned to Tuesday next.

div.head: LORD IIARTINGTON IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: LORD IIARTINGTON IN SCOTLAND.

On, Tuesday evening the Marquis of Hartington ad- dressed at Greenock a crowded meeting which had been arranged by the Dissentient Liberal and Conservative Associations of the town. He had been the guest of Sir Michael Shaw Stewart at Ardgowan, and during the day travelled by special train to Glasgow, where the members O f the Imperial Club entertained him at a private dinner. The public meeting at Greenock was held in the Town Hall— a building capable of accommodating fully 3,000 people ; and long before the speaking began, tke hall was filled to its utmost capacity. Mr. R. Kerr, the vice- President of the Greenock Liberal Unionist Association, occupied the chair ; and among others on the platform Were Sir Michael Shaw Stewart, Mr. T. Sutherland, M.P., Star Archibald Campbell, M.P., Mr. Anstruther, M.P., Sir Archibald Orr Ewing, M.P., Mr. Shaw Stewart, M.P., Mr. Thorburn, M.P., Mr. Hozier, M.P., Mr. Cameron Corbett, M.P., and Mr. Parker Smith, M.P. The Mar- qUis of Hartington on entering the hall was received With prolonged cheering, mingled with some hisses, and the singing of "He's a jolly good fellow."—The Chair- Man in a brief address, gave Lord Hartington a hearty Welcome to Greenock, after which the Burgh member, Mr. T. Sutherland, proposed a vote to the effect that that Meeting of Unionists offered to the noble marquis a cor- dlal recognition of the services which he had rendered in maintaining the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament and the umty of the country. The remarks of the hon. gentleman were, as a rule, received with cheering, but Nf.ere from time to time interrupted by manifestations of dissent.—Mr. Shaw Stewart, M.P., seconded the motion Which, on being put, was carried by a great majority, although there were some loud cries of dissent. Lord Hartington on rising to reply, was enthusiasti- tally received. He said that he repudiated, and with all the energy he possessed, protested against the word Which at a railway station, on Monday, was put intolis anouth, that he had ever in Scotland, or in any other Place, said any word as to the possibility of a surrender at the, position of the Unionists. When the day arrived --and it might be long—that a majority had been re- i turned in favour of Home Rule, that would he the time for Unionists to begin to think of the possibility of sur- render. and even when that time came he was afraid , they would be slow to admit the surrender of their Opinions. Till that time came they would utterly decline to recognise in any series of incidents a conclusion as to the issue, which would be presented in a very different 8-sPect when presented to the constituencies of the United Kingdom as a whole than it might appear to the constituents at elections in certain places. (Hear, hear.) Although in Scotland, according to some authorities, the people were down-trodden and trampled un- der foot, they had a knack of getting their own 'Way, and this had been shown even in the matter _of Scotch University Education and Free Education. ressing on to the question of Scottish Home Rule, he said Ile did na think that outside the Scotch Home Rule ' Association there was any great demand for such a change. But though a supporter of the Scottish Act of Union, he did not look upon Home Rule for Scotland With the same apprehension as he had in regard to Home Rule for Ireland. It would be a change for the worse, Nit it would not be, as Home Rule for Ireland would be, the result of an unscrupulous and mischievous rebellion against all authority and all law. Referring to the labour question he said he should be glad to see workers have More time to themselves. So far as it was possible, the state should aim at securing every one a fair wage for a fair day's work. A State, however, like this, in which Millions were dependent upon foreigners buying our manufactured goods, could not act always as it wished, a-nd in attempting to do good, it might do harm. They could not take a Chinese by the throat and make him buy British goods at prices fixed here. The Chinese would always buy in the cheapest market, and the same ?flight be said of other nations. He recommended this I..tnpertant question to the calm consideration of artisans, lor it mainly concerned them. A false move might bring atarvation to millions. (Cheers.)
TWO PLATELAYERS CUT TO PIECES.

, On Wednesday morning, a gang of about thirty plate- were repairing the London and South-Western Ilailway at Colvert Junction. between Queen's-road and Clapham, when a passenger train arrived unnoticed, and two of them were cut to pieces.
NATIONALISTS VISIT TO AMERICA.

Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien have received telegrams from their bondsmen at Tipperary, saying that they will be glad to pay the forfeited bonds if it is necessary. Mr. billon replied that there was no danger of the bondsmen being compelled to pay. The delegates have received a 4....nmber of offers to contribute to the funds ot the Irish ational League.

div.head: THF HOSPITAL SCANDAL
div.p: THF HOSPITAL SCANDAL

It is understood that Dr. Vacher, Medical Officer of yealth for Birkenhead, has appointed Dr. M'Adam Wallace as his deputy, in succession to Dr. Pinkerton, Vho has been stricken down by fever. The hospital scandal is still the theme of indignant comment, and 14eSeral fresh cases of typhus fever are reported.
HOW COLLIERY EXPLOSIONS ARE CAUSED.

On Tuesday, two miners, Henry Sutton and Hendal Lewis, employed at Llanerch Colliery, where six months ago 189 miners were killed by a terrible explosion, were charged before the Pontypool magistrates with having Pipes and matches in their pockets whilst working in the mine. It is believed the recent disaster was caused through a naked light. The magistrates severely repre- anded the men, and sentenced them to seven days' -imprisonment with hard labour.

ANOTHER IMPORTANT CASE TO AiI)LOYERS.

_ At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, be- fore Measrs. R. Garnett (in the chair), and Wm. Owen, Joseph Waterhouse, a sub-contractor, em- ployed at the forge of Messrs. Monks Hall and Co., , Atherton's Quay, was summoned on a charge of having, on the 4th of last month and on divers other days, unlawfully paid to his workmen their wages on the licensed premises of John Hill, land- lord of the Coach and Horses, contrary to Section 3 of "The payment of wages in the public-houses Prohibition Act,1883." This was the first case beard under this Act at Warrington, and caused a good deal of interest. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. P. Davies appeared on behalf of Mr. Waterhouse.—Mr. Browne said the Act under which Waterhouse was charged was one of those prohibitive Acts which were greatly to the benefit of the working ' class. This case arose in consequence of a dispute—a technical dispute—which was heard at that Court on ' Monday week, when a man named Brace sued Water- house for damages for unlawful dismissal ; and from the evidence which was given by defendant and other wit- nesses at the hearing of the case it appeared that the men were paid regularly at the public-house stated, and ' Mr. Brace would tell their worships that he was hardly raid anywhere else, but Messrs. Monks Hall and Co., were not in the slightest degree to blame for the offence. The Act of Parliament said that no wages should be paid to any workman at or within any public-house. Now one of the witnesses in the case last week said he was paid in the passage of the house cne time, and on another occasion just outside, in the yard, and this was an offence against the Act. After some further remarks Mr. Browne called his witnesses.—William Brace, said he had been employed under Mr. Water- house about 13 months, and a month last Saturday he was paid in the passage of the Coach and Horses,and wit- ness had been paid many times in the same house during the period that he had been in defendant's employ.— William Howell, who, Mr. Browne said, deposed last week that he had been paid in the public-house, now denied that he had. whereupon Mr. Browne said he would have to ask for a warrant against the witnesses for com- mitting perjury. The evidence he gave last week, he saiel, was taken down by a shorthand writer, and he (Mr. Browne) held in his hand the transcript. In answer to a further question by Mr. Browne, witness emphatic- ally repudiated ever having been paid in the Coach and Horace or even in the passage of the house.—William Brinksman,who also was on the side for the prosecution, made a statement to the effect that he had not been paid in the public-house, which was quite adverse, according to Mr. Browne's version, to what he said last week; and upon hearing this Mr. Browne characterised these two witnesses as hostile, and said he would read the transcript of the shorthand notes.—Mr. Davies, however, strongly objected to this, and said Mr. Browne was not au- thorized by the Town Clerk to take the present action.— Frederick Wm. Woods, reporter, for the "Liverpool Courier," was then called by Mr. Browne, and he said he was in Court on Monday week and was requested by Inspec- tor Cox to take a shorthand note of Brinksman's evi- dence. lie did so, and in his evidence Brinkman said he had been paid in the Coach and Horses, but he was not always paid there.—Mr. Brown suggested that the magis- trates had now better warn the witness Brinksman.—Mr. Davies contended that the man never made such a state- ment last week.—The Chairman said he thought witnesses in this case must be aware that they were swearing con- trary to what they said last week,and were, consequently, liable to be charged with perjury which was a serious charge.—Brinksman then admitted that he had been paid once in the Coach and Horses 14 months ago.—lnspt. Cox said he took a note of Waterhouse's evidence given in the case last week and in cross-examination, Water- house said" I have been in the habit of going to the Coach and Homes to pay the men up to three months ago."— ; Detective-Sergt. Monaghan gave corroborative evidence. ' —Mr. Davies, during the course of his speech for the defence, said he thought if ever there was a malicious case in this world it was the one before the Court, and a more frightful one belled never heard of; and the way that the case had crept into the Court was most disgraceful.— Mr. Browne told them he was prosecuting on behalf of the police ; but he (Mr. Davies) maintained that it was not his duty but the Town Clerk's duty to do so.—Mr. Browne said that those remarks clearly assailed him, and he could call Inspector Cox to prove that he was engaged to conduct the case for the police by him, and the In- spector would also say that Mr. Whittle requested him to ask him (Mr. Browne) to take the case.—Mr. Davies then proceeded to summarize the evidence for the prosecution and submitted that it was worthless. To put the facts short he said the gist of the evidence proved that the men had not received their wages in the public-house for at least three months back, for since that time altera- tions had been made. Several witnesses gave evidence in support of his statement, after which the Bench said they felt they must dismiss the case for the evidence given in reference to the payment of wages, on October 4th or any date since, in the public-house, was nob con- clusive.

div.p: T. A II ii:OSSE.
WARRINGTON V. STOCKPORT A. AT STOCKPORT.

This match was played on the Stockport and Cheshire County Cricket Ground and resulted in a win for the Warringtonians by 6 goals to 2. The grass was very long, thus rendering picking up very difficult. Bennett and Tyler faced at about 3.30, and the Warrington defence was kept very busy during the first quarter of an hour, by the sharp attacks of Stockport, who played a very nice, clean, and combined game. Repeatedly they were within an ace of scoring, but the visitors' gaol- keeper was there, and saved in brilliant style, one shot seemed almost a dead certainty being cleared away smartly by the hand. At last the Warringtoniana smartened up, and one of their homes received a neat pass and shot a beautiful goal. After some very even play, the visitors scored again, and the home attacks playing up managed to score, and at half time the game stood 2 goals all. After change of ends the visitors were not to be denied and quickly scored a couple of goals followed soon after by two more and thus the game ended in favour of the Warringtonians as stated above. Warrington stayed somewhat better than their opponents, pressing the game towards the end. Their attacks played well, getting loose and with combination, a great improvement on last Saturday's play. Walker and Tyler played best for Stockport. div.head: LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE GOVERNMENT.
div.p: LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE GOVERNMENT.

The " Mall Gazette "has the best of reasons for 1 stating that the rumours about " Lord Randolph Church- ill's return" are absolutely devoid of foundation in fact. I Not only have no negotiations for that "return," so far , as Lord Randolph Churchill is concerned, been in pro- gress, but Lord Randolph has had no political communi- ations of any sort or kind, direct or indirect, verbal or ,epistplary, with any politician or person connected with politicians, since the end of the session. So complete is P Lord Randolph Churchill's present estrangement from his old love, politics, that he is going abroad in a few days' time and will not be back till after the New Year.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY ACROSS ENGLAND.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY ACROSS ENGLAND.

The following paragraph has gone the round of the papers and has excited considerable interest, i but it is now stated that it has no solid foundation: —The Great Northern and Great Eastern Railway Companies are arranging to deposit a bill for the construction of a railway from King's Lynn on the I east coast, to Liverpool on the west. The route, which has already been surveyed, passes through Lincolnshire, Derbyshire, Cheshire, and Lancashire. One of the principal stations will be at Lincoln, and then the line passes through Chesterfield, Baslow, near Chatsworth Park, crosses the midland line on the east side of Millers Dale, and thence goes to Buxton, Macclesfield, Warrington and Liverpool.

' ELECTRIC RAILWAY OPENED IN LONDON, The Prince of Wales opened the City and South Lon- don Electric Railway on Tuesday, turning oa with a gold key the electric current that supplied both motive power to the train and illuminated the interior of the carriages. The journeys to Bennington Oval and Stockwell were made with remarkable success, and the Prince of Wales afterwards entertained at luncheon, said the new railway would do much to alleviate the congestion of traffic. It was a remarkable railway from a scientific point of view, land it had this great advantage, that in the tunnels there I was neither steam or smoke, and the ventilation was ample. The uniform payment of fare and the abolition of the ticket system also met with his commendation. Ele wished success to the new undertaking, saying the great- ' est credit was due to those who had contrived and car- ried out the scheme. Among the speakers were Mr. C. G. Mott, the chairman of the Company, and Mr. W. Mather, M.P. The latter said the working of a railway by electricity might be thought a rash enterprise on the part of his firm, but there must be pioneers in every new departure in the application of science to the require- ments of mankind. He added that but for a certain staff at the Salford Ironworks—a staff of apprentices who had enjoyed the benefits of our technical schools—his firm would not have been able to carry out with the same facility the experiments necessary to the satisfactory execution of the work.

fight. I firmly believe that, with a little education, the Latchford electors will change their representatives. It was a pity Mr. Stringer's address was not sooner in the hands of the electors, for on all sides I have heard it well spoken of since the election. At any rate Mr. Stringer has made a good impression, and I do not think it will be long before he finds a seat in the Town Council. With the exception of these two Wards, the answer of the ratepayers has been a very vigorous response to the "final blow to Radicalism in Warrington." Everybody is anxious to know how your Tory Con- temporary will account for its cocksure prophecies last 1 week; but it is only charitable to suppose that the I Editor had misplaced his spectacles and had cense- , queatly mixed his figures. I was amongst the crowd at the Town Hall when the results were declared, and I can assure you I felt sorry for;the Tory Aldermen. They have not had such a bitter pill to swallow for a long time • and they did not at all relish their work. Some of them would gladly have delegated their duties to others if they could ; but the work had to be done, and, by putting on the best face they could, they got through. The Tory paper has been constantly telling us that Litnalism was dead, but the Editor will doubtless have realised by this that it has a surprising amount of vital- I ity in it yet. It is not to be killed by Tory misrepresen- tation, by Tory meanness, or by Tory dictation. Such tactics only serve to stimulate the energies of the des- pised po.,ple ; and I trust that, having been roused from its lethargy, the Liberalism of Warrington will continue to make itself known, and thus rid the Town Council of the Tory majority that has so long dominated it.— Yours Rix.,
A LIBERAL.

TB.E LATE FEAST AT THE RUNCORN RATE- PAYERS' EXPENSE. Sir,—l see by a recent letter which appeared in the columns of your valuable journal that our worthy Corn- tnissioners have at last addressed the ratepayers through their Secretary Mr. Marshall. I have not the honour of knowing Mr. Marshall personally, but I am sure from the tenour of his letter he is a nice man, and clever —intellectually a veritable Goliath. Now I know nothing of any correspondence which has taken place on this subject, or whether "gross mis-statements were made by your correspondents" or not; but I am rather inclined to believe that a sore place has been touched somehow, judging from the alacrity with which the Secretary jumps into the pugilistic ring, cudgel in hand, to do battle for his employers, and lays so fiercely around him with all his might and main. Well,having thus got their best fighting man,as I ta.ke it, stiipped to the buff and well rubbed down, let me have a friendly round or two with him. I notice he says in his epistle in speaking of the feast—which was given to the Board's officials in connection with the late election that—" there were several officials present (i.e. who partook of the turtle dinner) who had not been engaged in the election, and the cost was 7s. per head "—a nice state of matters this sure enough. He admits the cost of the feast was £.5 145., and the charge 7s. per head, consequently, 16 must have feasted at the ratepayers' expense, nine of whom had in no way been engaged in the election during the day. I insist, sir, that he give the names of those nine highly-favoured individuals who thought it was consistent with their position to have a 7s. dinner at the ratepayers' expense; and also the names of the party in authority who authorised the dinner. May I further ask—were either of the reporters re- presenting the two local newspapers invited to this sumptuous feast? I trow not. Further on in his letter he says—" I know that I am speaking the minds of other officers concerned when I say that we are perfectly indifferent as to whether we have a dinner at the ratepayors' expense or not," Bravo ! bravo ! I should think so, considering the high salaries paid them. How is that for high Mr. Paylor ? There is a noble ring of real sturdy, manly independence in these words. In the face of this rebuff, it is rather amusing to recall the laboured remarks of the Chairman, who" in the green simplicity of his heart " so solemnly and feel- ingly pourtrayed the starved and famished appearance of the officers after toiling and slaving from 9 o'clock in the morning till 5 o'clock in the afternoon at the polling booths. Their condition, poor things, according to Mr. Taylor was even worse than that of seven other animals seen by a celebrated ancient Egyptian dreamer, the re- sult in both cases being the same, with this slight difference that our Commissioners' seven officials ate the cows after having been cooked, while King Pharaoh's seven were not so particular, and saved their master the expense of cooking.—l am, Mr. Editor yours very truly,
THOMAS ARROWS.
Mill-brow, Runcorn, Oct. 31st, 1890.

div.p: tettero to the attar.

_ "STANDING ET TO THE CLERGY, &C." Sir,-1 see by the Examiner Oct. 24th, 1890, a letter signed "A Churchman, Runcorn." The whole matter may be answered by three texts out of the Bible. "Let things be done decently and in order." As to his view of .4 doing as others do," remember we are "not to follow a multitude to do evil." The Biblical example as to when we are to stand up—whether on the entry of the clergy and choir, or at the commencement of divine service—is given in Nehemiah viii. 4.5., "And Ezra the Scribe stood up upon a pulpit of wood, which had been made for the purpose And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people (for he was above all the people) and when he opened it all the people stood up."—Yours OBSERVER. Nov. 3rd, 1890.

-- Sir,—The letter of " Churchman" endeavours to beg the question. The Parish Church at Runcorn must beat a low ebb if only such writer stands up under non de plume to defend a false system. This absurd question and tittle-tattle of whathe heard in Some church is beside the subject. I was at service in their churches all larger than Runcorn, lately, in which they did not stand, turn at Creeds, or intone the prayers. Did "Churchmen" never see a flock of sheep follow its leader? So it is with regard to standing ; people often do it becauae Mr. So-and-so does, and they do not want to appear singular. -Here it has been announced in the Sunday school that children must stand when the parson and choir enter church; they do not obey, neither do five sixth of the Vicar's " dear people." It is amusing to hear that people are being kept back from Christ through error being exposed. The truth has nothing to fear from controversy. Why does not Rev. J.Holden accept my challenge to discuss the subject ot apostolic succession Christ entered into controversy with the Priests, Scribes,Pharises, Sadducees and others. He not only put the truth before the people, but exposed the errors of those who led the people astray. I advise " Churchman" to take the advice of Augustine, "Let not these words be heard between us, I say' or you say' but rather let us hear, "Thus saith the Lord." Stephen had a dispute with the High Priest and told the I men and brethren, "That God dwelleth not in temples made with hands " ; called them stiff necked, for these sayings they stoned him to death. Let me tell " Church- men " that clergy, who adopt the eastward position are practically doing what Stephen denounced. Will he dare to say that during the late Mission the following Popish dogmas were not taught :—Baptismal regeneration, con- firmation, priestly absolution, Auricular confession and real presence ? Yours Sic.,
ROBERT FOULKES.
Frodsham, Oct. 29th, 1890.

" WHEER ARE E WEREIN NEAW r Mester Examiner, avent trubled yo lately, but ah thowt ad just tel yo that ad bin takkin a squint at th' lection fur th' Warriton Town Kounsellers. Wot a change as kum ore things sin ah wor a lad. Wen ah wor a youngster, at th' lectinn time theer wor plenty o' ale knockin about. Yo cud a got a tooth tam n out an' a blak eye just fur oppenin yore chops. But sin th' skoo boords ave bin on th' stocks, things ave awterd a lot. Last Seturty, yo cud a seed Radakels an Torys flyin about tryin to get ther men in—tha wer shakin bonds we one a nother. Yo mite a thowt tha aw belonged to one skoo. Th' only 'bit a nasty dirt ive seen throt'durin th' election wor that throt at th'Kanda,date fur St. Austin's Ward. It had tak summot stronger tun sun lite cope to wash them hoods cleon, as throt that ; they wa're durty above skin deep. Iv'e eard fellows spodin afore now on'th platform talkin abeavrt "the most cursery observer." Tha knoed wot tha wor sayin. But, Mester, crows cum worn to roost. It reminds one abeawt Barak wen he axt Balam to curse this people. We'er did th' curse drop, Mester? Ah' If yo con'no anser, Mester, just creep in th' Tory Club and put yore eye to th'-k'-ole an see that usuly quiet moo Robert Pierpoint slappin th' Tory babies afore puttin urn to bed, and hear im saucen urn :—" Yo nowty urchens go to bed an tak that wa vo, Ile giv yo more next time." Yole soon sea then we7'er th' mud dropt. Mester, if tha'd kept better hours, it wod a bin better fur um. Ah wonder we'er the " Observer " mon ad bin ore neet wen he settled th' lection afore it cum off —bloNsin th' Rad's to smithereens, not levin so much as a cote tale beind to devulge th' tale' o' wo. Him as lafs last—lafs best, Mester; "Ahab ah"—good neet ! Ah mun be of to bed; Robert's commin.—Gradely yors, A WORKIN MON.

THE LIBERAL VICTORY IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—' would thank you for the insertion of the ac- companying in your valuable paper. There is great wisdom in the words "Never prophecy unless you know," and no doubt by now the editor of your Tory gratis contemporary wishes he had followed the advice 'therein contained. The municipal elections just over were undoubtedly fought on political grounds, and were considered a trial of strength by both parties. On the one side was "the great Conservative party" backed by its powerful organisation, and its boasted majority of eight or nine hundred ; and on the other, 'the handful of puny Radicals, with ruin in their midst. And yet, Sir, what a result! " How are the mighty fallen"! They are scattered broadcast by the inhabitants of this.good old town. The Tory paper, not only predicted the return of all their candidates, which of itself was extremely ridi- culous, but circulated (as is the Tory wont at election times) a heap of slanderous statements. Undoubtedly, The "lying spirit has been abroad." The gentleman most bitterly attacked, was the" very unpopular candi- date" for Whitecross Ward, Mr. Henry Roberts, the man they said nobody respected. Sir, the statements put forward about this gentleman are as contemptible and ridiculous as they are untrue. He has himself totally refuted some of them, but, as one of the many workers on his behalf, allow me to say, that the editor of your "free-gratis for-nought" contemporary, must ho void of common sense, to circulate such a foolish lie as the one in which he said Radical canvassers were using Mr. John Roberts' name to mislead the electors. Just fancy, I sir, trying to win an election with the name of one who was so thoroughly beaten by the same voters, only a few months sinc, ! With reference to the chalk marking, I challenge the truth thereof, having canvassed almost all the electors ; but this is such an absurd statement as to not be worth further notice. Sir, we have won a grand victory over the united Tory party, who went so thoroughly into the affray that they brought out their old chief, in his yellow war chariot, . and paraded him round the town. The Bold-st. barrister, was also about, accompanied by the smaller fry of the party; but, notwithstanding all this, the weak, disor- ganised Radicals won three seats. I suppose they will now blame their poor Registration Agent for statements about their supposed gains at the Revision Court; but, be their excuse what it may, they are completely nonplussed. The lesson to the Liberals is this, that they have only to work in the same gallant way at the next election, as they did on Saturday last, and Warrington will again be represented by a follower of the Grand Old Mn, and take its proper position as one of the Radical boroughs of Lancashire .—Yours, ONE OF TUE ANNIHILATED RADICALS.
LAST SATURDAY'S ELECTIONS IN WARRING- TON.

Sir,—Allow me to congratulate 9my fellow Liberals on the grand success they achieved on Saturday last. It augurs well for Liberalism at the coming General Elec- tion, that in spite of the frantic efforts of the Tories to secure a victory, the Liberals were able, in so unobtrusive a manner, to almost annihilate the Tory party. It NY OS only by the skin of his teeth—as it were—that Mr. Rep- herd won in St. Austinms Ward, and there is not the slightest doubt in my mind that, but for the dispicable manner in which the Tory paper dragged to the front the family matters of Mr. Titchett, the latter gentleman would have also been amonost the successful Libera candidates. However, there is every reason for Mr. Titchett to congratulate himself upon the result of the contest, and to remember, when he fights again, the say- ing about the " third tone." div.head: DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORM AT RAIN HILL ASYLUM.
div.p: DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORM AT RAIN HILL ASYLUM.

On Saturday Mr. S. Brigkouse, coroner, held an inquest at Rainhill Asylum, touching the death of Catherine Maloney, a widow, 34 years of age, an in- mate of the institution and formerly of Liverpool Workhouse. Dr. Wigglesworth, medical superin- tendent of the asylum, was present at the injury. The Coroner, addressing the jury, remarked that the inquiry was somewhat important. The deceased was an inmate of that institution, and died on the 30th ultimo. For some reason it became necessary to put the deceased under chloroform, either for the purpose of undergoing an operation or for an exam- ination, but whilst she was under the effects of the chloroform she died. It was for the jury to say whether they thought it necessary that the chloro- form should have been administered, and whether or not they thought any one was to blame for the death of the patient. Dr. William Francis Menzies, senior assistant surgeon, said the deceased had been in a condition which gave considerable and grave anxiety to the medical officers of the asylum for about days previous to Thursday last, and presented symptoms which they could not exactly tell the import of without a full examination of the abdo- men. It was therefore decided, after consultation I with his colleagues, that an anmsthetic should be administered and a thorough internal examination made. The patient was accordingly prepared on Thursday morning to receive the anmsthetic, and at five minutes to two in the afternoon he com- menced to anwthetise her with chloroform in the presence of his colleague, Dr. Beaver. At fifteen minutes past two her respiration ceased, and the administration was instantly stopped. All the known methods of restoring respiration were resorted to. About half a minute later respiration was resumed spontaneously, and five or six f till normal breaths occurred. At that stage both respiration and the heart ceased. Their efforts were contined for three-quarters of an hour, until certain signs of death appeared. He added that he was present at the post-mortem examination of the body by Dr. Beaver, and he accounted for death as the result of tubercular tumour. That was the secondary cause, the primary cause being the adminstration of the chloroform. Dr. Robert Atwood Beaver, assistant medical officer at the asy- lum, gave corroborative evidence.—The coroner remarked a misunderstanding had arisen between him and Dr. Wigglesworth as to the right to have I post-mortems made in that establishment. He (the coroner) thought it was desirable that a medical man from outside should make the examination and tell the jury what he thought, and that was the rea- son he had asked Dr.;Knowles, of St. Helens,to make an examination, and to come and tell them vhat he thought.—Dr. Fred Knowles, of St. Ilelens, then deposed that on Friday night he made a re-examina- tion of the body. The organs were more or less diseased, the lungs being studded with tubercles, and formed the tumour to which reference hadbeen made. He had heard the previous medical evidence and agreed with it. Ile should have administered chloroform under the circumstances in the case of a private patient.—The Coroner then briefly summed up, and said he thought there was a necessity for; calling in the services of a medical man not con- nected with the institution, because, without sug- gesting for one moment that Dr. Wiggleworth or any of his assistants would say anything that was wrong, he thought they themselves would admit that it was better than an independent opinion should be given to enable the jury to give a verdict. The jury after 15 minutes' consultation, returned a verdict of "Death by misadventure," no blame being attached to any one. •

div.head: SERIOUS MILL FIRES.
div.p: SERIOUS MILL FIRES.

Low Folds Mills, Leeds, took fire on Thursday morn- ing, and the flock room and its machinery and stock were destroyed. Messrs. Hillas's mill, at Bradford. was destroyed by fire on Wednesday morning. The loss will amount to £12,000.

div.head: ATTEMPTED OUTRAGE.
div.p: ATTEMPTED OUTRAGE.

A carter named Shard, living at Bramall, was charged I at Stockport, on Thursday, with an attempted outrage upon a young woman in a railway train. The prosecu- trix was unable to appear. It will be remembered that in order to escape from her assailant she got on to the foot- board of the carriage and fell on the line, receiving an injury which necessitated the amputation of one of her feet. The prisoner was remanded.

div.head: MTh GOSCHEN AT HALIFAX.
div.p: MTh GOSCHEN AT HALIFAX.

-- The Chancellor of the Exchequer made a visit , on Thursday to Halifax. In opening a new Con- servative Club in the afternoon he referred to the subject of by-elections. He did not think these elections had the significance attributed to them, and urged his friends not to be , disheartened by reverses of this kind. In the evening Mr. Goschen ad- dressed a great meeting in the Drill Hall. His speech was largely devoted to a criticism of the recent Mid- lothian addresses of Mr. Gladstone. He complained that Mr. Gladstone had given no hint as to what his views were on various questions of great public interest, and in answer to "a man in the body of the hall" who remarked that he should give Mr. Gladstone" a chance" he said that they could not give a man a chance who refused to say what his policy would be if he were put into office.

div.head: VOLCANIC-AERATION COMPANY.
div.p: VOLCANIC-AERATION COMPANY.

The North-western Aeration Co., Ld., is formed for the supply of machines for the manufacture of aerated waters or draught, and in bottles' under Farrow and Jackson's. The capital of the Company is .£lOO,OOO, divided into 100,000 shares of .£1 each. As an evidence of the popularity which these patent machines have attained it is pointed out that Messrs. Spiers and Pond have fitted the refreshment bars at the Royal Military Exhibition, Chelsea, the great exhibition of the present season, exclusively with the Company's apparatus thereby indicating the confidence with which they are able to rely upon this process entirely for their supply of aerated waters. The prospectus of the Company will be found in our advertising columns.

div.head: DUKE OF ARGYLL ON THE IRISH LAND QUESTION.
div.p: THE DUKE OF ARGYLL ON THE IRISH LAND QUESTION.

Mr. Arthur Bennett, of Warrington, author of "John Bull and His Other Isllnd," a descrip- tive narrative of three journeys in Ireland, has received a letter from the Duke of Argyll in which , he says:—" I have to thank you for a very interest- ing little volume, which I have read with much pleasure. Many of the anecdotes you tell of con- versations with Irishmen of all classes are full of suggestiveness on points of great importance. Amongst others, lam struck by the evidence you have collected showing what an utter failure has been the attempt to regulate the price of the hire of land by the State. The result is that nobody is really satisfied of the "fairness" of the so-called "judicial rents." Each man thinks he has a right to judge the "judgments." And so he has. The Commissioners are not judges in any sense of the word. They administer no known law, but only exercise a purely arbitrary discretion."

div.head: LA.NCA SHIRE Ac UAL SESSION.
div.p: LA.NCA SHIRE Ac UAL SESSION.

-- -- ITS "FUNERAL OBSEQUIES." On Thursday, an adjourned annual session of county magistrates was held in the County Hall, Preston, the Right Hon. J. T. Hibbert presiding. There were fifteen other magistrates present. The Clerk of the Peace read a letter he had received from the Earl of Derby, who desired to know whether Mr. Jacson's proposal (for the abolition of the Lan- cashire Sessions Act) was only a formal matter, or the expression of an opinion of the magistrates. because he entirely agreed with the proposal, and would support it if in danger of defeat.—Eighteen members having been elected on the Standing Joint Committee for police and other purposes, the Chairman spoke of the unanimity with which that committee had worked during the past twelve months, and referred especially to their action in respect of the emoluments of the Clerk of the Peace. Mr. Jacson (chairman of the Finance Committee) drew attentioii of the court to the memorandum that had been circulated among me inetgistraLes, osmla was to show briefly the work that had formerly been done by annual sessions, and the very small amount that still remained to be done by that court. Having expressed an opinion that it might be desirable that the appointment of justices should be transferred to the County Council, Mr. Jascen proposed—" That, in the opinion of this court, the necessity for the con- tinuance of the Lancashire Annual Sessions Act no longer exists, and that it ought to be repealed." The Chairman said he could not avoid saying a word upon what might bethought to be the funeral obsequies of the annual ses- sion. He was sure they would not be doing justice to that body if, at this probably last occasion on which they would meet as an annual session, they did not speak in the strongest words possible of the great ability and the very great economy and good management which had been shown by the magistrates during the whole of that period, in the transaction of the county business. Mr. Higgin seconded the motion, which was then put,and agreed to unanimously. It was also resolved that appli- cation be made to the Secretary of State for an altera- tion in the order relating to the appointment of visiting committees of prisons, in accordance with the suggestion of Mr. Jacson. The court then separated.

WESLEYAN BAND OF Horn.--A meeting in connection with the above society was held on Monday evening in the schoolroom, Rush Green. There was not as large an attendance as usual. Mr. J. Thorpe presided, and several readings, recitations, &c., were contributed by the members. DRUNILENNESS.—A. labourer named James Skelhorn, of Broom Edge. near Lyrnin, was locked up on Sunday in the Lymm Police Station, on a charge of being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Ennion in the execution of his duty. He was brought up before Mr. R. H. Joynson on Monday, and fined ss. and costs for each offence. P.C. Ennion gave evidence in support ot the charge. A. VISIT TO TIPPERARY.—Mr. James Dodds, of Lymm, returned home on Saturday after spending a few days in Tipperaty, the scene of the recent extraordinary trials. It is stated that whilst he, in company with two or three members of Parliament, were inspecting New Tipperary, he was subjected to the rather unpleasant experience of being "shadowed." Mr. Dodds has brought back with him several photographs showing the extent to which the " shadowing " system is a vogue in Ireland. TICE FUSTIAN CUTTING TRADE AT LYMIL—The Lord Bishop of Chester, on tho occasion of his visitation to the Bowdon Rural Deanery on Friday, inquired whether the fustian cutting trade, both of Lymm and Oughtrington, was not being re-shaped. The Rector of Lymm, the Rev. G. W. Guest said the trade was dying out. The Bishop asked whether new machines were being intro- duced, and the Rector, :in reply, said he did not think any new machinery was being adopted, many of the young men in Lymm having gone to work on the Ship Canal. Probably when that was completed, they would return to fustian cutting, which was a demoralizing

trade. LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board took place on Thursday night. Present :—Mr. D. Rogers, in the chair; also Messrs. W. Brazendale, J. r Gibbon, F. Swallow, and J. Thomason; Messrs. Ridg- way and Mullard (clerks), James Mort (surveyor), and Severs (gas manager).—Dr. Fox called attention to a section of the Public Health Amendment Act which gave the Board powers over private slaughter-houses. lie pointed out that at present a slaughter-house once licensed remained always licensed, butunder this section the Board had power to grant licenses for any term not exceeding 12 months, and in case of violation of the terms of the license it may be withheld. He also called attention to section 47, which was of great importance. It stated that " It shall not be allowable to throw or place in any stream, river, or watercourso any cinders, ashes, stone, rubbish, filth, or other matter which is likely to cause annoyance to anyone, und€ r a penalty of Os. for each offence."—A letter was read from the Ship Canal Company complaining of the Board interfering with their frontage and hacking water oa their land by the syphon sill on Rush Green.—The matter was referred to tho surveyor.—This was all the business before the Board.

Madame Patti was announced to sing at Leicester on Wednesday evening, but was unable to fulfil her engage- ment owing to a sudden attack of illness. A Shanghai telegram says that immediately after the the termination of the recent Buddhist festival organised mobs set out to attack the Christian villages in the pro- vince of Szechuen, burning and looting in all d ions. At least twenty native converts were killed, their bodies being thrown into the Yang-tse-Kiang. Dr. James Frank Bright, the master of University College, Oxford, was shot, on Thursday night:, in the abdomen, by a lady who called to see him. She immediately left and and is still at large. The police are very reticent about the affair. The medical gentle- men in attendance have succeeded in extracting the bullet, and Dr. Bright is progressing satisfactorily. The motive for the conunission of the crime is at present a mystery.

div.head: HE CAME HOME TO DIE
div.p: HE CAME HOME TO DIE

One day in December, 1888, a British transport vessel arrived at Gosport. Only a brief look was needed to assure the spectator that she laad made the long voyage from India. There were soldiers on board; some on leave of absence to visit home, and others so worn and wasted that it was plain to see why they were come back from the East to the dear old Island. Of these poor fellows a few were able to go on to their friends, while others were just strong enough to bear the journey to the Navy Yard Hospital. Among the latter was one to whom we will introduce the reader.—You would have fancied him to have been about thirty years of age, yet the vigour and elasticity o youth were inissing.—Disease had done the work of time, and it was but the wreck of a man that entered the E al doors that day. It was a matter for wonder that he lived to reach an English port. Several months later, by accident, the writer of these lines heard that soldier's story from his own lips, and here it is substantially in his own words. "In the year 1683," he said," I enlisted in her Majesty's 51st Regi- ment, which was soon ordered out to India, where we arrived on the following Christmas ; and left there for lharmah Oct. 6th, 188 e, where we remained eighteen months, being present at Mandalay when King Theebaw surrendered to our troops. Here my good health began to give way. At first I had a sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach, and was so dull and drowsy I could scarcely keep up. I had pain in the right side and under the shoulder blades. My spirits were depressed, and everything seemed sad and melancholy. I couldn't eat, and lay in bed sleepless night after night, till I was almost wild for lack of rest. My skin and eyes turned yellow, as is so common with Europeans in India; my tongue was badly coated, feet cold and clammy, stomach sick and upset, vomiting, and constant diarrhea. Ia this bad form I lay in bed for four months in 1887. Both the Regimental doctor, and Dr. Bell of the Indian Government said I was suffering from dysentery. I was as weak as a baby, and passed nothing but slime from the bowels. No treatment availed to stop the diarrheea, which was fast draining the life out of me. Finally, I was sent home, and arrived at Gosport in December, 1888, where I lay in the hospital until Feb., 1889, when I was discharged as incurable, and placed in In the Army Reserve. "I returned to Warboys, in Huntingdonshire (my home), and tried to work. But it was impossible. I was so emaciated that old acquaintances did not at first recognise me. Then they said, Hodson, you needn't trouble to buy any more clothes. The only suit you'll require will be a wooden box." After eating even a little, I was obliged to hurry away from the table because of the terrible griping, gnawing pains in the stomach and bowels. My father and mother were alarmed, and I consulted a doctor at Warboys, but what he gave me had no good effect. At last it was Mr. Nicholl, the chemist, of Warboys (now of Croydon) who said to me, 'Hodson, you had better try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. On this I bought a bottle and used it, but I couldn't see it did any good. Mr. Nicholl said, " try it again, I have such confidence in it that I will give you the second bottle free of charge.' He did so, and before I had taken the half of the second bottle I began to feel relief. This was encou- raging, and I procured the third bottle. Before I had finished it I was so much improved that I was asked to go back to work. But I was afmid to risk it,and said, No ; wait till I have used three bottles more, for this Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup is doing for me what no Medicine in India or England has done yet, it is healing me from the very depths where I was ill and dying. So, as you may suppose, I kept right along with Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup until the fifth bottle was gone. Then I presented myself to the astonished people of Warboys as robust, strong, and well as I was when I first entered the army. I returned to my work, and my comrades looked upon me as one risen from the dead. With eyes full of wonder, they asked, "What has done this for you ?" and I answered, " I owe my life and health to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and am willing that everybody in England should hear me say so." I have le-o• ee hour's work since, and will gladly reply to letters of inquiry.—John Hodson, Warboys, Huntingdon- shire. Mr. Hodson's real disease was indigestion and dys- pepsia, caused by change of climate, food, and habits. The diarrhcea was one of its symptoms—Nature's effort to get rid of the poisonous matters in the stomach and bowels. Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup cured the diges- tive malady, and the symptoms vanished as a necessary consequence. But our friend did not get the right and only remedy a day too soon.

TECE REV. S. WILKINSON APPOINTED VICAR OF TIMPERLEY.

The Rev. S. Wilkinson, M.A., vicar of St. Paul s Church, Warrington, has been appointed vicar of Timperley, Cheshire, and will, we understand, leave this town about the middle of December. Mr. Wilkinson is, one of the most esteemed ministers in Warrington and his departure will be viewed with regret by the whole of the town but particularly by his own parishioners. His long connection with St. Paul's of eighteen years has been a period of active and successful work on the part of both Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson. During that time St. Barnabas Church was built and the separate parish of St. Barnabas constituted, and St. Paul's itself was repaired, the Mission Church was built in Hoyle-st., by Sir Gilbert Greenall, and the Girl's School at Heath Side by the late Mr. Beamont. Altogether during those years there has been expended in St. Paul's parish church and school building and other similar work a sum of not less than £ll,OOO. The Sunday scholars at the begin- ning of Mr. Wilkinson's ministration num- bered only about 3,00, but now there are about 1,300, and the day schools have also largely in- creased. Numerous parochial societies and other agencies for good have been set on foot by Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson, such as Mothers' Meetings, a Band of Hope, Mothers' Union, and a Girls' Friendly Society. In all their work, the Vicar of St. Paul's and his wife have been zealously aided by a large band of lay workers which numbers as many as 200 men and women. Mrs. Wilkinson has regularly conducted a large Bible class every Sunday afternoon, and Mr. Wilkinson has himself taken charge ,of a Bible class for young men twice every Sunday. The utmost har- mony and good-will have always prevailed between thA vicar end his pfirighio.ner.s. While never ceas- ing to maintain to his principles as a clergyman or the Church of England, Mr. Wilkinson has always held out the right hand of fellowship to those who differed from him on religion; and, with regard to another branch of work, it may be mentioned that he was elected the first president of the Warring- ton Temperance Federation, an office which is now held by the Rector of Warrington. Timperley, to which Mr. Wilkinson is about to remove, is a pretty country village near Altrincham. It has a beautiful comfortable vicarage, and three Church of England schools. The population is largely composed of villa residents—Manchester merchants and other business men, but there is also an agricultural population. The value of the living is given in Crockford as £320 a year.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Sr. JOHN'S PRESHYTERIAN CHURCH. On Sunday evening the Rev.J. Warnock, preached from the subject "The house that Solomon built, and how what he did concerns ourselves." There was a full congregation. THE ROSE AND CROWN HARRIERS. A meeting was held at the clubroom of the above club on Tuesday evening, Mr. Massey, of the War- rington llarriers, being oresent. At the close of the meeting, an enjoyable run round Thelwall and Grappenall Hall took place, the return journey being accomplished at half-past nine. Bradley and Jackson made the pace, and Vernon acted as , whip. SANKEY HARRIERS V. WARRINGTON WHEELERS. The above match was run off over a course ex- tending from the Coach and Horses, Sankey, to Bold Bridge and back, a distance of eight miles. The Harriers receiving twenty minutes start won by five minutes, Eastwood for the Harriers completing the distance in the fine time of fifty-one minutes, Barlow coming in second aminute later,Berry being third, Clark fourth, Williamson fifth, and James sixth. Wilkes finished first for the Wheelers, J. Forster being a good second, Mayall third, Dobson fourth, and Helsby fifth. The Harriers won by 15 points. WESLEYAN CHAPEL STOCKTON HEATH. The first public meeting in connection with the newly formed Band of Hope was held in the above chapel, on Thursday night. There was a good audience and an. excellent programme was pre- pared. Mr. Naylor occupied the chair and was supported by Mr. S. B. Stringer whogave an address. The following took part in the programme :—Thos. 13rereton, Beatrice Griffiths, Kate Guest, Charles Spencley; Venda Beswick, Lizzie Beswick, J. H. French, Ada Knight, Annie Brereton, Polly Guest, Mr. Whitfield, and Miss Annie Hooley. Mr. J. W. Spencley presided at the harmonium.

GUY FAWKES Dior. The evening of the memorable fifth of November was a most propitious one for the yougsters of Warrington, and the neighbourhood. The re- flection from large bonfires could be seen on every hand, while at intervals the sky was illuminated by the explosion of rockets and other pyrotechnical displays. Until far on into the night the deafening report of cannons was heard, while near at hand could be heard the hiss of squibs, and other like explosives which delight the hearts of the juveniles. In the cricket field there was a large bonfire, and a grand firework display. So far we have not heard of any accident resulting.
